EGG AND POULTRY PRODUCTION. That the- United Kingdom is capable of pro- ducing all the eggs and poultry required is recognised. In this connection will be remem- bered figures published three or four years ago in the Journal of the National Poultry Organisation Society, showing the capacity of each county in Great Britain, from which it was evident that upon the basis of three fowls per • acre of cultivated land production •would not only be equal, to present consumption, but provide fpr a very large increase. The diffi- culty is to bring these facts home to farmers aml others who have so great an opportunity if „they but took advantage of it. With a view of accomplishing what is so necessary, several of*our provincial contemporaries have -pub- lished --figures,,. relating to their respective counties, some of which are verr striking. For example, taking Sussex, in which production is probably greate'r than in any , other. English county, it is shown that the present number maintained is 547,353, whereas on the three fowls per acre basis there would be 2,243,130, or an increase of 1,695,777. Expressed in money values, the advance in annual returns would be £474,644 per annum.—Expert, in "Farm and Home."

div.head: PROFITABLE EGG PRODUCTION.
div.p: PROFITABLE EGG PRODUCTION.

Experiments have been recently conducted, under the direction of the North of Scotland College of Agriculture, on the small holding of Mr. Donald ,Gordon, Greenloanachs, Culbokie, in the Black Isle district of Boss-shire, with thirty White Leghorns and Leghorn crosses. In winter and spring the daily feed for the thirty fowls was as follows :-4113 bran, lb. thirds,' ilb. fish meal, mixed with well-boiled turnips and potatoes, sufficient to make the food into a soft crumbly condition. This mixture was fed hot in the morning. In the afternoon 41b. oats were given. In very cold weather, half the grain was boiled and given hot about noon. Vegetable food was always provided in the shape of kale, cabbage, and sliced raw turnips. Epsom salts were Also given once a week, as a corrective, three teaspoonfuls dissolved in the morning meal being sufficient. In summer the fish meal wasteduced to 2oz. per day instead of Boz. in winter, and the green food discontinued. The following is a summary of the results obtained:—

div.head: EGGS FOR WOUNDED SOLDIERS.
div.p: EGGS FOR WOUNDED SOLDIERS.
GARTER
FOR YOUR

Over half a million eggs for our wounded soldiers and sailors in the base hospitals in France and at home have been given to the War Office by the National Egg Collection, 154, Fleet-street, London, E.C., which is at the pre- sent moment contributing over 100,000 eggs weekly for the same purpose. To satisfy all the needs of our wounded, another 100,000 eggs per week are absolutely necessary, and any gifts of eggs, however small in number, will be welcome, and should, be sent to the society's central depot—Trevor-Square, London, S.W. _

_ Dear Sir,—We beg to inform you that in con- nection with the National Egg Collection, we are making a s'pecial Easter egg appeal during Holy Week on behalf of our "wounded soldiers and sailors, with the object of reaching, if pos- sible, the total figure desired of 200,000 eggs weekly. We are now in the position of supplying 130,000 eggs per week for this splendid cause, and the War Office, as a result of our work, is able to meet the needs of all the British wounded in ,every base hospital in France, in all the hospitals in London, and in a large number of provincial military hospitals. Very little additional effort is now needed to achieve the total desired, and we are making an earnest' appeal to every poultry-keeper in the country to send us during Easter week as ma. 47 eggs as can possibly be obtained. We are willing to supply (free of charge) boxes 'for the transit of the eggs, and they should be sent carriage forward under official labels obtainable from this office-154, Fleet- street, London, E.C. We should be grateful to every member of the clergy who will announce this appeal from the pulpit next Sunday, and. if possible, institute for this cause a special Easter Egg Sunday, when eggs could be brought to each house of worship. Concerning Neckwear. This is to be'a seagoti of accessories, and neck- wear will occupy a prominent position 4n the scheme of dress. Feather ruffles are well to the fore, and were never more charming. They are long and short, round and fiat, and When not more than a yard in length are finished with long and handsome Silk tassels or smart ribbon bows. There are raitivy most pleasing combinations of ostrich and marabout, especially in white and mole. Marabout is particularly soft ankbecoming, •and keeps in better condition than ostrich. The, flat short neckwear formed of alternate strands of these two, is very dainty, when finished With a :handsome choux Of wide, soft satin ibbon. Collars and fronts in tartans and military stripes are a new' feature this spring, and these as well as .turnciver collars are made in ribbed silk, satin and taffetas, also in organdie, and embroidered mnslins and voiles. Cravats, bows and knots are further adorned with paste buckles and slides.
About Footwear.

The wide skirt draws attention to the feet, and many women are having ankles and in- steps massaged with a view to making them more shapely,. The cut and fit of boots and shoes are more important than their design, hether for indoors or out. Pale coloured tops to , boots are fashionable, hut by no means economical. Black cloth is neater and more becoming, as if worn with black stockings it reduces the apparent size of the feet. Boots are worn just now, but shoes will come back with the warmer weather. Military designs charac- terise the newest boots, and one model is finished with a silk tassel; but it is not likely to be gener- ally worn. Some of the latest types lace at the side. Shoes for summer wear will have handsome buckles, similar to those worn in the seven- teenth century. Hosiery for day wear will be ornamented with clocks, but not extravagently embroidered -or patterned. Brocaded shoes are almost universally worn for evening, pithough an attempt is being made to bring back the Victorian satin sandalled type.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information in Popular Language.

Why We Work. One of the most essential things for appetite, for good digestion—for every vital function in the body, •in fact—is muscular work. The muscles are the furnace' of the body. If one does not use them, he is not consuming his food properly. His food is not burned as com- pletely as it ought to be, or as it would be if his muscles were used. The exercise which one gives ,his muscles increases the flow of blood through them, and thud increases the con- sumption of material which involves a change of material in the body. And it is this change that keeps us alive. Old age begins when the change of matter in the body becomes slow; and when this bodily change of tissues ceases, death comes.
Above All, Do Not Over-eat.

The appetite, if left to itself, is the best guide. Two meals a day is the preferable plan —a breakfast, say, at mine o'clock, and dinner at four or five. For,mest people the da.y's' work is so arranged that three meals are more practicable. In this case the evening meal should be light, consisting of a dish of cereals, and a serving or two of fruit, either fresh or stewed, or both, and bread and butter, with a cup of cereal coffee if desired. Especially should one avoid fried foods of all kinds, and dishes that are highly seasoned, pepper, horse- radish, hot sauces of all kinds, alcoholic liquors, tea, coffee and tobkcco.—Dr. Kellogg.

div.head: Toothache.
div.p: Toothache.

If there be a hole in an aching tooth, a little plug of cotton wool Stepped in glycerine or car- bolic acid is the magic cure; push it in with a bodkin. If there is not, a camel's hair brush steeped in tincture of iodine and pressed against • the gum will often similarly banish pain ,as by a fairy's wand. But in either ease see the dentist as soon as possible.

div.head: nraceful New Fashions.
div.p: nraceful New Fashions.

Fashions at the present moment are largely influenced by the styles prevalent during the First Empire, and the early part of Queen Victoria's reign. Designers ,seem unable to create new and original modes, and consequently have recourse to the past for inspiration. Much latitude is allowed, and there is a curious mingliing of styles. One dress may cleverly combine two or even three different periods in the general scheme, and its details, and strange to say there is nothing incongruous or ungraceful in the whole. The new fashions are exceptionally graceful, and retain the simplicity, but not the primness that charac- terised Early Victorian Modes. Straight lines, puffed sleeves and round decolletages are sure of a vogue, but whether the drastic changes that have been introduced will be generally adopted, is questionable. A welcome revival is the lace berthe, in which a full-blown 'rose is fastened. The' same flower is used to head the ilounces of white evening dresses,, just as it was at the time when the late Empress Frgderick of Germany was married.

div.head: HERE AND THERE.
div.p: HERE AND THERE.
The Gift of Life.

Livt your life while you have it. Life, is a splendid gift. There is nothing small in it: For the greatest things grow by God's law out of the !smallest. But to 'live your life you must discipline it. You must not fritter it away in "fair purpose, erring act, in constant but must ' make your thought, your words, your acts, all work to the same end, and that end not self but God. This is what we call Character.—Florence Nightingale.

Telling Him the Truth. Was it the sweet scent of the Mir in the conservatory, the beauty of the young girl's gilt hair, or the, excellent champagne he had taken with his supper—at any rate, after the two- step, as they Tested in the shadow beneath a palm, he proposed to the debutante in white. "It cannot be," she said. "I am unworthy of yon." "Oh, rubbish;" said he. • "It is true ; it is too true." And she sighed. "You are an angel," he said, ardently. "No, no; you are wrong," said the young girl. "I am vain, idle, Silly, utterly unfit to be yourhlPmate through life. He laughed slightly, saying in a soothing voice:
"Why, this is sheer; madness. What sort of a wife do you think I dught to have?" "A very wise, deliberate, practical woman," she replied; "one able to live on your small salary."

div.head: By MARJORIE.
div.p: By MARJORIE.

The Villa of the Duchess of Albany. The Villa Nevada at Cannes, whel'6 the Duke of Teck is recuperating from his recent illness, is the property of the Duchess of Albany, and came to her quite unexpectedly. It belonged for a number of years to Mr. Clifford Percival, and on his death passed to his sister, but before that it was lent to the late Duke of Albany, and there his Royal Highness died. )!Siss , Clifford, thinking that the Duchess,would like to possess the house, bequeathed it to her. It is one of the most delightful villas on the Riviera, beautifully situated on the shores of the Mediterranean, and has extensive gardens and grounds abounding in flowers and sub-tr9pical trees and plants.

Paris Returning to Normal Conditions. Despite the semi-obscurity of Park that once gay city, is gradually returning to normal con- ditions. French theatres and music halls are re-opening, whilst those of Berlin are closing. Parisians of all classes scan the lists of killed and wounded, and attend soldierS' funerals every "day, but after eight months of war, of sorrow, and of depression, there is naturally a reaction towards some recreation. Many Parisians who can afford the expense have gone to the South for the spring, but pedestrians increase.daily in numbers, awl the shops in the Rue de la Paix are opening gradually. The Parisian women, according to Dr. L. Garret Anderson, have not changed in spirit, in con- sequence of War conditions. They are as alert and ready as ever, and respond to new ideas with surprising alacrity.

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes and Useful Suggestions.

Why Cheese is Cheap. " Not one person in ten to-day uses cheese in cooking, yet cheese is _delicious when cooked, and makes nourishing and economical- dishes, admirable for family or individual use," writes Mr. Eustace / Miles in "How to Economise," a sixpenny book just published by, Messrs. Simpkin, Marshall and Co. "Scarcely anyone grates or, mills cheese. If cheese is finely grated or milled and then mixed with less concentrated foods it is generally easily digested by people who cannot eat it in solid chunks. Cheese has a genuine body-building value; and it must not be forgotten that three ounces of good cheese are to be bought for about half, the price that one would pay for four 'ounces of good meat."

High Cost of Food. On all sides we hear complaints of the con- stant increase in almost all varieties of food' and especially in, bread, which, is.'regarded by ,niany4-as the Oaf of llfe Althc,uh bread iti Engldild to-day is a great deal cheaper than it is in, the United States there the grain' is grown, still it is gradually getting dearer and the increased expense presses harshly upon the working classes: of society. Meat, too, is dearer, and so are eggs and milk and many other articles' of diet. But the fact remains that it is still possible to live well and main- tain found • health of body and brain on a smaller outlay of money than many might think possilile. There are tea, coffee and cocoa; for example; all of which are expensive luxuries and, in reality, with the possible ex- ception of cocoa, uselebss as well as harmful. Tea and coffee belong to the same category as alcohol, and are in truth drugs and in no sense foods. Men and women find a cup of telt refreshing just as they would find a glass of wine a pick-me-up. But the truth is that neither of these drinks actually add energy or

strength to the body. Hot water with a little milk added makes a perfectly wholesome and 'nourishing drink, and from the health standpoint is in every way superior to tea or coffee. Drinking tea is very largely a habit, and with a little self-denial and will power most people could substitute hot water and milk for tea with profit to both pocket and health.

div.head: WHAT LITTLE HANDS CAN DO.
div.p: WHAT LITTLE HANDS CAN DO.
Mr DEAR NIECES,-

What? Do I hear the boys asking, "What about us?' If so, .1 beg their pardon sincerely. By-and-by I shall pen them, too, a special letter; but this is for the girls. So I repeat, "My Dear Nieces." I 'don't know whether you ever read other parts of "The Examiner" besides our Corner, but if you do you would last week notice how a little Warrington girt had been rewarded for knitting a nice pair of soldier's mittens by re- ceiving a, splendid letter frodi a. "Tommy" in the trenches. And on another page of this number you will find how some more Warring- lon schoolgirls have been sending a number of scarves and mittens -which they have knitted right away to New Zealand for the soldiers there.
Now, these are grand examples, which I hope you will 'follow. Doubtless many of my nieces have already done so? If so, I shall be de- lighted to hear all about it.
Your loving UNCLE ,NEI).

div.head: CAMEL AND PIG: A FABLE
div.p: CAMEL AND PIG: A FABLE

4 camel said, " Nothing like being tall—look how tall I am !" • * A pig, who heard these words, said, Nothing 'like being short—look how short I am !" • The camel said, "Well, if I ail to ,prove the truth of what I said, I shall give up my hump.'' The pig said, " if I fail to prove the truth of
what I said, I shall give up my snout."

- "Agreed! said the climel; and they set out to journey together. They came to a garden enclosed by a low wall without any opening. The camel stood close up to the side of the wall /and reaching the plants within by means of his long neck, made a breakfast on them. Then he turned jeeringly to the. pig, who had been standing, at the bottom of the wall with- out even having a look at the good things in the garden, and said, "Now would you rather be tall or short?"

Next they came to a garden enclosed by a high wi.ll, with a wicket gate at, one end. The pig enteredllby the gate, and, after having eaten his fill of the vegetables within, came out, laughing at the voor camel, who had Icad to stay outside because he was too tall to enter the garden by the gate, and said, "Now would you be tall or short?"
Then they thought the matter over, and came Lo the canclusion that the camel should keep his hump and the pig his snout, observing: 'Pall is good where tall would do; Of short, the same is also true.

THE FISHING FROG.
This very curious fish frequents the southern coasts of England, and is sometimes 'seen in 'rather shallow water.

In appearance it is almost hideous. The. head is very large in, proportion to the rest 'of the body, and the Mouth is enormous. • On the upper'part of the head there are three long, slender feelers; two of these are placed near the muzzle, just over the eye, the third at the back of the head. They tan move in any direc- tion. One is longer than the others, and it has gt its end two flattened silvery tips. The pec- toral or fore fins are strong and broad,, and serve the purpose of what may be called hind feet.

The general colour of the upper surface of the body is brown, the under surface is white, the tail is nearly black. The fishing-frog has a voracious appetite. Being a slow swimmer, his, plan in taking his prey is to lie in ambush, selecting some favour- able lurking-place, under a rock, pefhaps. Re- posing on the sand or soft mud, and stirring up the mud with his fore fins, he forms around .hinvelf murky, indistinct cloud, above which

appears the..long feeler on the upper part of the head, already described, its silvery tip offering 4n attractive bait to other fish. In this manner 116 awaits his prey, as the shoals of the smaller kinds of fish pass'and re- pass, en the look-out for food. The glittering bait is soon seen, an unwary fish glides up to examine it; that moment its fate is sealed—the angler, aided by his feel-like pectoral fins, darts upward with his huge mouth open, and devours him in an instant.

His method of catching. food is so successful that fishermen often find in his stomach a great number of fish, alive, which he has just swair lowed! Sometimes he is seen floating on the surface of the water, ,no doubt on the look-out
, for prey of any kind that may come within his reach; but this plan is not FA.); common, and probably does iiot ansWer so well.

A SPRING SONG. (Br JESSIE Som.) 'Winter, forsaken, his leave now has taken; . The earth watch awaken e'er yet he is gone! The balm-breeze is blowing, the green grasses growing, The crazy cock crowing to herAld the dawn;

The bright buds up-springing, the soaring birds singing, The woodlands set ringing by children at play; • Old Solis clear Shining, benignant, unpining, Round each twig a-twining a sprightly spring - spray.
The faint flick'ring shadows merge o'er the still meadows, The heath-hag to bed goes—and dies, I pre- sume— •
No longer cloth wander, lohe, hither and yonder; Of Winter she's londer, the Spring is her tomb.
In trailings of glory the sum, golden-gory, Down sinks, and a• story of heroes is told . TO bairns beauteous bonny (Jim, Jennie and Johnnie) Bound bedward: anon in sweet sleep's fairy , fold.

`Neath sky soft and starry, with step light and airy, I walk with my Mary—my fairy, my Mary— I stroll with my Mary across the still moor; Till, weary worlds sleeping and dear dawn on- creeping, The stars we leave peeping,' pass homeward— and snore!

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.

Ctl-OPERATION IN AGRICULTURE. The Eastern Counties Farmers' Co-operative Association is held up as a practical example of the utility of co-operation as applied to farming enterprise. Its objects are to enablo the members to obtain the beat quality com- modities at prices which will compare favour- ably with those usually paid to merchants and middlemen; to open up, and render available for members, remunerative outlets for 'the dis- posal of farm produce and stock; to obtain in- formation and reliable expert advice for mem- bers on any subject connected with agriculture; and to promote the interests of the farmers generally.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

SOIL FOR POTATOES. Growers on a small scale can seldom choose the soil in which to plant potatoes, .but they may do much to enable such soil as they have to produce a satisfactory crop. Potatoes do best in moderately light soil with good. drain- age.. When heavy land must be used it should be thoroughly dug over during the autumn and winter, and should be prevented from becoming water-logged by being thrown up in ridges or narrow stretches if necessary. Twitch .(couch grass), docks, ,nettles, pr similaar perennial weeds should be forked out, and if there is any , reason to suspect that leather jackets (grubs of the daddy long-legs), wiieworms (grubs of the click beetles), or millepedes , (also known, as false wire Worms) are present in large .numbers, the land should be repeatedly turned over as far as, the 'weather permits. If the land is sandy or open in texture it may be improved by dding "humus" that is anything in the nature of dead leaves or decaying vegetable matter. Im- poverished.land should be enriched with -stable or farmyard manure, which may be dug in during autumn or winter, or before planting in spring. Lime should not be applied in large quantities to land on which potatoes are to be the next crop, as it may induce scab. Nevertheless, small quantites (say, ilb. per rod) are beneficial in rich -garden sOils and on heavy :"soils, or soils that have lain in grass for some years, 141 b. of lime per rod may. be applied. Lime corrects acidity and improves the texture of clay.

div.head: Time of Planting.
div.p: Time of Planting.

If the soil is in reasonably good condition, potatoes may be planted as soon • as mild weather , arrives in spring. If, however, wet weather has made the preparation of the soil difficult, planting should be deferred for. a time. It is better to plant at the end of April with the land in good condition than early in March with the land in bad order. In a very few districts potatoes may be planted in February, but March and April are the usual months, the former for the early varieties, the bitter for the main crop.

div.head: POTATOES FOR MILCH COWS.
div.p: POTATOES FOR MILCH COWS.

Potatoes are excellent food for Mulch cows, and, indeed, are far more suitable diet than turnips. In Lancashire the dairy farmers who supply the different towns with milk use potatoes for their cows very freely, ,and the milk is excellent. _ . _ _

An experiment was conducted by the Lyons Veterinary School some years ago, and the following results were noted: Dairy cows, when deprived of all other ndurishment than potatoes (which should be given raw and cut)„ will consume per day an average of seven per cent. of their live weight. Under the influence of this exclusive regimen there was an increase in the quality of milk, and a notable loss of live weight; this result was very decided and remarkable. The excreta, which were soft and whitish, contained some grains of undigested starch, and no sugar was found in the urine. Cooked potatoes were more readily taken.by the cattle; but when they were given alone and every other form of nourishment was excluded, rumination was affected or stopped, and diges- tion was hindered. The use of cooked potatoes could not, ! therefore, be persisted in. When they, are raw or, .cooked potatoes should be mixed with some other food to constitute a con- venient ration, both from the point of milk pro- duction and for fattening purposes. This mix- ture of rations is also favourable to the mechanical and chemical acts of digestion. ! From observations on a lot of dairy cows fed with a ration of which totatoes formed the half of the total dry matter, and on another lot of .which potatoes formed only 22 per cent., it was fully recognised that the first or larger quantity was clearly preferable to the secend or smaller. From other experiments it appeared that raw potatoes favoured the Production of milk, while an equal quantity which had been cooked fat- tened and increased the weights of the animals. Under the influence of a ration of which cooked potatoes formed the basis, the amount of sugar in the milk was found to rise, but the increase did not continue when the ration was changed. —"T.," in" Farm- and Home."

div.head: FARMYARD MANURE.
div.p: FARMYARD MANURE.

This manure is the most valuable at the dis- posal of the farmer, but at the same time it is one of the most variable in quality. When it is kept in an open dungstead and thereby ex- posed to rain, and especially when excessive water passes through the •dungstead from the roofs of surrounding buildings ff•r other sources, the „dung has its most valuable ingredients washed away. Rich. dung from ,highly-fed animals suffer); to the largest extent in this way. The urine of farm animals has a greater manurial value than their solid excrements, and this; 'therefore, should be fully utilised for watering the manure heap or in some other satisfactory manner. In a leaflet ,issued from the College, dealing with substitutes for im- ported potash, it is pointed out that the urine of farm animals contains from four to twelve times more potash than is contained in the dung, and therefore that the urine should be saved as far as ,possiblo by utilising all avail- able sources of litter, to absorb this, and by

It is also urged that thi,, winter's farmyard manure should be kept almost entirely for arable land, the need for farmyard Manure b43ing very small so far as pasture is concerned, and not much greater for land growing meadow hay. All potatoes and roots should receive, if at all possible, a dress- ing of 10 to 12 tons dung an acre for the coming season,

div.head: RAT EXTERMINATION.
div.p: RAT EXTERMINATION.

In. view of inquiries received as to method - of dealing with the depredations of rats on farm premises, the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries are re-issuing a. leaflet on the, subject contain- ing ,suggestions for concerted action for the ex- termination of these pests. Copies of the leaflet (No. 244, The Destruction of Rats) may be ob- tained free. on application to the Secretary 01 the Board,' 1. Whitehall Place, London, S.W.

div.head: IN THE GUDEN.
div.p: IN THE GUDEN.

THE GLADIOLI. Bulbs or iO-tris of these beautiful flowers may be planted Ir.im now onwards,,. but the sooner the' better. These look very charming with their tall, stately spikes of large flowers in the garden in autunin. The culture .very simple. Dig a hole about a foot deep and .add a layer of well-rotted manure about 6in. thick. Fill up with soil', to '3in. from stir- face. Then place a handful of sand under each corm :ind press corm into it. Fill-hole. Up_ with soil to g round level. They . look beautiful , planted in (-lumps of about six or eight trufh-• and are greatly admired,. , sortssvan bv had from tho local..seedMen 'Very cheap Lind--do very well, each bulb generally sending up two spikes.

The following are grand varieties and good growers. each giving large blossoms; Anierica lavender pink; Princeps, -crimson; Panama. rosy pink; Baron J. Hulot, dark blue: Hollandia, salmon and .yellow; Halley, pink of, white; Brepehleyensis, orange vermilion. Each of the above can be had. from the local seed men, and fine large corms can be had by order- ,. ing, early. •

SWEET PEAS AND THEIR CULTURE. Sweet peas are one of the most beautiful flowers. and their culture is very easy. They can be grown up walls on string netting or in . the garden on wire netting, 3in. .mesh pre- ferred, this being very cheap, or on sticks. Tip -- latter are very hard to obtain, Without of 'cOurse, resortinit to the nurserymen, who will supply these sticks or branches six to eight feet in height. at reasonable pfices. The culture fairly easy. Sweet peas don't like too much manure': in fact soil that has been well manured the previous season will answer ,verY well. Of eourse a little manure well rotted can be put under them about a spade blade deep or one spit deep. The rows should run front north to south if possible, and about 15 inche, . wide. The s4ds should be 'sown about two I inches deep in light or sandy soil, and about , one inch in heavy or clayey soil. They can be' sown in single or double or even three row--- according to requirements, but I like a good show and also good blooms, therefore I saw. three rows, each seed being four inches .awaY. •from , the other. Larger blooms can be obtained by planting two rows and the seeds six inches away from each other. I The seeds' of some varieties are generally chipped to ensure even germination, but if only for garden decoration they can be left untouched. When the seedlings -appear -put -black cotton over and around them, about two inches from the ground or the gardener's nuisance ,(the sparrow) will eat the lot. Seeds. can be sown in March or April, and your local seedsmen can supply 'yolt. with the finest -varieties in commerce without paying ''' fancy- prices elsewhere As the seed- lings grow insert thin twigs among them so that the feelers can get a grip of something to hold them up. As soon as they have nicely got attached to the twigs put your stakes up aria make them firm, so as .to withstand the fore.' of the wind later on. If you think they are not growing much, a slight "sprinkling of sulphate of ammonia, or nitrate of soda will be found beneficial washed in the ground. .Always soil your sweet peas up when they are a feW inches in height. Exhibitors pinch the tops off some varieties, but I want only to deal witb thoSe who are growing for decoration, so WY can be hit alone to grow at their own will. few varieties which I have found very satis- factery for bearing fours and being largo' blossoms and vigorous growers are:— . Maud Holmes,, crimson; Etta Dyke, white: Elfrida Pearson, pale pink; Mrs. \ltardcastle Sykes. blush; Barbara, salmon orange; Edith Tay-lor,, cerise; Hercules, rosy pink; Dobbies Cream, pale. primrose; King Manoel, deel/ maroon; B. F. Felton, lavender; Elsie Herbert, picotee; Evelyn Hemits. picotee; Nora trnwill• white; Bosabelle. carmine; and... Senator Spen- cer. chocolate flaked. There are plenty others. but the above Wll give 'every satisfaction and can bd obtained ax very low prices. When the flowers - are _showing, colour• weak liquid manure. can •be applie° (the colour of ~artie being like weak.- tea) to the ground Only. because it will kill the foliage,

div.head: DEMAND FOR TOTAL PROHIBITION.
div.p: DEMAND FOR TOTAL PROHIBITION.
We Are To Succeed.
The following letter from the King was issued from Downing-street on Wednes- day night:— • Buckingham Palace, March 30, 1915. Dear Chancellor of the Exchequer,—

The King thanks you for so promptly 'letting him have a full report of the pro- -eeedings at yestrxday's 'meeting of the .deputation of enoloyers. His Majesty has read it with interest, but also with the deepest concern. He feels that nothing but the most vigorous measures will successfully cope with the grave situation now existing in-our anna- nient factories. We have before us the statements, not merely of the employers, but of the Admiralty and War Office officials respontible for the supply of munitions of war, for the transport of • troops their food and ammunition. From. this evidence it is without doubt largely due to drink that we are unable to secure the output of war material indispensable to meet the requirements of our Army in the field, and that there has been such serious delay in the conveyance of the necessary reinforcements and supplies to aid our gallant troops at the front.

The continuance of such a state of things must inevitably result in the pro- longation of the horrors and burdens of this terrible war. am to add that if it be deemed advis- able the King will be prepared to set the .example by giving up all alcoholic liquor mMself and issuing orders against its con- sumption in the Royal Household, so that no difference shall be made so far as his Majesty is concerned between the treat- ment of rich and poor in this question.— Yours very truly,
_ Stamfordhatn. The Right Hon. D. Lloyd George, M.P.,
Chancellor of the Exchequer.
A REMARKABLE DEN TATION.

div.head: MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S REPLY.
div.p: MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S REPLY.
Greatest Of Our Deadly Foes Is Drink.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer, in reply, said--

You certainly need not offer any apology to any of us for the time which you have_occupied, because the statements which you have made are of the gravest possible character in the national interests.. .But although your state- ments are very startling, you have been able to support them, I am almost sorry to say, with evidence which ,appears to me to be quite irrefutable. I almost wish it were possible even to cast doubt 'upon statements which are so alarming. But not merely what you have told me to-day, but facts which have come to my knowledge, more especially since I have in- terested myself in the labour difficulties, have convinced nu' that what you have told us here to-day simply represents the truth. I note a certain amount of impatience—and I do mir regret it—at the faet that the Govern- ment have not up to the present taken even more drastic action than that which they have taken. But that is due to one or two causes. The first, and perha.pi the most important, is that before you take steps of this kind you must feel confident that yciu are not going in advance of the general sentiment, otherwise more harm will be done than good. You must feel that you hay every class in the community behind you when you are taking action which interferes, and must interfere very severely, with the individual liberties of men of all sections. But. lam sure that the country is beginning to realise the gravity of the position. (Hear, hear.) It is very difficult for Ministers to tell the country how serious it is. You who are employed in the yards connected with the output of war material- can draw a very fair inference as to the gravity of the position; and I am glad that the workmen thetnselves are beginning to be impressed with it, and that they are getting more and more prepared to accept very drastic action in reference to the question of drink.

div.head: DRINK AND MUNITIONS OF WAR.
div.p: DRINK AND MUNITIONS OF WAR.

Ytni have come the conclusion that the mere Curtailment of the hours of drinking would be an inadequate step. Some of you think it would hardly have an appreciable influence upon the evil. Others think that perhaps it might be of some use; but you are all agreed that it would be insufficient—(hear, hear)—to cope with the great injury Ntillich is being in- flicted upon the country in consequence of the excessive (kinking that takes place among a section, maybe a small section, but a very im- Tortant section, of workmen who are engaged in the production of munitions of war and the equipments for war in this country. I was glad from that point of view, tut only from that point of view, that Mr. llenderson stated quite clearly at the start that there were no teetotalers among. you. Mr. Carter: We could have brought some. _ _

The Chancellor of the Eichequer; Your appeal and the decision you have come to will carry all the greater weight for that reason; that you have not approached it from the point of view of men who have a Particular theory to promote. You have approached it from a point of view of men who have just got one end and aim in view, that is, -to help the country at the present 'moment successfully through its troubles. (Hear, -hear.) That is what will appeal to the country.

div.head: ROOT-AND-BRANCH METHODS.
div.p: ROOT-AND-BRANCH METHODS.

Having gone into this matter a great deal more closely during the last few weeks, I must say that I have a growing conviction, based on accumulating evidence, that nothing but root- and-oranch methods will be of the slightest avail in dealing with this evil. (Rear, hear.) I believe that to be the general feeling. The feeling is that if we are to settle German mili- tarism we must first of all settle with the drink. (Rear, hear.) We are fighting Germany, Austria and Drink; and, as far as I can see, the greatest of these three deadly foes is Drink. (Rear, hear.)

• Success in the war is, now purely a question of munitions. I say that, not only on my own authority, but on the authority of our great General, Sir John French. Ile has made it quite clear what his conviction is on the sub- ject. I think I can venture to say that that is also the conviction of the Secretary of State for War, and it is also the conviction of all those who know anything about the military problem—that in order to enable us to win, all we require is an increase, and an enormous in- crease, in the shells, rifles, and all the other munitions and equipment which are necessary to carry through a great war. You have proved to us to-day quite clearly that the excessive drinkifig in the works connected with these operations is interfering seriously with that output. (Hear, hear.) I can only promise you this at the present moment, that the words which you have addressed to. my colleague, and myself will be taken into the most careful consideration by my colleagues when we come -to our final decision on this -question. Coming as ney •do from those who know what the facts are, and have spoken with a due sense of their responsibility, they will, I am certain, carry very great weight in these quarters.

THE KING VERY DEEPLY CONCERNED. I had the privilege of an audience with his Majesty this morning, and that Lis the reason why I could not adhere to the original hour which was fixed for the deputation. I am per- mitted to say by him that he is very deeply concerned on this very question—very deeply concerned—and the concern which is felt by him is, I am certain, shared by all his subjects in this country. I am exceedingly obliged to you for the facts which. you. have put before me, and for the brave suggestions which you have also urged. If you have any further figures or facts beyond those which you have submitted to me now, I shall be very glad if you will let me have them; 'because I should like to summarise them and submit them to my colleagues with a view- to their 'considering the important sug- gestions which you have made.

div.head: RUSSIA DRINK-FREE. Activity and Efficiency Unimpaired By the War. "The Times" says:— •
div.p: RUSSIA DRINK-FREE. Activity and Efficiency Unimpaired By the War. "The Times" says:— •

The social and economic effects of „the temper- ance Policy enforced by the Russian Govern- ment at the outbreak of the war have been patent. Not only has the army taken, and kept. the field sober, but those who have remained behind have grown daily more efficient. Rus- sian workmen now work their six days a week, instead of only five or even four, and turn out better work. Pauperism and crime have every- where decreased and admissions to public hos- pitals continue to dwindle in number.

- The most striking feature Qf the *whole tem- perance movement has been the voluntary co- operation of the Russian people in promoting its success. They have shown themselves capable of a sustained moral effort and have nobly risen to a great occasion. The price and reward of this State policy of temperance can now ,be expressed in figUres. An authoritative estimate is furnished by AL Arthur Rafialovich, Commercial Attache to the Russian Embassy in Paris, who for nearly a quarter of a century has issued :that valuable publication "L'Annee -Econemique et •Pinan- ciere"

In a pamphlet whicl; he has just published in France, entitled "La Russie et la Guerre," he states that the Russian' Government, by re- nouncing its share in the profits from the sa,le'of spirits,. sacrificed a revenue of .266,000,000. There could he no doubt :that this deficiency would immediately be compensated. Fresh revenue, to-the amount of g 30,000,000, from sur- charges and new. taxes is alreAdy assured.
The remarkable thirg, hoive;er. is the in-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 3, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 3, 1915.

creaFe in national wealth, not only morally and in the abstract, but in actual money. During the six weeks from December Is, 1914, to Janu- ary, 15, 1915, the savings banks returns exceeded by no less than £4,500,000 the figures for the corresponding period of 1913-14. The lasting impression of this great war will be not so much the mobilisation by Russia of her vast resources as the spectacle of her people achieving freedom through 'service. Under the discipline of temperance the economic efficiency of the Russian working classes has increased by between 30 and 50 per cent. So great are Russia's reserves of men that, excepting the .area occupied by the. enemy in Pela,nd, the deficiency of skilled labour amount to little more than 'lO per cent. Women every- where have stepped into the breach, and have solved automatically a problem which has been responsible for so many heartburnings in Eng- land.
The manufacturing activity of Russia re-
mains unimpaired by the war. Indeed, never before has Russian industry been so efficient.

div.head: NEW ORDER.
div.p: THE NEW ORDER.
Late Opening and Early Closing
CLUBS AS PUBLIC-HOUSES.

The new Order curtailing the hours, of open- ing of the licensed houses in Warrington came into operation on Monday, notice to that effect having been given to the licensees on -Saturday evening, after the local licensing juftices had met earlier in the day, primarily, to consider whether the terms ,embodied in the military order issued by General Mackinnon. should also be made applicable to the local clubs, the matter of the later opening and earlier closing of the public-houses being one in which they had little option in view of the General's request. The meeting was presided over by the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), and thereat the Chief Constable (Mr. Martin. Nicholls), recom- mended the assembled justices to make the Order called for by the military authorities of the Western ,Command, under the provisions, of the Intoxicating Liquor (Temporary Restric- tion) Act, and to aPply the same restrictions as were laid down in the military order to club bars, as well as to other licensed premises. . The miltary order called for the closing of the public-houses at 10 o'clock at night, but the _ .

cominittee coneidered as to whether It Would not be advisable to go one better and to .fix the closing hour at nine o'clock, but the Magis- trates' Clerk ruled that their Worships had no power to vary the conditions submitted by the Chief Constable, and accordingly decided on 10 o'clock closing. As soon as practicable after the meeting all the licensees within the borough were served with a printed notice directing that the sale of intoxicating liquors in public-houses, club bars and the like must be suspended, "except be- tween the following hours " : Week-days : 10.30 am. to 10 p.m. Sundays: 12.30 p.m. to 2.30 p.m., and 6.30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
It was made clear in the Order that it does not apply to bona-fide travellers, or residents in hotels and 'clubs.

div.head: IN THE COUNTY.
div.p: IN THE COUNTY.
Warrington Petty Sessional Division.

At a meeting of the licensing justices of the Warrington, Petty Sessional Division of Lanca- shire, held at the office of Mr. Henry Greenall on Tuesday, it was decided to carry out. the Chief Constable's proposals, whioh embodied the military proposals, so that the hours for the sale of intoxicating liquors in the division will be r--
Week-days: 10.30 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sundays: 12.30 p.m. to 2.30 p.m., and • 6.30 p.m. to 9 p.m. These times .wero made to apply to clubs.

div.head: DARESBURY DIVISION.
div.p: DARESBURY DIVISION.

At a meeting of the licensing justices of the Daresbury Division of Cheshire, held at Mr. Hy. Greenall's office on Tuesday, the Order made a few weeks, ago was revoked and a new Order made in accordance with the recommendation of the military authorities. The closing hour of 9 p.m., as in the original Order was retained, so that the hours of opening in this division will be:—
Week-days: 10.30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sundays: 12.30 p.m. to 2.30 p.m., and
• 6.30 p.m. to 9 p.m. • These hours were made to apply to clubs, but there is only one club in the division, the Golf Club at Appleton.

div.head: TO CLOSE AT TEN.
div.p: TO CLOSE AT TEN.
Only Off-Licence Premises May Remain Open Later.

It having been argued that public-houses could remain open after the stipulated time if they did not sell drink, the Western Command at Chester issued a circular on the point, in which, it was made clear that
All public-houses must close entirely at 10 p.m., but in the case of off-licences the premises may remain open until 11 o'clock for the transaction of business other than the sale of drink.
This applies to the whole of the area affected by the order whiek came inta. force on Monday.

div.head: Weather.
div.p: The Weather.

The metereological returns for last week show that the 24th ult. was the warmest day we have experienced recently, 59 degrees of heat being. recorded. The mean temperature last week was 41 degrees, or two degrees higher than in the preceding week. The coldest day recently was Saturday last, when the glass droked to 25 degrees.

div.head: EARLY CLOSING OF PUBLIC-HOUSES.
div.p: EARLY CLOSING OF PUBLIC-HOUSES.
First-Day Warrington Experiences of Our Great Social

div.head: Reform.
div.p: Reform.
FROM ALL POINTS OF VIEW.
SPECIAL BY "THE

For some time now Warrington beer drinkers & in common with the rest of their kind throughout the isles, have had to pay extra for their favourite beverage, owing to the war tax unposed -upon it. According to tho brew they favour .they have been paying from a 'halfpenny on the most half-pint of what, in London, is known as "the bright- est "—but in Lancashire has for years been dubbed ." sixp'ny "—to twopewe on a pint of the more " headY " and darklyLhued concoction. And now, 'not only rust they pay.more for their "tipple," but they fire not allowed to, drink it—at any rate in their favourite haunts—from early morn to late o' niurky night, for on Monday came into force regulations made' under 'the powers of the In- toxicating Liquor Temporary Restriction Act, which forbid the opening of the public-house l! doors—save for the benefit of bona-fide travel- lers—before 10.30 in the morning, and en- joins their being closed at 10 o'clock at night. Thus'are five and a half hours knocked off the period during which; one short week ago, it wasjoossible for the workman to befuddle him- self in frowsy bar and beer-" scented " tap- room. On Sundays, too, the drinking hours will be curtailed, one hour being knocked off the period during which it is permissible to open for the sale of intoxicants in the even- ing.

div.head: CLUBS AND " PUBS " ON THE SAME FOOTING.
div.p: CLUBS AND " PUBS " ON THE SAME FOOTING.

When it. became known that there was to be some reduction in the hours of opening of licensed premises, clubmen looked up their membership tickets just to make sure that they had paid up their subscriptions all right, for, thought they, "when those other poor wretches are being unsympathetically turned out into the streets at the early call of 'Time, gentlemen, please!' we shall be able in com- foit to discuss our final liquid ' night-cap 1' " But they were doomed to sad disillusionment, for, 101 the Order applies to the clubs as much as to he "pubs." And so, not, Warring- ton nightly becomes what our friends, the Yankees; 'call a " dry " town from 10 o'clock each week-day mitil the sun is high up in the heavens the following morning.

In the matter of ordgring the earlier clos- ing and later opening qf tWpOlic-hoilses the local licensing justices' had no Option. The military authorities—who. have plenary power in the matter—commanded it, and and theirs was but to oheY, Atud they did so cheerfully, realising the object .behind the Order and its great importance in days such as these, when it is so essential that the worker shall come to his work fit and with a clear head, and when it is so necessary that he should conserve his material resources. But the justices went One better in including the clubs within the scope of the Order. Here was a matter in which the prerogative was theirs and theirs alone, and they decided to exercise it wisely, and to put club and "pub" on the same footing, realising' that otherwise there was some danger that the good results accruing from the earlier closing of the licensed houses might be, in some measure, annulled if it still remained possible for work- men to " wet their whistle" elsewhere.
Hence, clubs and " pubs " alike are now only open for the sale of intoxicants between the hours of 10:30 in the morning and 10 at night on week-days, and 12.30 and 2.30, and 6 and 9 on Sundays.

THE .ADAPTABLE WORKING MAN. An " Examiner " represeptative made in- quiries on Monday as to the effect of the later hour of opening, and found that on the whole it .was viewed with no groat disfavour by the better-class landlords, whilst needless to say it made no sort of difference to the great majority of the decent working men. There was no crowding round-the closed doors of thirsty beings, waiting for the, to them, welcome sound of the drawing of bolts; indeed, it appears to have been the experi- enCe of most landlords that trade between 10.30 and the dinner hour merely followed the normal conrse for such hours—an occa- sional caller of the female persuasion, with her jug under her apron, a chance dropper-in or two for his matutinal bitter, or a call from .a working man fresh frow his bed after sleep- ing off the fatigue of a night shift"!
The dinner hour trade was little greater than usual; in fact, one got the impression that the worker whose taste in beverages runs to the alcoholic. had already adapted himself
to the altered circumstances, and certainly was none the worse for them.
THE LICENSEE'S VIEW POINT.

" There's only one thing about it that strikes, me as being :a bit hard on us," said the landlord of a hostelry much frequented by men of the working class to our represen- tative, " and that is that if they curtail our sales they should also knock a bit off our licence dues, for of late years those dues have become so great that in many instances men who have scraped' all their lives to save a bit and have then invested it in an appar- ently well-doirrg ' house (the phrase is his) are called upon .to contribute such a dispro- portionate ' amount .of their income to the King's taxes, that they would be only too glad to sell out for what they gave to come in,' and to go back to work again. If our sell- ing hours are to be restricted, something ought to be knocked off' what we have to pay for the privilege sof carrying on our trade."

"In my view," continued the loquacious mine host, "this regulation is both a. reflec- tion on tile 'Trade' and on the working man, and it is ;nother instance in which the man who merely has his legitimate one drink, because he feels he needs it. is being made to sillier for the man who habitually 'makes a beast of himself.' However, I suppose it can't be helped, and if it's for the good of the country I don't tliiink you'll find many publicans seriously growling. If the authori- ties that be think that we like to see a man hanging about our bars all day, instead of attending to his Work—as we have to attend to ours—they make a huge mistake, for,--to put it on the lowest ground, we know very well that the working chap who is spending his 'bobs' with us is sconcing ' time and even if he does spend a shilling or two to-day will have nothing :at all—or, very little—to spend next week, and that, pretty inevitably, he will be coming round asking for tick.' We prefer the 'chap who works regular, and comes in for his pint regular, drinks it up, and goes off civil. I know there are lots of people who regard the public-houses as re- sorts of iniquity, but I think those people would have a pleasant surprise if, instead of surmising, they dropped in now and then and safr for themselves how we.try to run our -businesses clean and straight, and to per-. 'made stupid fellows not to make themselves more stupid than nature has already made them." ,

div.head: WILL PREVENT "BROKEN TIME."
div.p: WILL PREVENT "BROKEN TIME."
So much for the publican's point of view, and now a word as to the other side of the

div.head: EXAMINER" MAPh
div.p: EXAMINER" MAPh

picture. A foreman in a large works, where men only are employed, and which is .situate not a hundred miles from Bank Quay, wel= conied the regulation, though • himself not a teetotaler, and, as he himself expressed it, 4`..by no means 'faddy about teniperance.", "The new rule's a good One," he added, "especially in in so far as it applies to Mon- days and Tuesdays. Those are the only days when the chaps are inclined tb go 'on the booze,' speaking generally, the reason, of eirarse; being that ' they have the residue. of their wages in their pockets then and the cash would burn holes in their pockets unless they spent it. After Tuesday most of them are spent up, and they don't lose a single minute, if they can help it then—on to the end of the week. But? after all, the number of week-end fools' is very small. I remem- ber the time when if you got half your men in on Monday mornings you .thought yourself lucky, but now there's rarely more than a couple or so missing. Still, the new rule, if it does no good, will at any rate' do no harm,, and there's .not a decent working fellow that will seribusly grumble about it, once he gets used to it. And he's got to get used to it!" There is the non-teetotal working man's point of view, and it varies from the " In- fernal nuisance " (that's , putting it mildly) of the man who's "never happy unless he can get it "—and guzzle it—to the compla- cent " Well, I can do with it, ,or I can do without it!" of the decent pint-or-so-a-day man, who represents •the great majority of the frequenters. of public-houses.

div.head: BOTTLES AT HOME-INSTEAD OF GLASS
div.p: BOTTLES AT HOME-INSTEAD OF GLASS
out?

A third point of view is that of the off- licence holder, whose main trade is done in bottled beer, and he is rubbing his hands in something like glee at the new regulation, for, as he says, "If a man cannot drink his beer inn ' pub,' he can drink it at home, and it will come cheaper to him that way, be- sides which there is not the likelihood of his getting too much—the missus ' will see to that!" That there is something in his point of ,view is borne out by The manager of one of the biggest bars in the town, who said that last week-end he had done a bigger trade in bottled stuff than he ever remembered doing before. "There are some men," he added, significantly, "who don't mean to start work without their corpse reviver.' " Where the new regulation is likely to be most beneficial in ,effect is in the case of the man who too often has set out in the early hours of the morning to go to his work and ' has called in at a public-house just for a " tot." That " tot" has too often led to 'another and 'often to a third, a fourth follow- jug—and after that—well, theie would 'be at least one check that was not handed in that morning. The regulation will also serve a good purpose in that it is likely to ensure a fuller night's rest for many a working man, who hitherto has not sought to woo Morpheus until close on midnight.

div.head: NO THIRSTY THRONG.
div.p: NO THIRSTY THRONG.

An " Examiner " man beleaguered the pubs" in a certahi thoiloughfare 'which is mentioned with painful frequency in the Police Court, at opening time on Monday. Four or five houses clustered closely together, and 101 when the clock struck the magic hour and the portals of the hostelries were flung wide not a solitary customer darted in. In fact, some minutes elapsed before a devotee of Bacchus came along, ani then .the disciple wore petticoats, and was obviously, from her up-rolled sleeves and freshly-pink arms, but newly come from the family washtub. Jug in hand, she made her way into the inviting "Bottles and Jugs Only" entrance, and after due lapse out she came—with half a pint. "The first half-pint of war beer!" she exclaimed, to a crony, "and do you know I feel like taking the top off it now I" She didn't. The rush of workmen—whom it has been de- clared by the arch-al)ologists for drink • would not, or could not, go to work without their ." regular "--,was entirely conspicuous by its absence, and the wheels of the machines in the workshops whirred round as busily as usual—and, in short, "which marvelled many, none were a bit the worse," whilst several were doubtless much the better. And so—well, one wonders whether it will ever again be necessary to open the ", pubs " in Wprrington before 10.30 in the morning, or to keep them open after 10 at night. Perhaps, even who can tell?

div.head: BONA-FIDE TRAVELLERS SAFEGUARDED.
div.p: BONA-FIDE TRAVELLERS SAFE- GUARDED.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
WANTED TO ENLIST.
Thiers Explanation When Selling Stolen Cycles.

At the Borough Police Court on Thursday, a youth, of no settled abode, named William Patrick Moscroft, was sent to gaol for three months on charges of stealing four bicycles, of the total value of £ll 10.5., and a watch, during August and September last, when, said the Chief Constable, several local riders mys- teriously lost their machines. The prisoner took the cycles from outside different premises .in the town and disposed of them, telling some of the buyers that he was selling "his" machine because he wanted to enlist.

div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT..
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT..
SAW R DAY.
Before Alderman Tinnion (in the chair), Messrs. A. J. Jolley, J. Upson and T. Pem-
bertan.

Wrongfully Wearing Naval Uniform.—George Neild was charged on remand with having been drunk in Winwick-street on March 3rd.—When before the Court earlier in the week it was stated that he was supposed to be improperly wearing Naval uniform. It was now stated that it had been ascertained that prisoner was discharged from the 'Navy so long ago as last October.—On promising the Bench that he would cease wearing the uniform he was dis- charged. • Gave Herself Up.—Catherine Marshall. no fixed abode, was placed in the dock on rernan:l from Thursday, charged with having stolen on March Ist, five bed sheets, a snawl and a shirt, the property of Michael Hennessey, of Ship- yard. The value of the stolen property was 18s 6d.—Superintendent Williamson said the complainant kept several lodging houses in Ship-yard. The articles In question were missed from one of them on the 13th instant. On the Sunday morning prisoner absconded, and the matter was reported to the police. The whole of the missing articles had been pawned. Prisoner surrendered herself to the Manchester police the previous Weinasday. There was another allegation against her of stealing a lot of things two years ago, but the complainants concerned in the matter were not disposed to prosecute. Prisoner had been in Warrington about two years, but most of her life had been spent in Manchester.—Prist-ner pleaded guilty and had nothing to say.—She was committed to prison for a month.

Had Nothing to Say.—Mary 'Bridge, of no settled abode, was charged wtth having been drunk in Buttermarket-street on PridaY.—lt was stated that she tried to get into the Cross Keys public-house. A constable advised her to go home and she began to use very bad language and was taken into custody.—She had nothing to say in answer to the charge, and was fined Bs. 6d., including costs, the alternative being seven days' hard labour. Her 95th Appearance.—Margaret McClaughan, an old woman, of no settled abode, was in the dock for the ninety-fifth time on a charge of wandering abroad without. visible means of support.—A ccrnstable stated that he found her in Orford-road at midnight. He asked her where she was going and prisoner told him to go to —. Ile took her into custody.— Superintendent Williamson said that as far .as they knew prisoner had been up ninety-five times for various offences. It would be in her interests to send her to prison for as long a term as possible.—She was committed to gaol for a month.

Alleged Theft of Metal—John Grounds, .ta labcurer, of 204, Winwick-road, was brought up on suspicion of having stolen a quantity of scrap brass, &c.—Superintendent Williamson t aid it would 1e necessary to ask for a remand for 'a week. Prisoner was seen by a eon•lmble, tarrying a box which was subsequently found to contain metal, rubber and leather. Know- ing the prisoner very -well, the constable wtnt up to him and was in the act of examining the box when prisoner suddenly deah him a violent blow in the face and then belted. Prisoner was found in the early bouts of the m3rning.—There was a second cha-ge agaimt him of assaulting P.C. Clarke.—tie was remanded, in custody, for F evm days.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.
Before Mr. S. Wright (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, James Evans and Smethurst; Messrs. W. Furness; T. Locker, -G. Filling and W.
Roberts.

The Motor Missed.—John Mullins, labourer, of no settled abode, pleaded guilty to having been dnink in Bridge-street on Saturday.—A constable said he was staingering about, and almost 'got knocked down by a motor car.— The Chief Constable, having said the man was a stranger to the pblice, read an extract from the previous day's issue of a police journal, which criticised those who in these times of national strain; spent hours propping up bars and drinking. . The man, he continued, had not been in the town twenty minutes. He earned a good wage and had plenty of money in his possessiori.—A fine of ss. and 4s. 6d. costs was imposekl.
Heard Her Son Was Killed.—Mary Broderick, ma rried woman, of 32, Philip-street, appeared

for having • been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street at nine o'clock on Saturday night.—lt was stated that she was very drunk, and was making use of the most filthy language when arrested. All the way to the Police Station her conduct was disgraceful, and a " tremendous " crowd followed her.—Broderick said she had heard that her son had-been killed, and took the drink "to take it off her mind."— The Chief 'Constable said this was the woman's 87th appearance. She had been given a month for a similar offence.—The Woman: My Son was killed.—The Chief Constable: That should have kept you from the drink.—A fine of 10s. and 4s. 6d. costs was imposed, or 14 days! imprison- ment,

New Sort of " Tr i p per."—Thomas Cummins, labourer, of 12, Gandy-street, was charged „with having been drunk and ItisorderlY on Pig-hill on Saturday.—A constable told how Cummins was shouting absolutely filthy language, which he continued to use all the way to the Police Station, also trying to trip the two constables who had him in custody.—lt was his 35th appearance, and he was given a month's hard labour.

Wanted to See the Pictures.—Eliza Dagna.ll, married woman, of 72, Kerfoot-street, was charged with having been drunk and. disorderly in Church-street shortly after 10 o'clock on Saturday night. —A constable described how, very drunk, she went into the Star Kinema arid left at the attendant's request, being taken home by a woman. About twenty ,minutes later she returned, and refused to go away.—The
police knew of nothing else against her, and she was fined Ss. including costs, or seven days.

How They Walked.—John Wade and John Keefe, labourers, of Ford Farm, Norton, were brought up for having been drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street on Saturday night at about a quarter past eleven.—lt was stated they •came up from Market Gate arm in arm, staggering about and knocking people off the footpath. One minute they would be in the middle of the street, the next knocking against the shops. On the way to the Police Station, Keefe tried to get away.—The Chief s. Constable said the men were strangers, who drank whilst their (" or at least our ") fellows were fighting at the Front.-,-Each had to for- feit 14s. 6d., or go to gaol for 14 days.

Must Not Sleep There.—Patrick Richard Moran, loafer, of no settled abode, appeared for having slept out in the Cabmen's Hut, Win- wick-street, on Sunday, and for having gm visible Theans of subsistence, and being unable to give a proper account of himself.—Two, months before, it was stated, he had com- mitted the same offence, and he was now ordered to serve three months' hard labour.

" Between Two Stools."—George Miles was charged with being drunk On Sunday in Church-street.—A constable said the man stopped' 'people bn the footpath. He said he had paid for his lodging somewhere, but didn't know where.—The Chief Constable: He is a stranger to us. He goes from pub to-pub drink- ing and playing his whistle. He is a Scotch- man—or rather, he cows from Berwick-on- Tweed, so no one will claim him.—At this Miles smiled and nodded.—He was fined 10s. and 3s. 6d. costs, or 14 days.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

!Before Councillor, 11. Roberts (in the chair), Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes, T. Locker and J. Rymer Young. "The Bundles Di d lt."—John _ Turner, ! traveller, `Nof 67, Lovely-lane, appeared for having been drunk .in -Factory.lane shortly after ten .O'clOck the -previous night.—He pleaded not guilty.—A constable said he saw Turner fall acros the footpath, and found him helplessly drunk.=-2rwu other police officers gave evidence as to tie defendant's cliunken ton- dition.—The man denied, being drunk. He had come from St. Helens, he said, with three large bundles of photo-frames--big enough to fill a handcart. He, saw the two Constables at the bottom of , the station incline, . but when he caught one of de bundles against the railings and tripped and fell, instead of "giving a man a lift" they "came and took" him. He did not think it charitable at all. He had walked two thiles to St. Helens Station. Of course; he had had two or three drinks during the day.-- The Chief Constable said the man had a bottle of rum In his pocket. Theibundles, though large, were 'very light. As a Matter of tact, the man 'a-ifs always drunk, and this was his sixth appearance.—Turner: The fault is the bundles! I had no business to bring three: two were quite enough. (Laughter.)—A fine of is. 6d. and is. costs was ordered to be paid.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.
Before Messrs, C. Jackson . Hobbes .(in the chair) and W. T. Williams.

How Rum "Kept .Out the Cold."-?--jamey White, labourer, .of • no,„settled .abode, • ,was brought, up for using obscene language in Bridge-street the previouif_day.—lt was stated that he hail been 'drinking runi.—White,: I am very sorry; I had a bad .cold.—ln imposing a. fine of 7s. 6d., the Chaikaan told the man he had better leave the drink alone. Worked One 'Day in Fourteen Weeks.—Johu Dillon, labourer, of no settled abode, appeared for having been drunk in Bewsey-street at a quarter-past 'eleven the night before.—When charged, he replied "Yes,. sir."—A constable described how. the man was leaning against a wall, 'so drunk that he could .not walk along.— Dillon said he would take the pledge. The Chief Constable; He 'Till take the pledge every time he is brought up. He has worked one day in fourteen weeks.—The pyisoner was fined 7s. 6d., or seven days. •

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, APRIL 3, t9ts
THE KING TACKLES OUR GREATEST
ENEMY.

It is without doubt largely due to drink that we are unable to secure the output of wat material indispensable to meet the re- Quirements of our Army in the field, and that there has been such serious delay in the con- weyance of the necessary reinforcements and lupplies to aid our gallant troops at the Frent.—The King. .

We are fighting Germany, Austria and prink; and, as far as I can see, the greatest lf these deadly foes is drink.—Mr. Lloyd .Gebrge. The total time worked in almost all yards fivaS below the normal number of hours per wt.. In spite of working night and day, seven days a week, less productiveness was being secured from the men. The deputation INV of the opinion that this was principally flue to the question of drink.—Shipbuilding El/Violets" Federation deputation to Mr. Lloyd George.
plain duty ot the citizens of a great coan,try erer indicated in more striking or un- aingwerablo manner than in the above state- inesits P Slowly, but surely, we have been

approaching this point at which, we are stattlied into the realities of a grave and mewing situation. Fully to realise all that thexe quotations from the words of the men who know imply.. we must remember. that Kim=En and FRENCH are calling for mnni- Oleo that do not come forth in sufficient qutoatities and that the dispatch of men. and ammunition to the Front is not such as can corollate with the machine-like supply that is asgared to the soldiers of the enemy. What, aris-the facts of the situation? We have an immense and ever-increasing Army in the fient--thanks to the splendid patriotism of a tafge proportion of.our young manhomt The mat of this Army are striving to save the Win, of which they are so proud,. from the (lamination of a people who have proved them- selves of lower moral worth than the beasts of the field. At the 8141310 time, there are men ,at. lame, who, at all events nominally, love their country as much as their brothers who have gone forth to fight-in the field, but who. are such preys .to the luxuries of peace time dust they allow themselves • to be deceived in t*& state of criminal indifference. Nay, " worse, there is god ground for stating that many men at home are indulging their tastes more now than in time of peace, in conse- quence of the little 'extra money that war hours and war wages are putting in their way. The more fighting, the mqre slaughter abroad, the more wages at home, and, brutal as it may seem to say so, the more drink. If the result were not calamitous it might be erasable; but the results prove it Jo be blood money of the worst kind. The deputation to Mr. LLOYD GEOROR spoke of a battleship corn-
Zug in for immediate repairs and having those repairs "delayed for a whole day through the absence of the rivetters-lor the purpose

of drink afid conviviality." The. arrival of a battleship at a vital spot a day late might_ mean the downfall of an empire. But we have a battleship held up that rivetters may carouse—while our gallant sailors are in con- stant danger of being sent to the bottom. And, as the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, the one man in the kingdom who has the requisite amount of imagination to paint the picture for us in its true colours and accurate perspective, says, we have three deadly fdes to figh,t against, and the greatest of these is drink A nation, beset by dangers as is this

England of ours at the present moment, with three great enemies, clearly owes to itself the at:" of seeing how those enemies can he iso-. laW and defeated in detail. United they may het too strong for us; divided they may be atccessively rolled up. What are these enemies? Two are external foes, over whom we have no immediate control; the third-- attl the greatest—is merely a domestic habit that we could wipe out of existence by the simple exercise of our own will power and

'con:mon-sense. The time has gone by for arguing about the merits or demerits of alcohol. A nation in danger stands not on ce*mony ; it will not traffic in quibbles. It ratght, in peace time, smile at and consider extreme the admonition • that wine is a mocker; it cannot afford to be mocked to its deetruction in the midst of a world-wide con- flagration. What, then, is to be done? We nolght try voluntary self-denying ordinances, patkial prohibition of the sale of strong drink, ot total prohibition. Root and branch in a freedom-loving country such as this are not looked upon with, a kindly eye, but &operate diseases call for drastic' remedies. The shipbuilding employers say that partial cuttailment of the sale of drink would only aggravate the disease. It is not drunkenness they fear, but the drinking habit, and curtail- mint only concentrates the exercise of that habit and makes the result so much the worse. Iti) is therefore not to be wondered at that there should be a demand for total prohibi- tion for the period of. the war. The executive oltmnittee of a representative working men's organisation, the Transport Workers' Federa- tion, writing to Mr. LLOYD GEORGE, did not tut) total prohibition, but declared the wil- lingness of the Union to "support the Gov-

ernment in any drastic restrictions they may deem desirable, provided that they affect all districts alike and all classes alike, thereby removing any suggestion of favourite treat- tient." That is fair. All must be served alike, and the-Kt:lva, the very' head and fount , of British nobilitY stud aristocracy, hail under- taken to banish this greatest of enemies from his household. His great example is certain to be followed by others. LORD KITCR'LMER is one of the first to come into line with his Monarch. The KING'S Ministers of State • and jninisters of religion will join The ship-

uilding masters repudiated the idea that any one Of them was a teetotaler, but each and all demanded prohibition in the interests of the safety of the State. As to the men them- selves, the vast majority of them are doing "splendid and strenuous work, jitobably as good as the men in the trenches," the masters told the CHLINCELLOR ; and these men Will, we are sure, be - anxious to advance their patriotism a step as an object -lesson to their misguided mates, who disastrously reduce the average of the bows in works by their heedless indulgence. If the people, arc united to get rid of this greatest foe, the 'Government will be able to act effectively; and the overthrow of the remaining foes, Ger- many and Austria, will follow as a matter of course,
