div.head: PEACEFUL PARISH.
div.p: A PEACEFUL PARISH.

_ ' Of all the rural parishes in the neighbour- hood of Warrington. none is more peacefully or pleasantly situated than Appleton Thorn, an out-of-the-world village, known, chiefly to cyclists and pedestrian.s who pass throukh in the summer months on the way to Arley and other popular Cheshire resorts. At the crest of the long and winding road which rises steadily from'lumb Brook, stanas the beautiful little church of St. Cross. It is a modern building, constcrated in 1886, and is designed on simple but dignified lines. Mr. Evans's ser- vices were bright and devotional, and there was always a regular and loyal congregation.

THE FUNERAL. The interment took place on Tuesday in the graveyard attached to the church, the grave being but a few paces away from and directly opposite the vicarage. The church was full or sympathisers and the service was fully choral. Mr. Stanley Sewell presided at the organ, and the whole of the choir took part. The organist played Chopin's "March Funebre." The officiating clergyman was the Hon. and Rev. C. T. Cross (Rural Dean of Frodsham), and he was assisted by the Revs. H. G. Thompson (chaplain of Arley) and L. Roberts (assistant curate of Holy Trinity, Warrington). The other clergymen who attended the funeral were , the Revs. J. E. Edwards-Evans, 3. R. Jones, T. P. Owen; H. y Pigot, F. L. Snithett, W. S. Adams, J. C. Trampleasure, and E. W. Clarke, of Stockton Heath. - _ _ _

The chief mourners were the daughters of the deceased, the Misses Enid, Audrey and Vivien, and Mr. J. Sams and Miss L. Sams (brother and sister-in-law). Among others who attenked were Dr. and Mrs. Bower, Councillor Henry Roberts, Mr. F. Houghton, 3.l`r. Yessen,_Mr. J. Porter.

Flbral tributes were both numerous and beautiful, and were sent by the following : " Loving Wife and- Children," "Mother and Jack," Hamilton and Lilly," "Stella and Violet," Rev. J. T. Jones and family, " Lun- werth and T.P.," Mabel Roberts, Dr. and Mrs. Bower, "Millicent, Charles, Olive and Tom Bower and P 1111," Mrs. Henry Lyon, Lieutenant- Col9nel and Mrs. Lyon, Mrs. Piers Egerton- Warburton, • Misses Egerton-Warburton, Miss Robertson, Dr. Tong, Dick Whitehouse. Mr. and Mrs. Barnigh, Mrs.- Knowles and family, Mr. and Mrs. Pimlott and family, Mr. and Mrs. E. Marsh, Mr. Hindley, Mrs. Turner and family, "Stanley and Mabel," Mr. and Mrs. James Clarke and family, Mr. and Mrs. J. Mills and family, "From the Parishioners per S. Bate," "Choir and Day School Teachers," "Young Men of Appleton," "Elder Girls of Appleton," "Sunday and Day School Scholars," and the "Maids at Viewfield."

div.head: ANOTHER TERRITORIAL BATTALION.
div.p: ANOTHER TERRITORIAL BATTALION.
Recruiting Staff At Work.

Now ,that the original Territorial Battalion is at the froilt and the Reserve Battalion train- ing in the South is rapidly qualifying itself to fill up the ranks as they may be broken through the stress of war, a third battalion is to be raised.

The need for men to remain at work in War- rington. Amon war material is recognised; but it is clear that there are many eligible young men still in the borough who have no claims of work upon them to hold them back. To these duty calls aloud—for all our energies will have to be concentrated upon one object if we are to defeat the enemy and so end the war as it-must be ended.
The standard measurements are: Height, sft. lin.; chest, 34in. Age, not younger than nine- teen. All must enlist for foreign service.
THREE SOLDIER-BROTHERS MEET.

Mrs. E. e-Jones,, wife of the chairman of the Progressive Labour League, who lives at Knutsford-road, Latchford, has three brothers serving at the Front—Sergeant Davies, Canadian Light Infantry; Bombardier Davies, Royal Field Artillery; and Private Davies, 2nd Battalion Royal Welsh Fusiliers. They had not met for eleven years but, although they belong to different branches of the service, they met at the Front one evening last week and spent two hours together. They had been for some time only four miles apart.

div.head: Grand elothinq Hall for Easter
div.p: Grand elothinq Hall for Easter
SONG AND SUPPER FOR "TOMMY."
Enjoyable "Au Revoir" Gather- ing at Orford Barracks.

Another detachment .of the men who had been preparing for stern service at the Front left Orford Barracks, where they had been quartered for the past few weeks. on Wednes- day morning, their destination being a 1` finish- ing" camp by the sea. The night before they went they were given an excellent concert, a ollysupper party following. The chair at the concert was taken by Regimental-Sergeant- Major Quick.

div.head: HARMONY
div.p: THE HARMONY

• The programme, which was bright and in- teresting throughout, opened with a number of Harry Lauder's songs, played by the band. Drummer Hughes next gave a song, entitled "Nobody satisfied," while " Piccadily was made for you and me" and " Shirts " were the titles of two comic songs given by Private F Kershaw, of the 3rd Dragoon Guards. Mr. Wolfenden sang "-Here we are again," and Private Hyde delighted with his farmyard mimicry. Mr. Griffin contributed a recitation "Comrades," and Private Jones delighted the company with a ditty entitled "The old rustic bridge." The band next rendered a number of rag-time melodies, after which Mr. J. Jolley sang, to the accompaniment of Mr. Bates, the comic song "He's gone where they can't play billiards." "The magic of your voice" was the title of a song given by Drummer Hughes, and Private Webster rendered an amusing parody on the well-known ballad " Thora." Mr. J. Jolley was re-called after singing "You do so soon change your mind." Private Webstergave yet another gong, this time a parody on "Some- 'where," while Mr. Wilkinson caused great merriment with a comic song, entitled "Balmy Bill!" A duet "When sweet Marie was sweet sixteen" was given by Mr. Wilkinson and Drummer Hughes. A pianoforte solo "The student's first lesson," by Mr. Prow, concluded a thoroughly enjoyable programme. Mr. Wilkinson, who is well-known locally, and who was once a professional artiste, was loudly applauded, for his songs, as also were Private Webster and Private Kershaw, whose comic items proved exceedingly popular. The presence of the band, which was -under the con- ductorship of Mr. Cahill, livened up the pro- ceedings considerably.

div.head: – AND THE "TUCK."
div.p: - AND THE "TUCK."

After the concert the soldiers sat down to a, hearty supper, to which they did ample justice: The thanks of the men are due to Regimental= Sergeant-Major Quick and Sergeant Wynne, who worked hard in. the matter of the pro- motion of the concert.

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
div.p: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
Oddfellow's Well-Earned Presentation.

At a gathering of the members of the "Loyal Olive Branch" Lodge of the Manchester Unity of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, held on Saturday evening, an interesting presenta- tion was made to Past Grand William Hamraon, who has recently completed his term of office as Noble Grand and Grand Master of the lodge for the third time. The presentation consisted of a Past Grand's purple scarf. The gathering was presided over by N.G. Fred Broadhurst, and amongst those present. were District Grand Master Edward Spann, beputy, O.M. William E. Clare, I.P:P.G.M. Henry Lawrence, P.P.G.M. Frank Webster (district secretary), Lodge G.M. William Hammon, V.G. John Alex. Brown, Min- ute Secretary Richard Whitfield, P.G. Stanley Garnett, P.G. John Brown, P.P.G.M. George Higham, P.P.G.M. Walter Knowles, E.G. Arthur Cotterill (treasurer), and P.P.G.M. Alban Boyle (secretary). The District Officers made a special vbilt on this occasion, a fact which was much appre- ciated by the members of the lodge.

div.head: DUTIES FAITHFULLY DISCHARGED
div.p: DUTIES FAITHFULLY DISCHARGED

Grand Master Spann, in making the presen- tation, said he could assure the members that it gave him great pleasure to be asked to pre- sent the special purple scarf to P.G. Hammon. He had visited the "Olive Branch" Lodge on many occasions, and could truthfully say That Bro. Hammon had always carried out his duties .faithfully and well. P.G. Hammon had carried out the various offices on three occasions, and he (the speaker) thought that fact should be an incentive to many of the other members to go through the same offices. He hoped the recipi- ent would not relax his efforts, but would try and qualify himself for district honours. He further hoped that Bro. Hammon would be spared a long time to wear the scarf.

div.head: AN ARDENT WORKER.
div.p: AN ARDENT WORKER.

Deputy G.M. Clare thanked the offieters and members of the lodge for-the cordial welcome they had given the district officers, and said ,he was pleased to be present at the presentation of the scarf to P.G. Hammon, as he thought the brother had been a very ardent worker. He hoped that Bro. Hammon's example would be emulated by other members of the lodge. Prey. C.S. Webster said that was the only presentation of the purple scarf that he could remember during his experience. It was due to the work of members like Bro. Hammon that Oddfellowship had attained its present position. P.G. Hammon, in responding, thanked the officers and members, and said he had always tried to carry out his duties to the best of his ability. If any difficulty ever arose in the lodge he would gladly come forward and -render any service he could. _ _ _

The meeting was brought to a close by the Noble Grand reading the extended ritual of the Order, and the singing of the hymn having special reference to members of the Order serv- ing in His Majestyls Naval and Military Forces.
ONLY THREE DAYS TO THE TRENCHES.

Sergeant Davies, writing to Mrs. Wynne- Jones, to acknowledge the recevt of a cake she had sent, said it was delivered to him in the trenches three days after dispatch, showing the efficient state of the means of communication now existing between this country and the Army. Sergeant Davies said the cake was thoroughly enjoyed, and twelve other members of his company sent "their compliments to Mrs. Wynne-Jones."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATIJRDAY, APRIL 3, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATIJRDAY, APRIL 3, 1915.

The Rev. F. E. Evans was 55 yeirs- of age. He was educated at London University and Exeter College, Oxford, *here he obtained his degree in 1886. Before coming to Appleton he held curacies at Hollinwood, Oldham; All Saints', Portsmouth; St. Stephen's, Twicken- ham, and Tilehurst, Berks. He was a close student of Church history and archeeology, and had travelled a great deal. Eight years ago he visited India as chaplain to the troops. FIFTEEN YEARS AT APPLETON. The Rev. V. E. Evans went to Appleton Thorn as vicar 15 years ago. ' Although the parish is a very Amall one, much had been in- augurated and kept going by him, including a parish magazine, which paid its way without trouble. Up to quite recently there was a flourishing musical and dramatic society which Mr. Evans started. This was a means of pro- viding excellent entertainments for the long winter evenings, besides having a refining and beneficial influence on young -parishioners. Recently missionary work and work for the Red Cross Society had taken the place of the musical and dramatic society. Mr. Evans succeeded in raising considerable sums of money in the parish for religious and charitable objects, the chief amount being £230 for a new church organ to replace the instrument prhich had been in the church since its oPening, and had become worn out. He had the work par- ticularly at heart, and was backed up by a united body of waters, and so was enabled to carry it to a successinl issue. The organ proved a great help, the services from a musical point of View at Appleton being above the average for a small village choir. Another object which the Vicar worked strenuously to attain and, indeed, succeeded in attaining, was prictically the re-building of the school some seven years ago.

div.head: BELGIANS WAITING FOR HOMES.
div.p: BELGIANS WAITING FOR HOMES.
Thousands Need Succour.
MR. PARKER'S APPEAL FOR FURTHER LOCAL HELP.
Collective and Individual Effort
Ts the Editor of " The Examiner."

Sir —The aets of Carnage, cruelty, lust and brutality, which the' Germans perpetrated upon the Belgian people during the first six weeks of the war shocked the world. These acts have indelibly marked the German nation, and no victory, no • indeinnity,. no lapse of time can erase the damned stain. A sense of horror and „amazement was felt through . the civilised , world, and quickly efforts „were ,jnadet.o heal,..as far as coulftbe, the wounds, „and to comfort this Suffering peeple. ;Since these early War days so many happenings have crow ded upon ,-us in rapid succession that our thoiights -and Sympathies are in some danger of being .diverted from Belgiunf,s rmattyrdonv and .Belgium's need., The wrongs inflicted . cannot be righted by emotionalism or by a few Weeks' effort. For long, we British people must take the larger share in bearing up the Belgian people in our strong arms, must do all that is possible to re-establish their shattered- lives and for- tunes, and help them again to become self- sustaining and. self-reliant.

div.head: WHAT CAN WARRINGTON DO?
div.p: WHAT CAN WARRINGTON DO?

What are the facts ? In London there are over five thousand being housed in large buildings like the Alexandra.ltalace, waiting for homes. There are also many thousands in Holland waiting to come over. Holland cannot sustain all that sought refuge on her soil. The Dutch are doing more than their share. The Belgians waiting for homes both in England and Holland are living under conditions physically and mentally unfavour- able. They have no regular employment, no duties to keep them from brooding over their undeserved sorrows and misfortunes, simply waiting for the time when some kind hearts will prepare for them some place that can be called a home.
What can Warrington do to plitce more of iese in conditions healthy to mind and body? Warrington made a _ satisfactory start in

this work; the Borough Committee took up with all seriousness the caring for a limited number of these homeless ones, and brooded over them with zealous care. Somehow the committee was not very suc- cessful in eliciting the support of all sections of the community. The work and its inter- ests were limited to the few, and as time went on the movement appeared to lose its driving power. An impression was, unfortunately, created that we had done enough, we had done our share, and we .should husband our resources. However necessary it may be to husband resources, it is more important to call forth the resources that can be enlisted. I am confident that this can best be done by awakening the interest of groups of our townsmen already associated by some com- mon bond, and by the Central Committee in- flaming such groups with their own enthu- siasm, and going to some trouble to encour- age these to provide Belgian homes. These homes would be managed by their own. com- mittee, thc subscrlbers would be brought into human contact with the people they are help- ing, an interept would be created which (except to the very few) is absent when homes are run on subscribed funds by a cen- tral committee. Working on these lines, I feel sure Warrington would take as proud a place in helping the Beigian people as she has already done in other directions of national war effort. NOT A CASE FOR COMPARISONS.
We should not be concerned with compari- sons With other places. The •extent of our work should be determined by our individual duty, by the great need, and by our capacity

, for sacrifice and service. Few- towns are so generally prosperous as Warrington. I say generally, because here, as elsewhere, some indivisluals are hard hit through the unequal effects of the war. But taking Warrington as a whole, there are few towns more pros- perous, and where so much is given much is required; and much should be given. I do not ignore the practical difficulty of homes; I am aware there are few houses available in the borough. But supposing we filled every empty house in the town, houses could be secured in neighbouring townships.. The question of separate homes is not the only way in which the Warrington people can help. There are small units, possibly husband and wife, or Tucrther and child, or a single individual, who could l be accommodated in existing homes. Much has been done in other places in this way, and niany lonely people have had their lives enriched, their outlook broadened, by taking in Belgian guests. I am surprised that the committee has notinade an, effort in this direction. It can scarcely be expected that individual gi will come forward' with offers of hospitality unless invited and assured of getting suitable guests. I The authorities in London admit that, in the early stages, it. was impossible to give much atten- tion to the question of selection.. They nOw fully recognise the necessity, and are pre- pared to do all that is possible in selecting suitable guests, if intending hosts or hos- tesses will supply, thiough their local com- mittee, particulars of their requirements. I have this promise from Sir Ernest Hatch, as well as from those in charge of the London centres. I wish I had time to describe my visits to these centres; perhaps for your next issue I may be able to find this. CHARLES E. PARKER. London, March 31, 1915.4

div.head: MERCIFUL NEW ACT.
div.p: MERCIFUL NEW ACT.
1189is1ra1es Able To Deal With An
Embezzler.

The first case to be heard locally under the Criminal (Justices') Administration Act 1914, which only came into force the same day, cropped up at the Borough Police Court on Thursday morning, when Arthur William Tanner, an electrician, of Sheffield, in the employ of Mr. Harry Rogers, Friars' Gate, was charged on remand with having embezzled the sum of £3 28. 7d. from his employer, Mr. Harry Rogers, an electrician.—Mr. T. S. Steel prosecuted and Mr. Arthur Browne defended. The prisoner had been remanded on bail since the Thursday of the previous week in order that other accounts that had been col- lected by the prisoner, on behalf of his employer, might be inquired into. After a prolonged hearing, during -the -course of .which it was stated that other small sums had been collected by the prisoner and not paid over—the defence contending that the young man was arrested before he had time, to pay the other money in—a fine of £2O was imposed, the Bench trusting that Tanner would realise that he had been very leniently dealt with. Prisoneit's explanation as'to why he took the sum mentioned in the charge was th,at he had got into the hands of money-lenders. The new Act, under the provisions of which the prisoner's case came, enables magistrates to deal With charges of embezzlement in which sums not eceeding £2O are at stake. Hitherto, cases where the money embezzled exceeded 40s. they had no option but to commit the prisoner for trial. Under the new Act deliquents are liable to a penalty up to £5O, or to imprison- ment.

div.head: MORE MEN WANTED!
div.p: MORE MEN WANTED!
Hon. Local Agents Appointed To Assist In Recruiting. ••••••=111•••• EFFORTS IN THE RURAL PARISHES

Still the cry is "More men and yet more men!" and the more that come forward the sooner will dawn the day when the call need no longer be heard in the land. To ensure that the call to arms shall. reach . every town- ship and village in the neighbourhood of • War- rington. the Chief Recruiting 'Officer for the 40th Recruiting Area (Lieuteant-Colonel Mocatts.)-*--whose headquarters are at the Police Station, Warrington—has invited the various Urban District Councils and Parish Councils within his area to form small Recruiting Com- i mittees and to nominate honorary recruiting agents to assist and co-operate with him in the grand work of finding soldiers for the King. The honorary recruiting agents will be supplied ' with suitable badges and their duties will be to pass along likely young fellows who come forward to the chief recruiting officer, who will, subject to their being up to the require- ments demanded, see that they • are duly attested and that they take their place in the ever-swelling ranks of those who have offered their services, and, if need be, their lives. in the glorious cause of their country. The honorary recruiting agents will also be required to assist the Chief Recruiting Officer and his staff in every other way polsible. So far a good number of the local and parochial auth- orities approached have formed their com- mittees in accordance with the Chief Recruit-
ing Officer's request and have nominated their honorary recruiting agents.

HON. RECRUITING AGENTS APPOINTED. Mr. B. S. Newcombe has been appointed the hon. agent for the area controlled by the War- rington Rural District Council, and a number of other agents for the different districts embraced within the area under the jurisdiction of the Council will work in conjunction with him, and by means of their efforts it is confidently anticipated that many suitable young men may be brought to see where their duty lies. A list of the hon. agents so far appointed to act with Mr. Newcombe, together with the names of the parishes for which they will act, is as follows : Southworth-with-Croft : Mr. J. Cawthorn°. Winwick: Mr. G. P. Greenway. Poulton-with-Fearnhead : Mr. G. Mather. , Houghton, Middleton and Arbury : Mr. S. Walker. Woolston-with-Martinscroft : Mr. E. Donned. Rixton-with-Glazebrook : Mr. J. Robinson. Burtonwood : Mr. Fred Btuideley. Great Sankey; Mr. A. H. Lowe. Penketh and Cuerdley : Mr. D. J. Griffiths. Windle : Mr. F. C. Davies. Rainhill : Mr. Frank Lowe. Lawton: Mr. Charles Canfield. Mr. W. T. Thornley has also been appointed hon. agent for Culcheth, and Dr. Dowling, J.P., for the Haydock Urban District Council area.

GREAT SAN KEY PLAYING ITS PART. The matter was referred to at the annual parish meeting at Great Sankey on Monday niight, when Mr. W. Furness (chairman of the Warrington Rural District Council) presided over a fair attendance, and explained in detail the military authorities' new scheme for encouraging recruiting in rural areas. The Government, Mr. Furness told the meet- ing, were very charry about putting a scheme of compulsory service into operation. They were proceeding along the lines, of voluntary service as far as they possibly could, before applying the principle of compursion, and they were desirous of forming, in every rural dis- trict, small sub-committees with a local resi- dent as honorary recruiting agent. The primary object was that the military autliorities could be kept in touch with the agent, who would inform them as to the progress of the recruit- ing in his area. By this means all possible moral pressure would be brought to bear upon the district, through the medium of the sub- committee, the recruiting agent and the , Government recruiters. He hoped the residents would assist the 'Committee and the gentleman who had been appointed honorary recruiting agent for the district (Mr. A.H. Lowe) as much as they were able. Sankey, so far as he could gather, had done fairly - well in the matter of recruiting. He had gone through the district with Lieutenant-Colonel Mocatta, organising those committees, and found that every village had taken the scheme up energetically. Prior to the parish meeting, Lieutenant- Colonel -Mocatta, who is the chief recruiting officer for the 40th Kecruiting, Area, had attended a meeting of the Great Sankey War Relief Committee, with the result that a local recruiting committee to assist Mr. Lowe was appointed, the following consenting to serve thereon: The Rev. J. R. Jones (vicar), and Messrs. C. A. Littler, F. T. Newbold and Joseph Smith.

div.head: SAVED BY HIS SISTER.
div.p: SAVED BY HIS SISTER.
"Falaba" Musician Persuaded To Prolong His Holiday.

A sister's persuasion most probably saved the life of Mr. Walter Brandreth,. a musician, whose home is at 109, Padgate-lane. Mr: Brandreth had arranged to make '.no the orchestra aboard the ill-fated s.s. Falaba for her trip; indeed he had written • a postcard announcing his intention of joining her at Liverpool, prior to her setting Out for v.rhat proved to he her last voyage, but as the time for his departure drew near he was distinctly " 'seedy " and on the earnest solicitation of his sister, and rather contrary to his own wishes, he did not post the card, but consented to pro- long his vacation and, accordingly, wrqte a sub- sequent message to the effect that he wbuld join the next boat, 'a course in which his employers quite acquiesced.

div.head: Torpedoed by a Submarine.
div.p: Torpedoed by a Submarine.

The boat on which he originally intended to have sailed left Liverpool at six o'clock on Saturday evening, bound for the Canaries and West Africa. She was an Elder Dempster liner and had hardly begun her long voyage; in fact, she had only got as far as Milford Haven, on. the Pembrokeshire coast, when she was tor- pedoed by a German submarine and, of the 242 people aboard her, only about 140 were saved. The newspaper accounts say that as the vessel was nearing Milford a submarine rose and gave three whistles as a signal to the liner to gat out her boats. Before these boats could be launched, however, the submarine torpedoed her in a vital part near the engine-room. Three boats were swamped, and the ship sank almost at once. The people were thrown into the water.
Brutal Germans Laugh at Drowning Passengers.

The submarine made a circle round the drowning people, her vrew laughing at 'their struggles, and without making any attempt to help them, sheered off A Lowestoft drifter, the Eileen Mary, had seen the submarine some time .before, and suspecting mischief, followed. She came up in time to pick up from the boats and water about 140 persons, and of these she landed 110 at Milford.

Mr. Brandreth, who was formerly employed at "The Examiners' office, was solo violinist in the ralaba's orchestra, and on her last trip figured prominently in the programme of a grand concert gis‘en aboard the vessel.

div.head: SOLDIER'S RETURN.
div.p: THE SOLDIER'S RETURN.

Private John Rhooney, King's Liverpool Regi- ment, was brought before Monday's Police Court for having been an absentee since the previous day.—Superintendent Williamson stated that man first said he had been absent since eight o'clock on Sunday morning, and later from eight o'clock on Sunday night. He also sail be would be all right till midnight. The police had previously put him in the train, but he came back again.—The magistrates ordered him to be handed over to an escort.

div.head: SECONDARY SCOOL SCHWAS.
div.p: SECONDARY SCOOL SCHWAS.
As War Fund Raisers. OVER £135 TO DATE.

The pupils of the Warrington Secondary School coniinned'Oeir patriotic- effiiits' in the direction of helping the war funds, by means of a bazaar held on Saturday in the School- room. The arrangements were in the hands of Forms I. and H., under the capable guidance of the Form Mistressee—Miss E. J. Forsyth and Miss M. Jolley. There were stalls for all kinds' of art needlework and fancy goods, sweets, second-hand books, woodwork and toys, fruit and flowers, and refreshmentsl and a pound stall. Handsome gifts of greenhouse plants and flowers were received from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. T. H. Lyon and Mr. W. A. Powell, and in addition worked articles received from the staff and students of the evening domestic depart- ment.

div.head: BAZAAR PROCEEDS £47.
div.p: BAZAAR PROCEEDS £47.

The pupils were fortunate in securing the services of Mrs. E. Fairylough. wife of "Colonel Fairclough, to'open the bazaar. The Principal (Mr. Robson), in introducing Mrs, Fairclough, alluded to the splendid work she and her family had done on behalf of the Local Territorial Regiment, and trusted that the parents and friends would show their appreciation of her presence by their heartiest support of the work done by the pupils. Mrs. Fairclough, in formally declaring the bazaar open, expressed her keen pleasure in accepting the invitation from the pupils, who had rendered valuable assistance in connection with her school knitting Scheme. After the presentation of a bouquet by Mildred Isaac, a vote of than:-..s to Mrs. Fair- dough was proposed by Mrs. H. Jolley and carried with acclamation.

The attractions provided by the organisers of the entertainment received the heartiest sup- port, and the sum of £47 was realised. This amount will be divided among the following funds. 2 The Serbian Relief Fund and the Local Territorials' Fund, the Wounded Allies' Relief Fund, and the Sailors' Comforts' Fund. The staff and pupils of the Secondary School have now raised over £135 for the various war funds.

div.head: ENTERTAINMENT.
div.p: THE ENTERTAINMENT.

During the afternoon and evening a most attractive programme was presented. It was opened by the singing of Elgar's fine chorus "Land of Hope and Glory," with Mildred Isaac as soloist. Eileen Morton next recited "Seem' Things," after which Margaret Scotson sang "My Treasure." A Morris dance, in which the following girls took part, followed: M. Isaac, E. Knowles, M. Scotson, E. Baird, M. Southerden and M. Knight. "Our At 'Ome Day," in which the Misses A. Duckworth, C. Willett and May Weston appeared, proved a most amusing dialogue, and Mildred Isaac was warmly applauded for her rendition of "Some- where a Voice is Calling." Two well-delivered recitations, by Gwendoline Humphreys and Emily Sutton followed, after which the follow- ing boys appeared in " Macnamara's Band": J. Padmore, E. Woolridge, It. Barrington, S. Brayshaw, C. Bayliss, F. Lowe, J. Mills and E: Birtles. The Misses A. Duckworth, M. Weston, M. Pass, R. Persons, C. Willett, L. Plinston, G. Humphreys and D. Collins danced a pretty country dance, and Masters D. Jones, It. Den- nett and W. Simcock appeared in a sketch entitled "Custards." A hornpipe by the Misses M. Southerden and M. Houghton brought the programme to a close.

div.head: OLD SCHOLAR'S GIFT.
div.p: OLD SCHOLAR'S GIFT.
Technical Institute Student's
Clever Working Model.

Mr. S Appleton, a student in the Building end Plumbing Classes at the Warrington Technioal Institute, who has recently left the town to join the Royal Flying Corps, has kindly presented to the Building Department a complete working model of a domestic hot- water Supply apparatus. The model is well- made, and is entirely Mr. Appleton's own work.' "

It is arranged on the combined .cylinder and tank system. Practically the whole of the apparatus, which stall& about 4ft. high, is made in copper, and the skill and judgment dis- played in its execution are highly commendable. In the opinion of Mr. Marshall, the head of the Building Department, the model will prove

div.head: GIFT AND THE GIVER.
div.p: THE GIFT AND THE GIVER.

a valuable asset for demonstation purposes, and the Technical Institute is very much indebted to Mr. Appleton for the gift, which may be regarded as a mark of appreciation for the benefits he has received by attending the classes.

div.head: IN THE HANDS OF THE lIUNS. Vt'arrington Lance-Corporal's Fate.
div.p: IN THE HANDS OF THE lIUNS. Vt'arrington Lance-Corporal's Fate.

Lance-Corporal J. Harrop, of the Cheshire Regiment, who, until he death of his father a few months ago, had his home at 53, Elles- mere-street, is at present a prisoner in the hands of the Germans. Since the death of his father, his mother has taken up her abode with a married daughter, Mrs. Robinson, at 13, Tanner's-lane.

The gallant Lance-Corporal had • finished twenty-one years' service in the Army and was on his *ay home from abroad when the war broke out and he volunteered his services for a further fieri(xl. lie is forty years of age and is single.

div.head: Another Local Prisoner of War.
div.p: Another Local Prisoner of War.

Further news of her husband, Private George Latham, of the Ist Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment, is anxiously awaited by his wife, who lives at 73, Bostock-street, Warrington. , Private Latham was working for the Wir- rington Slate Company when the war broke out, and he was called up as a Reservist. He Went to the Front early on in the campaign, and months ago he was reported missing. Since then, however, his wife has received several postcards from him stating that he is a prisoner of war and is interned at Munster, in Bavaria, hi,s last 'message being received five weeks ago, when he asked her to send him along some white bread and a tin of treacle, which she duly forwarded, together witli a quantity of other suitable foodstuffs.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
THRILLS AT THE ROYAL COURT

In that alwaye-thrilling and consistently popular melodrama. "The Frozen North " whioh attracts large crowds to the Royal Court this week—the,principal. part. is .most cloves:lY filled -by Young Buffalo. a dashing here Of great personal charm, undaunted courage: and never-failing luok. Thus in the climax—that great sensational episode in which Young Buffalo rescues a clever little child actress from the clutches of a gang of, wicked and desperate men by imeans of a rope hanging over a seeth- ing mass of flame and lava—he contrives the deed unharmed. His careless. deportment only serves to enhance the heroic effect.

Miss Kathleen L. Russell gives a moving study of Alaska, the lovable Siwaah girl, and Mr. Edward G. Millins very cleverly sustains the humorous element in the role of Sambo, the negro. Big Canter and Baptiste—the cun- ning evil-mongEtrs whose schemes are so happily frustrated—are realistically portrayed by Messrs. 'Edward Dobson and Frank McLellan; and, Miss Dolly Stamp renders lively and ' cap- tivating songs and dances, Mr. Gus Ruhlan providing the cornet solos in great style.

div.head: CAPTIVATING REVUE AT THE HIPPODROME.
div.p: CAPTIVATING REVUE AT THE HIPPODROME.

Gay scenes- hold the boards this week at that popular and comfortable amusement resort, the Hippodrome, for Messrs. Ray Bros. (owners and producers of the successful revues—" Have a Dip," &c.) present London's latest aquatic revue—" Have a Plunge"—" a delicious slice of seaside life, in four scenes and a dip." The production is one long laugh from start to finish—although at the same time some mar- vellous exhibitions of diving and swimming are given by a talented troop of dainty damsels. The five leading entertainers in the piece are specially worthy of commendation, whllst tableaux and scenic effects are remarkably excellent. Other items include Johnson and Bert—who present the character comedy absurdity. "A Queer Customer." This is easily one of the best sketches ever given at the Hippodrome, • and earns loud applause at every performance: Florence Cowper's repertoire of (contralto) "old and new successes" is quite a novel one, and she proves a great favourite. Les Andreo give national 'dances in all sorts of costumes and styles. Their performance is perfect. Bert Castle—" he of the catchy songs"—also scores a marked success. Perfection pictures are shown as usual.

div.head: Holiday Week Fare.
div.p: Holiday Week Fare.

The Seltini Trio will present a novel acro- batic act—quite one of the best things of its kind to be seen on the vaudeville stage—and other artistes booked include the Martelloni Family, who are smart lady tumblers; the Brothers St. John, musicians, humorists and dancers; the, Five Joy Belles, a quintet of charming young ladies in an amazing frivol; Harry Rogerson, in his latest novelty, "Old and Young," and Dalkeith,_ the illustrating comedian in his amusing chalk-and-chaff show:

div.head: SAIART TOPICAL SKIT AT STAR – KINEMA.
div.p: SAIART TOPICAL SKIT AT STAR - KINEMA.

A novel departure in picture-plays has proved a great attraction at the Star Kinema 4.tbj°, week. Whilst the "star" film for the Jars' j half of the •week was a smart and up-to-datefr military skit, that being shown now is the famous masterpiece, "The Miracle "—an ex- cellent contrast!

The first excellent programme included "Her Last Chance," a quite new and hilarious comedy. The race for the 1915 Grand National' was. shown ‘practically in' its entirety, with remarkable clearness. "Pathe's Animated Gazette" turned attention, this week, to the progress af our Colonial troops and the troops of our Allies—besides home football. "The Revenge of Mr. Thomas Atkins," a smart topical skit on the Hun Army, absolutely con- vulsed the audience with laughter. "AD Actor's Downfall and His Regeneration" was a most touching story, showing how the ,wounds a worldly wife inflicted upon the heart of her husband, were healed by the loving solicitude of his daughter. Incidentally it afforded a forcible object-lesson on the curse of drink. The entertainmeht 'concluded with "The Boob's Legacy "—another fine comedy:
Of 'course, opportunities of seeing "the Miracle" are rare, and all film-lovers ,who can should to-itight pay the Kinema a visit.
Exciting Adventure Next Week.
For next week "star ", films totally different in chanicter .from this week's are booked—for the first three days " The Abduction," and on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, "The Trap."

So varied was the action in this excelleht film that it could not fail powerfully to appeal to picture lovers all and sundry. A beautiful Frencli scenic film concluded a "Grancf" bill of fare. div.p: Emmanuel Fellows' Study

The doctor took the line that Christianity and war Were totally incompatible in the light Of.the four Gospels, and .claimed that Paul epitomised what should be the attitude of every Christian on the sub- ject when he laid it down as axiomatic that they must overcome evil with good. They were enjoined to. love their enemies, do good to those Who hated them, and pray for those who despitefully used them and persecuted then:, it , and before they could harmonise that leaching with warfare they must call black i!hite• War was not only unlawful, in the ight of the Gospels, but was alSo.unnecessary knd inexpedient; it was a negation of the very ~f(nplidation of Christ's teaching—the universal "rotherhood of man.

div.head: Mr. Charles Dukes.

At the annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of Trades and Labour :Councils, Mr. Charles Dukes (the secretary of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council) was elected to the secretaryship of the parent body, tributes being paid to his fine record of work for labour.

div.head: St. Ann's Sale of Work.
div.p: St. Ann's Sale of Work.

The annual sale of work in connection with St. Ann's Parish is to be held in the Dannett- street Schools on Wednesday and Thursday. next. Emphasis is laid upon the fact that the sale is being held not to provide luxuries for the church, but for necessities, else it would not have been held at such a time as the present. The sale will be opened on the first day by the Deputy-Mayor tDr. Joseph), and on the second day by Mrs. Richardson, of Holly Bank, Walton.

div.head: "The _End—and Beyond."
div.p: "The _End—and Beyond."

At the Christadelphian Meeting Room, Bold- street, will to-morrow evening be delivered by Mr. G. H. Denny (of Walsall) the last of a series of special lectures on "The Divine Plan of the Ages. The title and theme, will' be "The Millennial Age "—the long-promised Kingdom of God established on the earth: a fime of peace and blessedness for 1,000 years: the end and beyond. Mr. Donny previdusly lectured at Bold-street in winter, and his visit is by a large number eagerly anticipated.

div.head: Local Leather Trade.
div.p: Local Leather Trade.

In his weekly review of the local leather trade in " The Leather Trades Review," a-local cornespoudent writes :—" The market was very strong again last week, the current prOduction, although increased, being too slow for the de- mand for all classes of Army leathers. Con- tractors pressed for deliveries all round, and were generally open to buy any surplus from contract requirements. The inquiries that cam 6 to hand were of a fairly wide character. Al- most all classes of bends were sought, and it seems that medium to light weights are now 'just as difficult to get as the heavies. Nry business has been' largely confined to prompt .or early date, ,there being little inclination to venture far ahead. A definite pronouncement as to furtliqr Government orders would un- doubtedly do much to clear the situation. As matters are, all kinds of rumours obtain cre- dence for a time."

div.head: Youthful shero.
div.p: A Youthful shero.

James A. Gilbert (16),. of 39, Marsh House- lane, was presented at the Borough Police Court on Monday4with the certificate of the Royal Humane Society—in recognition of his gallant though vain attempt to rescue Andrew Sauce from drowning in a reservoir at Cock- hedge Mills on Febtuary 6th. Fully dressed as be was, Gilbert dived into the water, but failed to find any trace of Sauce. He did all he could td try to find the drowning lad, but failed, although he dived twice. He had- to leave the water owing to exhaustion, and when he did sof summoned further assistance. . He was in the water between five and ten Minutes, and the gallantry of his act is enhanced by the fact that he had never tried to chi any- thing of that sort before.—ln the absence of the Mayor, the Chairman (Mr. S. Wright) made the presentation, telling the ,recipient that the • Bench felt indebted to him for his courageous act.' They realised that it was lads possessed of Such gallantry, as he had displayed who were fighting our battles at the Front. He hoped his conduct would be an example to others, not only to try and save life at home, but also to go forward and save life, wherever possible, at the Front.

div.head: OLD FOLK ENTERTAINED. Latchford Wesleyan Bible. Class's "Annual."
div.p: OLD FOLK ENTERTAINED. Latchford Wesleyan Bible. Class's "Annual."

The annual Old Folks Treat, promoted by the "United Bible Class of the Latchford Wesleyan Church, took place in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Wednesday evening. About one hundred old folks sat down at the tea tables, over which the lady members of the church and Bible Class presided, assisted by the members of the Men's Bible Class.
"ON THE SUNNY SIDE OF SEVENTY."

The Rev. A. J. Morton presided over the sub- sequent proceedings and, in the course of a few opening remarks., said he was glad to see so many present. There were some on the sunny side of seventy, but they should all try to, keep their hearts young. He was very glad that the Bible Class took upon themselves that glorious event once a year. Touching upon the war, he said that they should not get downhearted about their losses on land and sea, but should "ace them fearlessly and heartily. He heard that evening that a German submarine had been run down by a French gunboat. Let them hope that it was one of the submarines that had committed such outrages on their peaceful passenger boats. (Applause.) Hanging was too good a death for such men as those. (Hear, hear.) THE ENTERTAINMENT.

A most enoyable programme was submitted, and all the items were well received. A quartette party first gave a 'selection, for which they were re-called. Miss , Isherwood, who possesses a very sweet voice, rendered a solo, while Miss Butterw,orth gave a pianoforte solo. Mr. Clare skilfully played the violin and, With Miss Butterworth, joined in a duet. Messrs. W. Grounds and Rushton also gave solos. The sketches "Four to One" and "The Matri- monial Mart" created considerable merriment. The pianoforte accompaniments were tastefully played by Miiss Butterworth and Mr. 4.. A. Fairclough.

At the close Mr. S. Ackroyd proposed and Mr. Cook seconded a hearty, vote of thanks to the artistes. Chairman and lady helpers. The arrangements for the concert had been admir- ably carried out by a small committee.
First Casualties Among The Officers.

div.head: ONE KILLED AND ONE. WOUNDED.
div.p: ONE KILLED AND ONE. WOUNDED.
The list of casualties in the local Territorial Battalion at the Front to hand this week includes the name of one officer killed and one wounded. The additions to the roll of honour so far are
KILLED IN ACTION. Lieutenant A. Seymour Jones.
DIED OF WOUNDS. Private W. Bridgen.
WOUNDED IN ACTION. Captain H. Gordon Roberts. Private W. Smith. Private H. Huniphries. Private W. R. Cross.

div.head: LIEUT. A. SEYMOUR-JONES. " He Lived, As He pied— A Man."
div.p: LIEUT. A. SEYMOUR-JONES. " He Lived, As He pied— A Man."

On Saturday morning of last week, we regret to state, Lieutenant Arnold Seymour-Jones, of the 4th South Lancashires, and eldest son of .11. Ir. Alfred Seymour-Jones, -of Pendower, Wrex- ham, was, killed in action. •

div.head: SHOT THROUGH TEMPLE.
div.p: SHOT THROUGH TEMPLE.
The sad news was contained in the following letter, sent, from Flanders, to his father, by Lieutenet-Colonel Brereton Faircloogh:—

Dear Sir,-1 regret to have to inform you that your son was wounded this afternoon about 4.15 p.m., dangerously, and that he died almost in about an hour. He was shot through the temple, the bullet passing right through the head and coming out at the other temple; without disfiguring him in any way. Our trenches are within 200 yards of the Germans. The doctor states that he must have been unconccious from the moment he was hit. I have not seen Ma.!or Cary, who was in command of the trench he was in, as he clops not come out till to-morrow night. The trench is unapproachable by day. I have arranged to have him buried in the soldiers' burial ground, in a village about three miles away, as we are right away from anywhere. May I offer you and your family
ICilled in Action.

on behalf of the whole Battalion the most sincere sympathy? He had endeared himself to all ranks,- and I considered him one of my best subaltern officers. Always cheer- ful, always willing, he lived, as he died—a Man.-1 am, sincerely yours, BRERETON FA I RCLO UGH, Lieutenant-Colonel, • 4th South Lancashire Regiment., P.S.—I enclose a list of personal belongings found on him. These will be placed in his valise. The valise will be sent to the base for transmission to England. It is quite possible there may be some delay before it arrives.—B.F. EDUCATION AND SPORT.

-13°rn in May, 1889, the gallant officer was only 25 years of 'age. During his short life, however, he had gained a most creditable repu- tation in the world of education and business: Educated at Wellington College, Salop—where he had a very successful career—and after- wards at Leeds University, he was a B.Sc. (Honours) and M.Sc. (Leeds); and held the Le Blanc medal for technical chemical re- search_in his last year at the University. In addition to success in his studies, he took a keen interest in games. He captained the University hockey team, and also obtained con- siderable prominence in • the "noble art" of boxing.

In the course of time the Officers' ,Training Corps was inaugurated. Promptly joining it, Mr. 'Seymour-Jones attained commissioned rank therein, transferring to the 4th South Lanca- shires on leaving Leeds to take up the position of physical chemist with Messrs: Crosfield. A few years ago he was awarded the Royal Humane Society's certificate, for a gallant attempt to save a girl from drowning at Felin Puleston, near Wrexham. He has two brothers serving, one at the Front since November with the 4th Welsh Fusiliers, and the other with the sth Royal Welsh Fusi- liers.
The deepest sympathy will be extended to Mr. and Mrs. Seymour-Jones in their bereave- ment.

At Warrington the Lieutenant took a pro- minent part not only in the Boy Scout move- ment, but also in furthering the campaign for National Service. He on one occasion spoke on Lord Roberts's platform at the Free Trade Hall, Manchester.
LIEUTENANT SEYMOUR-JONES

div.head: FINE MILITARY CAREER
div.p: FINE MILITARY CAREER

The story of his Army career is a most -ex- emplary and honourable 'one. From 1909 to 1911 he beloriged to the Officers' Training Corps at Leeds University, and for some time acted as quarterfaaster-sergeant. He was 'ultimately gazetted second-lieutenant on the unattached list (Territorial Force) for service with ,the O.T.C. On July 13th, 1912, he joined the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, and en April 18th, 1914, became a lieutenant. He held the Coronation Medal in recognition of the fact that he had formed one of a Territorial eontin- gent 'which was on duty in London on the occasion of the Coronation of King George V. Of the Crosfield Troop of Boy Scouts he was one of the most enthusiastic and energetic pro- moters, and he had held the position of Scout- master ever since its formation. He took a keen personal interest in the lads, and accom- panied them to every camp, sparing no effort to Maintain the high traditions and aspirations of their movement •

CoUrteous, cheerful, considerate and sociable, Lieutenant Seymour-Jones enjoyed the esteem and friendship of a very large circle of War- ringtonians, although his residence in the town was of but a few years' duration. By his death has been created a gap which will not easily or quickly be filled.
DISTINGUISHED CONDUCT MEDAL FOR SOUTH LANCS. CORPORAL.

In a list of distinguished conduct medals awarded to 452 soldiers, appears the name of Corporal J. W. Windsll, of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, who has been decorated for conspicuous gallantry on October, 21st, 1914. During an attack he assisted in withdrawing a gun from a house 400 yards in front of the firing line and subsequently with- drew a 'machine gun under shell fire. On both occasions he acted voluntarily, and has rendered good service throughout the war.

div.head: DIED OF WOUNDS.
div.p: DIED OF WOUNDS.
PRIVATE W. BRIDGEN.
Gallant "Terrier" Who Lost His
Wife Since 'Listing.

News was received on Wednesday morning by Mrs. Bridgen, of 104, Cartwright-street, that her son—Private William Bridgen—one of Warrington's gallant Territorial contingent— had been seriously injured. The news was con- veyed in the following letter, dated March 28th: Dear Mrs. Bridgen,—Your son, Private W. Bridgen, of the 4th South Lancashires, has asked me to write to you for him. I am _ very sorry to say that he has been wounded and is in hospital. If he is well enough he will be ranoved to-morrow Ito the base hospital,, or over to England. He is anxious that you should not worry, but I am sure it would be a mistake to buoy you up with false hopes, as the doctor says his wound is, quite serious. On the other hand his case is by no, means hopeless. He sends you much love, aild especially sends love to his children. I am indeed sorry to be the writer of bad news, and it is hard in a letter to express consolation, but it is a great honour for. you to have had a son wounded for his country, and our God has a loving heart for all who are afflicted and distressed.—l am, yours sincerely, Marshall (chaplain).

div.head: His Most Recent Letter.
div.p: His Most Recent Letter.

A letter of March 22nd, received from Private Bridgen on Tuesday morning, ran:—Dear Mother and Sister,—l wi-ite these - few lines hoping you are keeping in the best of health, as it leaves me at present. I received your letter and parcel yesterday. I am glad that you and the children are comfortable. It makes me feel content to know that they are being looked after. Continuing, he writes: 'I am glad to hear that our Jack got leave to attend my wife's funeral; I thought he would have been out here. ,

div.head: Twice a Widower.
div.p: Twice a Widower.
Private William Bridgen's wife, Mrs. Eliza- )(Alt Bridgen, died of consumption on March

Ist, and he was unable to attend her funeral. She was 36 years of age, amt. was Private Bridgen's second wife. His family of three young children by the second -wife are now left to the care of their grandmother. There are older 'children by the first wife. Private Bridgen, who was an engine-driver on the L. and N.-W. Railway, had , ten • years' military experience befOre joining the Terri- torials in August last. WOUNDS PROVE FATAL.
Dead Warrior Leaves Six Orphaned Children. Yesterday morning Mrs. Bridgen received the following letter:— Dear Mrs. Bridgen,-1 am afraid 1 have

very bad news for you. After rhad written to you your son became rapidly worse and at three o'clock yesterday (Sunday) afternoon, he passed away peacefully. I was able to be with him at the end and to commend his soul to his God and also to take his funeral this afternoon. We have buried him next to other fallen soldiers in a meadow near the church. A little wooden cross is erected with his namo burnt in on it. The soldiers have set flowers on the grave and the place is carefully recorded so that after the war you . may know the spot where he rests. He bore his sufferings more bravely than any I have known. He was thinking much of you and .all his little ones at the end. Let them know as they grow up what a brave father they had. That God will give of His Easter con- salation to you and a happier, fuller life be- yond the grave to him is the earnest wish of yours sincerely, H. Marshall, chaplain. Private Bridgen was buried on Sunday after- noon, exactly a fortnight after his second wife, who was also interred on the Sunday afternoon. The deceased's mother, who is 72 years of age, and suffers from a distressing complaint, is now left with the six little orphan grandchildren to bring up as best she' can. There is a child of 15 months and the eldest is but 14 years of age. Doubtless there are large hearts in War- rington who will see io it that the 'hapless offspring of a heroicjather are properly cared for. This, at least, the town owes to the memory of one of the most gallant of its citizen soldiers.
PRIVATE W. BRIDGEN Died of Wounds.

div.head: PRIVATE T. SMITH.
div.p: PRIVATE T. SMITH.
News Of His Death From Wounds Confirmed.

The news of the death of Private T. Smith, of Church-street, which was recorded in our last issue, has now been officially confirmed. " Only too true !" said his brother, to our repre- sentative, "as you will see from the following letter, which I have received and which is dated March 22nd:—

"Dear Sir,—l any sorry to have to inform you that your brother, Private T. Smith, died from wounds received the same day, the 17th inst. He was a good soldier and is missed by all. You have our deepest sym- pathy in your sad loss.—Yours faithfully, H. GORDON ROBERTS, Captain, Command- ing 'B ' Company, 4th South Lancashire Regiment. " P.S.—He was buried in a little graveyard here on the 18th of March, and a cross has been erected over the grave." A "PAL'S" TRIBUTE.

Private Robert Robinson, a comrade, writ- ing to Mrs. Wrench, of School-brow, says:— "I daresay you will have heard the news about us. I am very sorry to say that Tom Smith, who used to work in David's mill, was killed on St. Patrick's Day. Poor lad I was tipset altogether about it. It will be sad news for someone when they get to know. But, all the same, he served his Bing and country well. It is very hard to part with one of your com- rades, and especially with him. He used to cheer us up in the trenches. Every one has expressed their sympathy. I hopeeDavid will tell the lads in the mill that he was a good soldier—one of the best and brightest. Ile did his duty very well."

div.head: ' WOUNDED.
div.p: ' WOUNDED.
CAPTAIN GORDON ROBERTS SIIOT IN THE LEG.

Captain H. Gordon Roberts, A Company, 4th South Lancashire Regiment, has the somewhat unwelcome distinction of being the first of onr local Territorial officers to be wounded. The news to hand shows that last Friday the officers of several companies.- 44had .4 to. inspect inspect some trenches prior 4to the Battalion taking them over from troops who were to be relieved. On returning from the inspection, and when only: &Jew( minutes',walk from safety, and the bullets were getting few and far between, one of them caught Captain 0. Lyon Whittle, son of the Town Clerk, in the calf, and pierced lug puttee. It only made a slight bruise or burn. The same bullet, however, caught Capt. Gordon Roberts, who was just in front of Capt. Lyon Whittle, above the ankle and went clean through his leg, fortunately missing the bone. Captain Roberts received immediate_qtentibn and was taken by the ambulance to the nearest hospital three miles away,. whence he at once
CAPTAIN H. GORDON ROBERTS. Wounded in Action.

wrote home saying he was going on all right, and that there were not likely to be complica- tions. He is now in hospital at Rouen, pro- gressing favourably. - Capt. Roberts, who has been musketry in- structor to the Battalion for some years, is one of the most active men in the auxiliary. forces of the country. He began his military career
in the Volunteers fourteen years ago, with a second-lieutenant's commission. He is, like his father, Councillor Henry Roberts, an ardent advocate of National Service.

_ Outside military affairs, Captain Roberts is managing director of the Warrington Slate Go. He takes an interest in the Citizens' •Guild of Help. He is chairman of the Stockton Heath District ,of the Knutsford Division Liberal Association, and is one of the youngest, if not the youngest, of the justices of the county of Chester., Some ten years ago he married the only daughter Of the. late Mr. Henry Milling, -And has three children. His home is at Brant- wood, 'Hill eliffe. 4

div.head: PRIVATE WILLIAM SMITIL 0 Shot In Both Thighs, But Is "In The
div.p: PRIVATE WILLIAM SMITIL 0 Shot In Both Thighs, But Is "In The
Pink."

In an undated letter to his parents, Private Williant Smith, whose home ,is at 95, BewseY- road, says—" I have no proper address yet. because I am. on the boat going to Dover. I have been wounded, in both thighs. It was done by a German sniper whilst I was going to the trenches on. Wednesday. I am going on fine and am ',in the pink,' so don't worry, but keep on smiling, as I shall soon be at home." A letter card, dated March 16th, came to hand
PRIVATE W. SMITH Wounded in Action.

before the foregoing letter. It was written from Lincoln Hospital, and says: Just a few lines to tell you I am getting on fine. I sent a letter to you but you must not have got it. I have been wounded in both my legs. lam lucky I was not killed, because I just missed being hit by a bullet in the head and back. Cheer up, I will soon be home again."
DOING FINE AND SOON BE ALL RIGHT.

—lnlnother letter the Titil-an—t private says ""i am 'in the pink.' My legs are doing fine and they will soon be all right again. I am able to smoke in bed and get up after dinner and toddle about a bit. •My left leg is healing up a bit, but my right one has a tidy big hole in it, but I am out of all danger." His most recent letter from hospital bears the date March 24th. In it he says: "I am still doing fine and you have no need to trouble about me. My right leg still has a hole in it. I have had a good ivalk and felt champion after it, but the nurse choked me off' for walking so far. Cheer up!" TWO YEARS A "TERRIER."

Private William Smith is twenty years of age, and has been in the Territorials two years. Before going to the war he was in the employ of IWhiteeross Co., Ltd. As a boy he was a member of St. Paul's Boys' Brigade. He has a brother, Private Thomas Smith, at present in training with the Territorial Reserve Battalion in the South of England.

div.head: Easter Music at AA y (.liffe.
div.p: Easter Music at AA y (.liffe.

The an;U-a-l-Easter services .at the Wycliffe Congregational Church were commenced on Sunday evening, when Stainer's "Crucifixion" was most impressively rendered by the choir. The Rev. T. T. James occupied the pulpit, and Mr. W. H. Payton presided atAhe organ. The soloists (Messrs: H. Hawthorn lind W. Booth) invested their parts with true devotional at- mosphere, whilst the choruses—as well as the hymns—were finely and reverently rendered. Yesterday morning the Pastor conducted the customary qood Friday service, speaking upon' "The Message of the Cross." • With Mr. Payton at the organ. Mr. Booth gave a solo.

Wounded' in Aetion.

'death of his, cousip, Private Reginald Humph- ries, whose death, was recorded in our last issue, he says: I was at the listening post when my cousin got shot. The bullet went through his mouth and his last words were 'I am hit,' and then he dropped dead." Private Harry Humphries is 27 years of age, and was attached to the military police section of the Territorials.
PRIVATE HARRY HUMPHRIES.

div.head: PRIVATE W. R. CROSS SHOT IN THE THIGH.
div.p: PRIVATE W. R. CROSS SHOT IN THE THIGH.

Private W. R. Cross is among the wounded now lying at the Ilkley Hospital, which is situate in the lovely Wharf Dale, Yorkshire. The official news that he had been wounded was received on Friday of last week at his home, 2, Dudley-street, Orford-lane. Private Cross is attached to the "B" Co. of the Warrington (Territorial) Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment. He was first in hospital in Belgium, then in Baillieul and Rouen, subsequently being sent to England, first\ to Leeds and then to Ilkley. While lying in hospital at Leeds he wrote home describing his experiences in the trenches, saying that he had been up to the knees in " slush " and telling how he was left alone in the trench when the company was removed. He adds that he had a singular, but, as it transpired, fortunate experience, walking alone in the dark for nearly two miles beiare he caught up with his comrades, and that he lost his equipment on the way. Hopes to Go Back Again Later On.
He was wounded in the upper part of the
thigh, but is now going on satisfactorily, and hopes to be home again soon and ready to go into the. trenches again later on, if permitted to 'do so.

Private Cross is a single man, 37 years of age. His father, Mr. William Cross, died some time ago, but Mrs. Cross, his mother, still lives at 2, Dudley-street. He was in the old Volunteers before they were merged into the Territorial Force, and altogether has 14 years' service as a citizen soldier ;to his credit. When the Boer War broke out he offered his services, but they were declined. In politics he is a Conservative, and prior to going to the Front he was employed in the Wagon Works Of the Cheshire Lines Company.
PRIVATE W. R. CROSS. Wounded in Action.

div.head: "FAREWELL, DEAR DEAD, FAREWELL!"
div.p: "FAREWELL, DEAR DEAD, FAREWELL!"
A Humble Tribute To Warrington's Fallen.
Farewell, dear dead, farewell !--though far thou sleep, 1 And o'er thy lowly grave we. may not weep; The hearts that love thee in the homeland here Are mourning thee to-day, deep and sincere.
Farewell, brave dead I—thy hands we could
not hold, Or gentle mother on her bosom fold The dear brown head, she pillowed in the years When broken toy had caused the childish tears.

Farewell, dear dead, farewell !—to England's shore, Kinsfolk and friends shall welcome thee no more; On foreign strand, 'mid strangers and un- known, , Thou'll sleep, and take thy rest, till break of dawn.'
Farewell, dear dead !—thou hast answer'd
duty's call; No nobler death than thine, to fight and fall. That England's flag, the flag that freedom gave, Shall ever float afar o'er land and wave.
Farewell, dear dead !—'tis but a little while, And then we, too, shall tread the lone dark
m Ile That leads to Home, re-union 'mid the throng, Then life for evermore one long glad song. M. B. Warrington.

div.head: II MOWS SCIOLL.
div.p: II MOWS SCIOLL.
THE LNIE CORPORAL GEORGE MGHAM.
Tributes To "A Good Man And A Good Soidleo."

Writing in the current issue of the Orford Parish Magaziite, the Vicar (the Rev. G. Vale Ipirein) makes sympathetic reference. to the death of Corporal George Higham, one of the first of the Warrington l'erriteriale to .he of wounds received in action. • t Mr. Vale Owen refers to the deceased Cor- poral as "one we all loved and honoured :n hi 6 life here, as we do now that he has passed on before us. His name will still remain in nut prayer list, for, although his life and work is in another sphere, yet he is still one a us. for Death is no wraith, of visage pale, But waits attendant on our bitrth Out of the darkened womb or earth, To lead us gently through the Veil: To Realms of radiance, broad and free, To Christ and immortality." • "Straightest_ Chum a Man Could_ Have."

Another of the Territorials who belongs to Orford, has' written to the Vicar to say that he has learned the name of the churchyard in which Corporal Higham is buried, and adds: "I will find out his gravt, for I am determined he shall not be amongst -the many 'unknown heroes. I 'can manage French all right, and I expect to get some French people in the dis- trict to rook after the grave. They are only too proud to do these things. In George I have lost a chum whom I considered the straightest chum a man coca have." Another Orforellart at the Front writes to Mr. Vale Owen as follows :—" We were all sorry when we heard of the death of Corporal Higham. He was liked very much by the boys of his sec- tion. He died with a cheerful heart. God bless him .!"

Yet another of the village boys serving with the "Terriers" says: "The death of Corporal Higham upset us all, ,for he was the most re- spected man in our company, because he did not bully the men under him, and ho always had a good word for anyone.

div.head: DECEASED CORPORAL'S BROTHER PROMOTED.
div.p: DECEASED CORPORAL'S BROTHER PROMOTED.

"I was present at his funeral, and it brought tears to all who were there, for he was a good man and a good soldier, and he treated his men just as he liked them to treat him. We can ill afford to lose such men as he. His brother, William, has been promoted to lance-corporal, and he fully deserved the honour."

Still another Orford lad t writes to his Vicar on the same subject "God," he says, "has ,taken one of oar best soldiers into His keeping,. G. Iligham. He will be missed both here and' at home, as he was a good soldier and a good workman. But I. am very glad to say he had a burial service and he rests in a very pretty churchyard here."

div.head: SHOT THROUGH' THE ARM.
div.p: SHOT THROUGH' THE ARM.
One Of The. First Men To Cross To

France In Hospital. Private George Worthington, 22 years of age, of the South Lancashires, who wife and child reside in Stoney-yard, off Bank-street, was on the 20th of' March transferred from the Front to a convalescent home at Shrewsbury. On February 21st he was shot through the right arm and was for some time in No. 3 Stationary Hospital, Rouen. He was subsequently re- moved to England and after being treated in another hospital, was transferred as stated. He was a reserve-man and' was called up im- mediately on the outbreak of war and was one of the first to be sent to. France. His wife, Mrs. Ellen Worthington, received a letter from him on Wednesday, saying that he was going on well. The latest official note stated that he was' suffering from myalgia—a morbid state of muscles. Private G. Worthington was prior to being called up, employed by the Whitecross Co., Ltd.

div.head: SAPPER REGAN KILLED IN ACTION.
div.p: SAPPER REGAN KILLED IN ACTION.

Scion Of A Military. Family. Official intimation has been received at his home, 56, Orford-lane, that Sapper Harry Regan has been killed in action. Details as to how he met his end, barring the fact that the date was March 12th., are not to hand. The official intimation is corroborated—if corroboration were needed—by a service post- card forwarded to the family. By trade Sapper Regan was a printer, and he joined the Royal Engineers about two years ago. When war broke out he was stationed at Chatham and he was, early on, drafted to. France, and had played a part in several engagements before he met his fate.

div.head: Two Brothers at the Front.
div.p: Two Brothers at the Front.

His last message home was contained on a service postcard, dated February 28th. The gallant soldier belonged io a family with mili- tary traditions, and at the present moment two of his brothers are serving with the Expeditionary Force—Private Charles Regan being with the South Lancs., and Private P. Regan with the Scottish Borderers. At the time Sapper Regan enlisted he was accompanied by a friend, Mr. William Henry Perry, who was also desirous of joining the Army, but was not accepted. Instead, he went to Canada. Anxious to return home he hooked his passage on the ill-fated s.s. Empress of Ireland, and went down with her in the Gulf of St: Lawrence in the spring of last year.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.
T,.venty-first Year Clouded By
The War.
The annual meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood Was held on Sunday afternoon, when the Rev. T. T. James presided. _ _
It was reported that the year began with a balance in hand of lIS is. 7d., and finished with one of tli is. 3d.

The Secretary (Mr. B. Farrar), in the course of his annual report, said that the Brotherhood was: grateful and joyful because it had lived through twenty-one years of ser- vice. Their twenty-first year had been one of great experience, trial and disappointment. The cloud that was hanging over Europe, nay, over the world, had affected them very much, between thirty. and forty of the brethren having gone into the Army. Several had participated in the actual fighting and one had been wounded and had again gone back to the firing line—Brother Yeates. Since. the beginning of the war, the attendances at the weekly gather- ings had, been seriously affected. The work of the Brotherhood during the vet year had been of a quiet and plodding nature. They had not only met to pray and to praise, but they had also tried to benefit those around them. As well as by the war, they had been affected by, strikes, which had helped them to see the misery around them. Whilst they took no sides in the disputes between masters and men, their feelings of compassion went out to all who had to undergo privation-and suffering.

div.head: CONTRIBUTIONS TO LOCAL FUNDS.
div.p: CONTRIBUTIONS TO LOCAL FUNDS.

During the year the Brotherhood had con- tributed the following sums to various objects: Mayor's War Fund, £6; the Belgian Distress Fund, £3; the National Institute for the Blind, £1 is.; the' Tanners' Strike Distress Fund, £2; Dr. Barnardo'S Homes, .£1 10s.; Dr. Stephenson's Homes, and the Wycliffe Fund for Christmas Comfort for those members who had volunteered for active service, £2. In the twelve-month just ended 280 prize books were distributed, making a total of 15,300 since the formation of the Brotherhood, an average of 695 per year. They had had good, helpful and happy meetings, and all that was needed was a larwcr membership. NEXT YEAR'S OFFICERS.

The following officers were elected for the ensuing year: President, Rev. T. T. *James; vice-presidents, Messrs. B. Farrar, W. Beswick, H. Osborne, A. Healey, C. Cotton and J. div.head: JOITINGS BY AN OLD JOUKNALIST.
div.p: JOITINGS BY AN OLD JOUKNALIST.

" Wasn't that a Dainty v, The name or a prisoner who was before the Borough Bench last week reminded me of " Mosscrop "—the. cotton grass which grows abundantly on some f t;,e moors in ti,ese northern latitudes, and .s so-e;liliA by the natives. Some of the latter :II an East Lan- cashire town in which 1 spent severai yeats told me that in a former generation local weavers had ingeniously contrived to produce from the yield of the wild growth in question enough material of substantial manufacture to make a handsome waistcoat fit for the reigning sovereign. That was in the, days when George the Third was king. The gar- ment was sent to his. Majesty, who was said to have been delighted with it.

Cricket—Then and Now. The local Cricket and Bowling Club's reso- lution respecting recreation "as usual" caused me to turn up an old copy of "Bailey's Magazine," containing an article the writer of which quaintly reflects that when cricket was first played it was really a game—actually just a game that people played for recreation and mutual amusement. Only fancy, on a fine day our ancestors would make up a game of cricket and repair to sore meadow where " they drave their wickets in." The star bowlers usually selected themselves the actual pitch from personal motives, and incidentally by this proceas avoided any risk of a drawn ganie; whilst the two sticks from each of which for every run a notch was cut to score the game did not always show signs of exces- sive damage when darkness—darkness, mark you, and no 5 or 6 o'clock p.m., or a reflec- tion of our mythir!al sun upon a window— stopped play. Conti net this with modern county cricket. As a journalistic acquaintance once humorously put it, can anyone who is not a high sheriff or one intimately associated with ELM. prisons, think of a more gloomy spec- tacle than a county cricket team breaking covert; infrequent amateurs crawling from one hutch, professionals from a remote but similar bolt-hole, all with an obviously forced air of gaiety and playfulness trifling with the ball that with its successors is to be an instru- ment of so much distress for the more sensi- tive of them daring sederal subsextuenthours ? Having decided upon play "as usual," let our cricketers determine to win matches, weather or no. Let them in obedience to the Marylobone Club defy Law IX. of cricket in order to get a game, and no longer sit for hours with folded hands, slaves of a shower. What Girls Read. - -

This is suggested by last week's Lymm f amp aph, " What wounded warriors read." L recall a contribution which Miss Constance Barnicoat made to a leading magazine a while ago comparing the reading of the colonial girl with that of her English sisters, and it demonstrated that "Edna Lyall " was then an all-round favourite. So, far as Brit- ish girls were concerned, 'other authors ranked in this order: Henry Seton Merriman, R. L. Stevenson, Stanley Weyman, Anthony Hope, F. Marion Crawford, Mrs. Gaskell (nearly always "Cranford "); Lytton, Marie Corelli, and Allen Raine. In the compara- tively brief. interval since that information was obtained, there have been great changes in the tastes and habits of even girl readers. There is an unfortunate tendency to neglect if not positivery to despise the classics, and to prefer simply books of the day, in which sex problems are discussed with a freedom that would have shocked and scandalised the wcmen of a former generation of readers.

div.head: An Expert's Test.
div.p: An Expert's Test.

Dr. Robert Collyer, the famous New York divine (who came from the neighbourhood of Fewston, in Yorkshire, and was baptised by —his parents having also been married by —my - great-grandfather, who was vicar of that parish for upwards of half a cen- tury), truly said: "If when I have read a book about God, it has frit Him farther from me; or about man, that it has Int me farther from him; or about the universe, tlyit it has shaken down upon it a new look of desolation, turning a green field into a wild moor; or about life, and it has made it seem a little less worth living; or if I have read a book about moral principles, and they are not quite so clear and strong as they were when this author began to talk; then I know that on all those five points that, for me, is a- bad book." And so, I Should say, it is for anybody else, even the modern Miss.

Lunacy Question. I have no comment to make en the discus- sion at last week's Guardians' meeting *re- garding the Winwiek Asylum arrangements. The information is insufficient for one to pre- tend to give an opinion on the merits of that particular case. On ,the general subject, how- ever, I may just state that on January 1, 1859, there were 36,762 persons notified as insane in England and Wales, and on January (last year there were 133,157, an increase of 962.2 per cent., while during the same period • the population had only increased 85.8 per rent. The situation is even worse than the figures imply. I remember a case of a sufferer from , neurasthenia who hanged herself in the belief 1 that she had another and an incurable disease. 4She was really on the borderland of insanity, and a doctor who might not have cared to czrtify for her removal to an asylum might 'Lave hesitated just the same to assume the _ _ _ _ _

responsibility of discharging her if they had happened to get her there. On the other band, I ,recalLan instance of a deaf mute who was quite sane being sent to an asylum -in error., That, of course, is a serious matter, and, while magistrates are largely guided by the certifying doctor, they should take the utmost care to satisfy themselves that the alleged insane person is one whom it is abso- lutely necessary to detain. I confess to mis-
Continued in next column. 0
JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST-
continued.

givings about the present system, though I have no doubt whatever as to the bona-fides of the medical authorities anywhere. It has been reasonably enough suggested that we are very urgently in need of greater know- ledge of the subject. Until the doctors know enough to pronounce definitely upon the sanity of any person who may be Submitted to them for examination there must be a most thorny path for the administrator to tread. As things are at present, while I mil- not but suppose that more of ,the inmates•of the lunatic asylums might safely be released, a certain proportion of those now in full en- joyment of • their liberty ought really to be under restraint. Yes, dear sir or madam (as the advertisement circulars have it), doubt- less I lay myself open to smart retort, and of course you are equally entitled to your opinion.

LETTERS should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information not abuse..
