div.head: SANKEY-STREET HOOLIGANS.
div.p: SANKEY-STREET HOOLIGANS.

. , • Sir,—On night recently, at nine o'clock, there was a gang, of young hooligans in Sankey-street, opposite Springfield-street; making night hideous by their squeals and foul language. They Were passing some very uncomplimentary language about everyone that passed, and one respetable citizen of Welsh descent Wp howled at in a scand4lonS manner. "Go to if—, you b— Jew." Re may be of a very dark "com- plexion, but his phyAiogatimy is certainly not Oriental. I consider it a disgrace that such conduct should be allowed in our main public thoroughfares, and an example or two might prove most beneficial.
A TI WE BRITON.

div.head: NEWSBOY SHOUTING NUISANCE.
div.p: NEWSBOY SHOUTING NUISANCE.

Sir,—it is surely time that some action was taken by the authorities to minimise the news- paper shouting nuisance as it prevails at pres- sent, particularly on Sundays. Is there any real reason why on that day there should be continual shouting until 11 p.m.'? It is surely most desirable—nay even necessary—that peace and quietness should be assured the community at least one day in the week, and that people NS not kept' in a -continiiir whirl of excitement. Very often on Sunday evenings the news pub- lished and heralded is of an uniniportant or trivial nature, or what was published the same morning, or even the previous night; and very often, I am afraid, to put it mildly, not quite true:- The last point is not confined to Sundays. As an example: a few nights ago a boy was shouting,,“ Capture of four German cruisers!" I venture to suggest that the reason is to found in the unrestricted competition—the- great number of boys selling papers. I under- stand that those boys only who are authorised by the police should sell papers, and that such boys are to be recognised by a badge worn on the arm. Then why is it that so many are -without badges, and that boys wearing them are the exception, and not the rule? The conse- quence of there being so many selling papers on the streets is that shopkeepers who are so heavily rated, and cripples who cannot get a living otherwise, are subjected to a most unjust competition _ _

Again! Why should boys be shouting and hawking papers about the streets until 11 p.m., and not only so, but lately they have commenced before six o'clock in the morning? This is surely beyond,all reason, and the early morning business is a matter which employers would do well to take note of. A newspaper in the pocket of a workman is no asset to a master. Referring to the evening papers, those issued at six or seven o'clock usually, contain the news of the day, and anything important coming out after such are printed is sure to appear in detail the following morning. Another point for consideration is that there are boys and youths selling papers during the day„ who, considering the scarcity of labour at present, should_ be engaged at far better em- ployment. The betting evil is quite had enough, and its 'indirect propagation by allowing bet- ting papers to be thrust at people at every hour in the streets and at works' gates is a matter which demands stern action.

I must protest that I have no desire to pre- vent the sale of newspapers, neither week-days nor Sundays. What I do strongly protest against is the exploiting of the peace and in- terests of the town for the mere purpose of paper selling. People have a perfect right to buy and read papers, but there are ways of procur- ing the same by other means than of the pre- vailing and growing nuisance. It would be a boon, or, at least, it would be no disadvantage to the town generally, if the heralding in the streets were stopped altogether, but as this might be considered to be too drastic, I ven- ture to suggest :--

1. That Sunday shouting be prohibited.‘ 2. That shouting on week-days cease at 8 p.m. 3. That boys selling papers, and who are. not authorised to do so should-be rigorously prosecuted. 4. That boys and youths who are able to work should not be allowed to sell papers.

I trust that those of your 'readers who agree with my sentiments will write and express their views to you, and so promote healthy agitation which will prevail upon the Watch Committee to take strong action.
JOHN RIcHARDSON. 86, Buttermarket-street, Warrington.

Scouts and Good Friday.—Yesterday the ileatley troop of Boy Scouts attended morning service at the Oughtington Parish Church. Another Red Cross Resignation.—Miss Nichol- son has this week tendered her‘ resignation of the position of nurse at the Lyinm Ped Cross .Hospital.
Lymm Longevity.—The four deaths recorded in the April Parish Magazine show that the :.verage age attained was 65 years. Reports of Lil the deaths have already appeared in The Examiner:' •

--Nine Wounded Men at " Brookfield,r —Two more recovered " ToMmies "—Private' w Cohen. and Stowell (Leicestershires) Jeft the Red Cross frospital on Wednesday. There are now 'nine' wounded recuperating there. '— Coke Dearer.—lt has been decided by the Jrban District Connell, acting on a. recotn, aendation of the Gas Committee, to increase the price of coke, as- from April Ist, from Us. Bcf. to 13s. per ton. "Somewhat Denuded:'—"Our Y.aster services," ,ays the Rector, "will be somewhat denuded ..3y :the double fact that school holidays,tici not oegin till the middle of April. and many of the vounger men are away on active service." The Fifth Cheshires at Ole Front.-3,10ng :etter, by an officer in the sth Chebhiretti, giving experiences of ;the local -,Territorials oU arrivalin France, appears in °Ur war stories under the heading "Gigantic Firework Dis- play."

Forthcoming Football:—On the Pepper-street ground. theiLymm. Wednesday hope to play, the Manchester Post. Office. on Wednest.laY. Twice\before they have met them this season, winning. At home (4-0); and drawing at Man- chester (1 goal apiece). . • Street Lamps Damaged.—A dikussion arose at Monday night's meeting of the Council on a proposition to rescind a- resolution of the Council to prosecute • certain boys for having broken street lamps.—lt .was contended that the better Way would be to bring the lads be- fore the Council instead of taking them before the magistrates, and after discussion ,it was decided to have the offenders before the Coun- cil and reprimand them.

Allotment Land.—lt was reported to the Urban District Council at their meeting on Monday night that at a meeting of the Sani- tary Committee held on March 22nd it was de- cided that land near the Sow Brook Sewage Farm be bought for allotment purposes. The land in question is at present in the occupa- tion of Mr., W. H. Winstanley, and it was stated that it would be "seeded down" by him, and that no charge for labour would be made.

Altering A Road.—Arising out of a minute presented by the Roads Committee at the monthly meeting of the Urban District Coun- cil on Monday evening was a letter from Mr. Segar Owen, 'arehitect, of :-,:Warrington,(.- who wrote on behalf of the Development company with reference to the proposed widening of the footpath in the New-road.—The Clerk was in- structed to ask for a sketch of the alterations proposed. "Thank You, Mr. Chairman!"—Monday night's being the last meeting of the, Ufban District Council for the official year, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman tMr. T. H. Warburton) for his services during, the past year.—lt was proposed by Mr. Groves, was seconded by Mr. Gotobed.. was supported) by Mr. Cowper and was carried unanimously.—; A similar compliment was accorded the Vice-, Chairman air. F. .Lockyer).—Both votes -were suitably acknowledged by the -recipients. Rolling the Roads.—At Monday night's meet- ing of the Urban District Council it was re- ported that the Lancashire, Road Roller -.Co. had written in reply to a letter from the Sur- veyor stating that the hire of any weight of roller from 41- to 15 tons, including fuel, water— cart, driver and flagman, would be 21s. 6d. per day. They added that they had recently added to their plant one of the latest Aveling and Porter types of tar macadam rollers. The Roads Committee decided to recommend that the tender .be accepted and the Council ac- quiesced in that recommendation.

Present at • the Council Meeting.—At the Monthly meeting of the Urban District coun- cil held on Monday evening there were pre- sent: Mr. T. H. Warburton (in the chair), and Messrs. A. Mclntyre, R. H. Gotobed, G. 11. Parker, Fred Lockyer, W. G. Groves, C. E. Cowper, F. Ingham aud S. Critchley; with Mr.W. Mullard (clerk and collector), Messrs.W. Timperley, and: Cecil 'Mort (assistant clerks), Dr. de Jong .(medical officer), Mr. D. Mort (surveyor), Mr. T. H. West (gas manager), and Mr. C. T. Barnes- (water manager).

Rector's Son and New Font.—ln his monthly letter in the April Lymm Magazine, the Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston) says: "I cannot close without expressing here my great joy that our little son was born at the Rectory, where I have spent so many happy years. It is an event for the dear old house, which has not been so similarly favoured for close upon sixty years. The new font will be placed in the church directly after Easter and I hope to have the pleasure, with the consent of the kind anonymous donor, of christening the font by baptisixt my own little son in it. My wife and I are very grateful for all the kind, good wishes we have received; we deeply appreciate them."

Infants' Opinions ,of Kaiser.—ln the ,April Parish Magazine appear the following wisdom whiffs fromi the pens of the Lymm infants:— "The Kaiser as got a black hat with a 'pont on is hat, and he is the King of Germany." "The Kiser has two wiskers sticing up like two nales and he doesn't want us to win and he isnt a :nice man becors he is a German and he is a very wicked man." I think the Kiser will dye when he gets an old man and then he cant kill the Eritish." "The Kaiser is a bad man and we wont give up if. we do he can get in England." "The Kiser?) wiskers turn up and he is at the war." "The Kaiser is bad and he is a. German and he wont give .up and he is funny." "The Kiser Is not going to win and he is a nasty man." "I dent like the Kiser and he is trying to win and he-cant Win."

Congregational Gatherings.—The Lymm Con- gregational Church anniversary was celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev. W. D. Thomas, of Broadheath, occupied 'the pulpit, preaching to very fair congregations. The title of the address in the evening was "Follow-Me;'-We understand that the collections proved highly satisfactory.—On Monday the annual tea-party was held in the ,schoolroom, under the presi- dency of Mesdames .Bladen. 'Brearley, Cook, C. Lewis, Miller and Smith; Miss Forrest, the Misses Hesketh -and other ladies,. 'Afterwards the Rev. T. A. Penaliggon presided.-whilst Mr. S. Lamb (of Bowden, who has travelled con- siderably in Germany) discoursed most in- terestingly on "The War: Its Causes and Results." A cordial vote' of, thanks to Mr. Lamb was carried on the proposition of Messrs. Hardy Holt and W. Bladen. During the evening the choir sang a number of glees, Mr. A. Leather accompanying.

Neuve Chapelle Rumours.—ln the course of a letter from the Front to the Rector, Sergeant H. Clare refers to the action at Neuve Chapelle. "I was so sorry" he says " to learn of those rumours that had been circulated concerning us, and I am sure it was comforting to all our men's mothers, fathers and wives when they read your letter in t4e magazine. The news I send has been and continues to be, of the very best; I am pleased to say we are all enjoying good health just now; about a dozen. of our men have been a little seedy for a few days, but all are quite well now. We took part in a very big attack the day I received -ycitir letter; it was very successful and the lads behaved Splendidly under very heavy shell fire, not one of us was hit, undoubtedly the prayers offered for us were answered: When we reached our billets at midnight we Lyrum men held'n thanksgiving service and thanked God for His mercies to- wards us. I feel sure you will be glad to know we often hold a service, ,and Tthough sometimes dead tired, how refreshing it is. Private

loinley, takes a leading part, and we all have small Prayer and Hymn books. You will be sorry to hear that the room where we held our church parade has been struck and shattered by shells, in fact this village, like a good many more in Belgium, is ruined. This is a lovely spring Sunday, the birds are singing as I write, and the air is quite warm. Whilst lam writing you are holding the beautiful morning service; I am thinking so mach of you all."

Level Crossings..7--A • letter from, the London And.'North-Western Railway, Company, placed, before the Council at their meeting on Monday, regretted that the regulations for train-Working did not permit of the corapany keeping the gates across.the railway at Statham. They had (the Company, wrote) never, at any, time re- Ceived complaints from, people, • owing to the fact that a man was on duty all day. The detention of road 'passengers was of. short duration unless a train was approach,ing.— After a discussion a letter was ordered to be sent to the Railway Company saying that un- less the wishes of the Council were acceded to an appeal would be made to the Board of Trade.

Church Inn Licence Transferred.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions on Monday, Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, Warrington, applied for the transfer of the licerke of the Church Inn, Lymm, from Mr. William Allman to Mr, Tom F. Green.—Mr. Steel said that Mr. Green had
had charge of The Grange, Hartford (the home of some Belgian‘ refugees), and was highly spoken of by the residents in that district. He

, had served several years in the 15th Hussars, and resigned in 1913 with the rank Of sergeant- major, his character sheet being marked "excel- lent." Mr. Allman's wife .had died suddenly, and that was the only reason for his desiring to give up the liouse.—There was no objection by the police, and the transfer. was granted.

Lymm Prisoners In Germany.—Private Massey, who served at Mons with the Ist Che- shires, writes to Mr. F. E. Evans from Lager 2, Barracke 68, Soltau, Province Qf Hanover, Ger- many, to say that he is quite well. . "Ted Woriall," he continues, "is also here a pri- soner-of-war. I ~ttm pleased to hear that Sam Lewis -got away from Mons. . . They will let you send small parcels, with cigarettes, tobacco, &ea If you send any put them in a strong box."—This letter is in reply to one which Mr,: Evans sent to Private Massey. Pre- viously Mr. Evans had sent five communications to the • private, hut apparently only one, sent several months ago, yet was received by him. The reply quoted was written on Jani,ary 11th and came to Lymm on .Tuesday afternoon.'

Funeral of the Late .Mr. J. E. Joynson.—The Rector conducted, at the Parish Church on Monday afternoon, the funeral of the lath Mr. J. E. Joynson, of Pepper-street• Lyram. (whose death was reported in our last issue). A ser- vice having been held in the- Church, a large number of friends and acquaintances of the deceased gentleman gathered. at the graveside to pay their last tribute,of -respect. to him. 'The *toffin was borne ,by. four of the deceased's _ _ _

fellow-postmen Messrs : Knowles, Robinson, Davies and -Platt. The Postmaster (Mr. J. Arnell) and Mr. A. Sutton also attended, to- gether with six bellringeis, .who afterwards rang a mated peal. The principal mourners were the widow and eldest daughter, Messrs. filbert and Thomas Wright (brothers-in-law), and their wives; Mr. and Mrs. N. Seymour (brother-in-law and sister), Mr. and Mrs. Light- foot (brother-and-sister-in-laW) and Mrs. Dingle (of Bowdon).—Several beautiful wreaths were laid on the grave, including those from the widow and children, Mr. and Mrs. G. Wright, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Wright, Mr. and Mrs. Holt, Mrs. Dingle, the Post Office Staff, and the neighbours.

div.head: lIELP IN HOME DEFENCE! Judge Spencer Hogg Addresses Drill
div.p: lIELP IN HOME DEFENCE! Judge Spencer Hogg Addresses Drill
Hall Meeting
CALLED BY COUNCIL.

The Volunteer Defence Corps is the third and last line of defence. And therefore until we come to that bad day when the first and second lines must have assistance it will not be called* upon for active service. But if and when the Volunteer Defence Corps is called upon and is found deficient either in numbers or quality, then defeat for England Is assured—and the only thing we can then do is to make peace in the best way we can.

These words formed part of the powerful appeal for Cheshire Volunteers which was made by Judge Spencer Hogg at the Lymm Drill Flail on Tuesday evening. As announced in our laSt issue, the public meeting had been called by the Urban District Council, at the request of the Lymm Volunteer Training Corps Council.

Councillor T. H. Warburton (chairman of the Urban Council) presided over a good assembly, and there were also upon the plat- form: His Honour Judge Spencer Hogg; Coun- cillors C. Cowper, S. Critchley, R. H. Gotobed, W. G. Groves, F. Ingham and G. H. Parker; Messrs. W. Mullard (clerk to. the Council), G. Williamson, W. Molesworth, A. de C. Parmiter and A. Watkin; the Rev. E. E. Lovell and Captain Hawkins.

div.head: UNRECOGNISED RESPONSIBILITY.
div.p: UNRECOGNISED RESPONSIBILITY.

Mr. MuHard having read messages of apology for non-attendance from Messrs. A. S. Bleckly, J. Coxon and W. Peter Rylands, The ,Chairman proceeded to explain the ob- jects of the meeting. They had had a com.- pany formed in that district, he said, and the meeting was to form a- new corps for the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment. When new regu- lations came along they did not appear to recognise the meaning or responsibility of the thing, and the strength of the corps dropped. Now, in a place like Lymm, would it not be a disgrace if they could not form a company? Just think of the-lads who had gone away, and of their example! He himself, as a lad had paced that room times without number, as one of what were called "The Saturday Night Soldiers." They were now' called upon to shoulder rifles, so that if invasion did come they would be pre- pared to take their part in the country's defence. If they were trained they could be called at once and say "We are ready !" And they could take up arms and meet the enemy as their lads were doing now. (Applause.) "Gentlemen," concluded the speaker, "it behoves you as much as you can to push this thing forward! You have splendid opportuni- ties and leaders--applause)----you can be taught, and feel when you have gone through your drill that you know all a soldier requires to know to face the enemy if he comes along." Applause. )

div.head: WHO MAY JOIN.
div.p: WHO MAY JOIN.

Mr. MuHard then read the letter received some months ago from the War Office, in which were stated all the regulations 'neces- sary- for the obtaining of official recognition. Amongst 'these was one to the effect that only those would be allowed to join who were certi- fied unable to serve in the 'Regular or Terri- torial Armies. Another said that no arms, ammunition, or uniform would be supplied from public sources, whilst a third stated that acceptance of the ordinary military ranks, titles, or uniforms would no be allowed; and that they must provide their own officers.

div.head: LET 'TOMMY" GO ABROAD.
div.p: LET 'TOMMY" GO ABROAD.

Judge Spencer Hogg, on rising to address the meeting, was enthusiastically received. The reason for the existence of Ole corps; he said, was obviously Defence. There were several possible duties which members might be called upon to do. If it was desirable for some mili- tary reason that the trenches on the East Coast—which were now filled by men who were better able to fight than they—should be re- filled, or if for military reasons it was abso- lutely mcessary that men who were now in this country, and who were, better able to fight than they, should be at once drafted out to the fighting area, then they might be called upon—and be hoped they -would respond—to
ill those empty trenches and to do that patrol ;cork, or otherwise, which, would under ordin- Lry circumstances have been done by those non who had gone to take their place in the trenches.

div.head: Attitude of War Office.
div.p: Attitude of War Office.

The attitude of the _War Office towards tle 30r1)s had 'aliriost completely changed. (Ap-' olause.) His Majesty the King had himself thown the utmost interest in it. And there- ...ore they must not assume the somewhat cold letter, written some months before, repre- iented the view of the War Office on the corps to-day. In fact, the ,corps had been used 'Already, having in' the ~South .'done'' valuable work in relieving those men—who would other- wise have had to stop in this country—to go to the Front.

'The Lymm section would be in the Altrinc- ham Parliamentary Division, which extended right up tO Stockport. The business was man- aged by a committee, of which. Messrs War- burton_ and Williamson were members—so, that Lymm's interests would be well looked after.

div.head: Rifle Ranges and Transports.
div.p: Rifle Ranges and Transports.

Then tlwy were arran,gin. g for suitable rifle ranges; and also for motler car transports; so that when, it became necessary or advisable they could join other sections and be enabled to drill better. The question arose: Are the corps _wanted? .Yes, they were!. Every man Was wanted: the War Office corroborated it. The Germans were not heart-beaten—we had not started attacking them yet, or got half of our men at the Front. Others said we should beat the enemy. Aye, and we should beat them; but it would only be when every man put his hand to the plough. (Hear, hear, and applause.) _Again, Some said invasion might have come three months age, but was impos- sible now. Nothing was impossible in war!. A moment's hesitation or doubt on the part of the Generals—who, after all, were only human —might lend itself .to great catastrophes. And could,' it be doubted that the Germans would take the very 4rst opportunity of, invading England? . .

div.head: " Excessive Modesty."
div.p: " Excessive Modesty."

This was not a recruiting speech. To people with feelings of patriotism and decency such would be an insult., and if they had neither one wasted tithe talking to them,. but there was a certain excessive modesty on the part of some of the older men, who said: "Oh, I couldn't do anything." That was the Wrong view. They ought to say: "Oh, lam only an old Crock; but they malt- find me something to do, and I'll do my best." ' _ _
lie hoped that if be ever again had the good fortune to address them, he might do so not by the name of "Gentlemen," but 1)y the far better name "Fellow Comrades!' (Loud aP- plause.)

div.head: FUNDS NEEDED.
div.p: FUNDS NEEDED.

Mr. Williamson made a strong financial áp- peal. If a Inan could not provide his own uniform,. he stated, generous assistance would be given. The cost of outfitting a man with rifle, &c., ready for the field was a matter of and the man himself could not be ex- pected to bear all that. The matter would be gone into by a special committee, and an impartial appeal to the Lymm public made at a later date. If a man's uniform was pro- v;ded for 'him he himself must contribute 10s. by instalments,. and it would become his own when he had put in forty drills-and passed at least in the 2nd class on a miniature rifle range. Uniform con.sisted of tunic,- breeches, puttees,, cap; and badge' (the last provided by the regiment). lie thought the Lymm district might • raise . tWo Platoons—sixty men. (Ap- plause.) 4 - HELP FOR THE 130*S. ,

The Chairman: then proposed" the following: "That thisAnteting approve or: the object of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment, and agrees to support the same in every way in their power," Councillor-Cowper,..in seconding said-it mw4t. be in the heart of every man to stand with the Allies at the.•tresent time. They were not, too old—they should be 4' as old as they felt"—(laughter and applause)—and they had not half so many-men us they ought to have. The men •in the trenches were fighting for them without a murmur. And_they were asked to conic, forward and let them go. Surely they would do so if they were Englishmen—help their own boys! (Loud applause.) The resolution was unanimously and heartily carried. -. COMMITTEE ELECTED.
The following committee was then clected:— Lymm : Messrs. A. Watkin, Molesworth, Cowper and Farrar. Heatley : Messrs. A. Crompton and Fred Willis.
Broomedge: Messrs. Gavon, Cook and Land- lass.
Oughtrington : Messrs. W. Perry and Fred Tomason.
Thelwall : Messrs. James Hampton and Arthur Bleckly. .Warburton: Messrs. Wood and J. R.. Newton. Mr. Frankland Garside was chosen as secre- tary, and Mr. John Thomason as treasurer, amidst applause.

GOViERNMENT SUPPLY NOTHING. A number of questions were asked in con- nection with the work and equipment of the corps. One gentleman having inquired if the Government would..s.upply the'..drill.'sergeants, Mr. Williamson replied that the Govern- ment would supply nothing. They would have to provide their own. Councillor Gotobed moved a vote of cordial thanks to the speakers. It was about thirty years, he added, since he first shouldered a rifle, but he could see in the near future the prospect of renewing his acquaintance with an old friend. Lymm had done royally with its young men, and the few who were left he hoped would •soon make up their minds to go. Let them help in every way possible, and have a strong detachment ready to do its duty to their native land--bne which would be a credit to Lymm.

Councillor Groves, seconded. As another old "Saturday Night Soldier" he hoped all who could would join the ranks. The motion . having been carried, Judge Spencer Hogg suitably replied; after which the Chairman's services were appreciated on the motion of Messrs. Williamson and Watkin. The National Anthem concluded the meeting,
HIS LIFE-STORY:

"The Examiner" representative, having been the first to break the news to Mrs. Taylor, was informed that the wounded soldier will be 21 in seven weeks. He is unmarried. As a boy he attended the village school under the head- mastership of Mr. Richard Oddie, and at the age of 14 he went to work at Statham as a file-cutter for Mr. W. Moss. After six years, however, his health began to fail. On the advice at Dr. de Jong he then took up outdoor work, joining his brother (Mr. Henry Brooks) as a gardener, in the employ of Mr. Champ, at Foxley Rouse, Broomedge. Four months after, however, the call of King and country came, and he enlisted in the Territorials. At the August mobilisation he went into camp at Aberystwyth, and, after a fortnight, to Chester, thence to Cambridge, Nortitssmptou, Stow- market, Northampton again, and via Cam- bridge to the Front.

div.head: MAKING LADIES AND GENTLEMEN
div.p: MAKING LADIES AND GENTLEMEN
OF THEM.
Are The Workers' Children Over- Taught?

At Monday's meeting of the Urban District Council, Mr. Cowper had some caustic. remarks to offer concerning modern education. He had, he said, *ever found out yet what the children of to-day were taught, and he opined that millions of money, were being thrown away in teaching the workers' children to be ladies and gentlemen—taught to develop such an inflated opinion of themselves that if one asked one of them to carry a parcel they looked at one as if they were going to eat him.—The Chairman's remarks were /suggested by a circular letter from the Hale Urban District Council, which stated that that 'body had recently had under consideration the question of. the cost of educa- tion in Cheshire, and they were somewhat alarmed at the constantly increasing demand of the Council for purposes of education.

div.head: How Education Touches the Ratepayers' Pockets.
div.p: How Education Touches the Ratepayers' Pockets.

The cost of education was included and col- lected in the poor rate, and in the Hale district alone the poor rate had more than doubled itself during the last ten or eleven years, and a pro- spective increase was now threatened. The in- crease was due principally to the increase in the cost of education, which in 1903 stood at 4d. in the £ and was now is. 4d. Every ratepayer was not au fait with the principles of rating, and where the district poor rates ' were collected together, as was the practice in the Hale dis- trict, ratepayers were inclined to cast reflections on the District Council when they were called upon to pay more rates than was previously demanded, consequently upon an increase in the poor rate for educational purposes. This gradual increase in the poor rate hampered urban and rural councils in the administration of their duties under the Public Health Acts. In abnormal times such as the country was now passing through, the Hale Council thought that education authorities should exercise the greatest economy, and with this 'end in view they suggested that some•united action should be taken in making representation to the County Council on the matter. On the proposition of Mr. Gotobed, seconded by Mr. Cowper, the Council agreed to join in a representation to the County Council on. the matter.
PRIVATE JAMES TAYLOR.

div.head: Family of Fighters.
div.p: Family of Fighters.

Thus the gallant- private has been serving in the war-zone for about two months. His brother, Private .Hen.ry Brooks, also belongs to the sth Cheshires,.and is now at the Front; whilst his father (in peace times a fustian- cutter) is with the 9th South tancashires in the South. Private Taylor, sen., also rendered his country service during the Boer War.
"They'll Pop at _Me!"

Several of Private J. Taylor's letters have been published from time to time in our columns. Upon being told to "take care" as he went away, he laughingly replied: "Oh, if I get the chance of having a 'pop' at the Germans I shall have a ' pop'—and I daresay they will have a 'pop' at me!"

div.head: WHERE "TERRIERS" ARE NOW. In Beautiful Village ,Unhit By, German Shells.
div.p: WHERE "TERRIERS" ARE NOW. In Beautiful Village ,Unhit By, German Shells.
MOST CHEERFUL LOT.

Sergeant R. Clare's word home' says: "We had another man, I am sorry to say, wounded—. in the back. Re comes from. Birkenhead. Ho will soon be all right. 4. . ' . I am enjoying' the best of health. The village from which. I am writing is about five miles from the village I told you of in ray last letter. It is indeed a grand sight to see all the buildings intact; not one has been hit by the German shells, and it is a lovely spot. '

div.head: Marvellous Spirits.
div.p: Marvellous Spirits.

• "We are living in a house opposite a church, and it was a treat this morning to hear the bells ringing—so much like being at home. "I am glad to say the health of all our men continues to be very good, and a more cheerful' set you could not possibly find. Their spirits are marvellous, and they face danger as true Britons can.
"One of our men—from Latchford [Private J. Watson]—unfortunately met with an acci- dent whilst cleaning his rifle. He shot himself in the foot."

div.head: Wrlll MACHINE-GUNNERS. Lymm " Tommies" Dare Not Move
div.p: Wrlll MACHINE-GUNNERS. Lymm " Tommies" Dare Not Move
During Daytime.

"By the way, do not send any more cigar- ettes—as we get plenty. My mess-tin is full of them now!" writes Private S. Gibbs in a letter received at 'Henry-street two days ago. "The thing we like here is chocolate; I should be very pleased to have some from you. . . . It is a lovely day, and we are having an easy time .of it just now. What is the English opinion of the war? Around here they seem to think it will finish very soon. I hope so. . .

div.head: Hundred Hymn-books.
div.p: Hundred Hymn-books.

"Mr. Linley (of Pepper-street) has sent to Lymm for a hundred hymn-books, as we have a service every Sunday night in our billet." "Jeff. Watson," he adds, "had an accident with his rifle yesterday, and got shot through the foot. . .

Writing on March 25th, Private Gibbs said: "You will be surprised to hear that (Privates Percy (Clare) and I have moved about eight mites away, and are billeted with the machine-gunners. We dare not move in the daytime, as we are so near the firing. line, and we have to wait till night so as to get a wash, &c. We dare not have a fire at any cost, so we look like roughing it a little. • • •
"We can go down the village at night for a few oddments," he adds. "This last fortnight Percy' and I have not. seen the trenches, as .we .are going under instruction for range-finding.

div.head: Little Rain.
div.p: A Little Rain.
"By the way, the Scotchmen are in these parts in their kilties, oui, oui! , Half of our men are in the trenches now. We are having sbme rain to-day."

div.head: LUCKY LYMM LADS.
div.p: LUCKY LYMM LADS.
Quite Used To Terrors 01 War-Zone.

Private J. Clare writes home to Booth's Bill :—" The Lyzum lads 'are in the best of health and quite happy. . . Things are very. quiet, save when we are in the trenches. I "expect the lads round Lymm are getting very few. I was surprised to hear that Harry Daniels had gone {Mr. Daniels has joined the Artillery], but he has gone to a nice place..." A Luxury.
In a note to Mr. D. Daniels the gallant private says :—" I must thank you very much for the cake. It WaS quite a change, for I had

never tasted any since we left Old England. Well, I am all right and in good health. We are doing very well out here, and have got used to hearing the guns and seeing shells burst. But the sooner it is all over, the better; and we must do our best!

am hoping to see you all again before long. We have had a, few :easuoltiekin .our, battalion, but the Lymni lade. havo beeehicky• . . . . It is getting better weather now, so that will make things better for us. Remem- ber me to all."
TRADESMEN AND WAR BONUSES.
Association Protests To Council That Time Is Inopportune.
That all employes:Ad the Council, not including officials, have an increase of wages of 2s. per week during the continuance of the increased prices of provisions.

• Over this proposal of Councillor tockyer's. some discussion arose at the ,meeting of the Urban District Council on Monday evening. and against it a protest was lodged by the Ideal Tradesmen's Association. Representatives of the Association have since availed themselves of the opportunity offered by "The Examiner "of explaining their attitude.

div.head: Increased Cost of Living.
div.p: Increased Cost of Living.

. In moving the resolUtion at the Council meet jug, Councillor Lockyer referred to the sacrifices —owing to the increased cost of living—now being made by the employes. Therefore, he said, it was fair that some consideration should be shown to them; the amount named was reasonable. Councillor ..Parker seconded.

div.head: Councillor's Vigorous Proted.
div.p: Councillor's Vigorous Proted.

Councillor Cpwper vigorously protqsted against th'e motion. The men, he urged, were well paid, and other ratepayers were suffering quite as much from the increased price of pro- visions as the Council employes. The Council were treating their men magnificently. He did not suppose there was any man who had suffered more than he had; he had suffered in thousands, not pennies. They would have to put 6d, on the rates, if not Bd. or 10d., if that sort of thing went on. He therefore strongly' objected to the increase.. Councillor Gotobed moved an amendment: That the matter be referred for consideration to therGeneralsTurposes-..Committee, as the mem- bers of, the Council had no intkmation that the matter would be introduced until the receipt 01 the agenda. .(Hear, hear.) Councillor Ingham seconded.

Another Objection. The Chairman informed the meeting that upon entering tb,e room that evening he had re- ceived a letter from "the Tradesmen's Associa- tion, protesting against the gran,ting of a scar bonus. The letter (which was signed by the President, Secretary, and twelve other mem- bers) pointed out that the present was not an opportune time for any increase of Council ex- 1 penses, and expressed the hope that "nothing would be decided without a full inquiry at a ratepayersr' meeting." 'I think," added Coun- cillor Warburton, "that the matter should be referred to the General Purposes Committee." The amendment was then carried.

div.head: TRADESMEN INTERUENVED.
div.p: TRADESMEN INTERUENVED.

Interviewed by "The Examiner" representa- tive, a member of the Tradesmen's Association explained that the half-pay now being given tO Council employes who had enlisted put an extra penny on the rates„ and, if the WO:r. bonus Pr°- posal was Carried it would further increaie the rates by twopence. It must also be remembered that the gas and Water bill for the Red Cross Hospital (about,P-45) fell on the rates, and the same applied to the Belgian Refugees' Home. The bulk of the rates, he continued, vr4re paid by the tradesmen; and at a time when trade was so "hard hit" economy in the rates was therefore alnaost essential--especialy when si' many appeals were regularly issued on behalf of war charities. Moreover, the workers proposed to be benefited

had never asked for the bonus. PADGATE• Wesley Guild.—The closing social of the session in connection with the Wesley Guild was held on Monday evening, the programree being provided by members of the Leigh Wesley Guild. The entertainment took the form of an old English fair, the members being dressed to represent the styles of bygone years. Old part-songs such as "John Peel," "0, Who will, O'er the Downs so Free f" and "Cherry Ripe" were given, and the duet "'Where are you going to my pretty maid?" was also sweetly rendered. Old English games were played at intervals, the gathering concluding :with an amusing sketch entitled " Majesty's Mails." The Rev. A. J. Morton pre- sided; and the. usual votes of thanks were moved by Mr. Duckworth and tit.. Plinston, Mr. Birchall replying on behalf of the Leigh mem- bers.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

Successful Lecture.—ln the Wesleyan School'. room on Monday evening, the Rev. E. J. Galva(' gave an exceedingly vivid description of the Passion Play as he saw it Performed at 01)!1, Ammergau. The collection, which was in ala of the church fund, amounted to about EN:" Mrs. C. E. Parker was in the chair.

£55 Raised at Anniversary Services.—On Sun- day the Penketh Wesleyan Church held their anniversary services,- the preacher for the day being the Rev. E. J. Gawne, a former minister. In the afternoon a cantata entitled "The. Good Shepherd," by T. Mee Pattison• was rendered' by the choir and was thoroughlY appreciated by the congregation, who were present in full force. Mr. Frank Aickman, the organist of the Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel!, Warrington, presided. The anthem in tbe. evening was "At Even ere the Sun was Set.' The collections for the day amounted to .255 155., and were ,set aside to reduce a deficit of £lOO in tile chapel funds.

Nearly Forty Years in the Same Employ.-- On Wednesday afternoon the remains of the late Mr. John Henry Brooks, of Warrington - road, were interred in Sankey Cemetery. The deceased, who was a well-known resident, had lived in this district for some ;.ears, having charge of Messrs. Hayward and •Tomlinson' works at Fiddler's Ferry. He had been in the same employ.for 38 years. Born in Lincoln citY 55 years ago, he passed away after a short' ill- ness. His fellow employes made a special point of following him to his last resting place, four of them acting as bearers, viz., Messrs. Appleton, Ireland, Goodman and Wheeler. Mr. Hayward, jun., represented the firm, being accompanied by Mr. Frank Ward (the de- ceased's co-worker' at Fiddler'.s Ferry). Wreaths were received from “The Firm," Mr. F. Ward, Mr. G.- Kirkham, and Membefs of the FamilY•

April Fool. An American authority, answering the ques- tion—Why does the custom of fooling peOPle prevail on April 1? says :-7-The origin of the custom is • unknown. Some people have attri' bated it to the fact that :the weather during the month of 'April is uncertain and fools the PoPIe and that it is well to accustom :peoPle to getting fooled by generally starting the fooling on the first day of the month. .

div.head: MEMBER'S SUGGESTION.
div.p: MEMBER'S SUGGESTION.

Cenncillor Henry Roberts war unaniincusly re-elected chairman of the Warrington Ecluca- Illn CGmmittee. at the annual meeting of that ,u.'d3r, held in the Town Hall on Monday even- A.t the same time members 'A)ok the oPPortunity of publicly expressing to him their qmpathy with his gallant son—Captain H. Gordon Roberts—who, that day it had been l,earned, had been wounded whilst serving in the fighting line with the Warrington Terri- torials. CHAIRMAN SHOULD BE A REPRESENTA- TIVE MEMBER. The re-election was proposed in felicitous terms by Mr. E. Plinston. It afforded him he said, the very greatest pleasure to propose that Councilor Robert be 're-appointed to the chair for a further term" of twelve months. Be would have liked .to see Mr. Jolley have turn in the chair, but it was thought necessary that the chairman of that committee should be a representative member—one who held a seat on the Town Council—and that being so it 'would be hard to find a gentleman more _ .

Iliinently fitted for• the position than was, Councillor Roberts—(hear, hear)—especially in ,Y;_ew of the fact that it was probable that in "le next twelve months they would be everi more criticised than they had been in the past: liruder those circumstances he thought it tisential that the most capable representative ilieraber sitting on the committee—he said that IlTith no disrespect to the other members— ilhould be the chairman.

Sympathy With The Chairman. lie would, like to take that public oppor- tunity of expressing on' behalf of the members their deep 'sympathy with Councillor Roberts and his family in the news they had received that the Chairman's gallant son—Captain Roberts—had been: wounded, and also to express sympathy with the Captain himself. div.p: WARRINGTON'S DOLEFUL DAY.
Improved Dewsbury Team Beat Them By 27 Points.

div.head: VISITORS' ALL-ROUND FEEBLENESS.
div.p: VISITORS' ALL-ROUND FEEBLENESS.
Notes by " Centre."

Dewsbury confirmed the improved form they have recently been showing, when, on Saturday, they gave -Warrington. - their second ' worst whacking of the seaion. To say that a defeat by 27 points came .as a surprise to local football enthusiasts is to say the least of it; it was a positive staggerer. We had, of course, heard and read much about Dewsbury's better form, but we never anticipated that the improvement would prove to be such a real one as to enable the team that had been so easily beaten by teams we had ourselves defeated to turn the tables upon us in such thorough-going fashion. Twenty-nine points to two, and that from a team standing considerably lower in the N.U. table than we do ourselves! Phew I It is enough to give one pause and to set one a- wondering whether a not over-glorious season is going to filter out in an ignominious fizzle, so far as Warrington are concerned.

from the kick off Dewsbury put on pressure and less than a quarter of an hour had elapsed before they had assumed the lead, which came per a penalty goal,--langed by , Stringer. Em- boldened by their success they made a series of dashing onslaughts on the Warrington line, but for a time their dangerous movements were frustrated by the superb defensive work of Jolley, ably assisted by Laws, who finds his real metier in the half-back line. But eventually there came a breakdown, the pace proving too hot even for the übiquitous Jolley, and Dyw was enabled to nip over the line for a deg& try. A moment or two later Robertshaw threaded his way through the defenders and had a clear run to the line, but just as he was about to cross dropped the ball. .6-

div.head: DEWSBURY'S WIN DESERVED.
div.p: DEWSBURY'S WIN DESERVED.

Saturday's score by no means flattered Dews- bury, for they had the measure of their oppo- nents, and were the better men in all depart- ments. Their forwards were markedly superior and their halves* were an adroit 'pair, who kept the ball well up nearly all the time. Fortun- ately Jolley was in great form, for had he slacked or been off colour, what was a very nasty defeat must have been turned into a per- fect debacle. Laws also did some fine work for his side; in fact he was quite one of the best men on the field, both in attack and defence, and he pregented several opportunities to his three-quarters, but they were nearly all allowed to pass unheeded. The inability to make good shown bST the Warrington three-quarters was exasperating, and, of a generally weak team, they were by far the weakest section. The Dewsbury three-quarters, on the other hand, were a tower of strength to their side, and time and again initiated the movements which,led to Points.

div.head: RUNAWAY VICTORY AT VULDERSPOOL.
div.p: RUNAWAY VICTORY AT VULDERSPOOL.

Runcorn were the visitors to Wilderspool yesterday. These teams last met on October 10th at Runcorn, when Warrington were the victors-by 20 points to 7. A The following teams did duty yesterday :- Warn i n gt an. B. Jolley. , _ _
B. Bradshaw, E. Brookes,- T. Laws, J. Baker. J. Dainteth, S. Young. • • H. Cox, 3- Fearnley, W. Cunliffe, T. Cunliffe, M. Green, Bombardier Chesters.
Hughes,. R. Richardson, E. Shields, Nickson,
A. itieliOxdson, J. A. Stevenson. C. Butterworth, J. Jolley, sen. C: Bown, Co*hill, J. Shaw, J. Hoxworth J. Jolley, jun. Runcorn.

The officials weret—Referee, Mr. C. Platt (Swinton); touch-judges, Messrs. R. J. Pye (Salford) and A. Roscoe (Broughton Rangers). Warrington kicked off in a deluge of rain, before a small gate, and pressed immediately. Chesters rolled over simply after a scramble on the Runcorn line, and Jolley added the goal. Fearnley ran through all opposition and Jolley .added 'goal No. 2. After thirty minutes' .play Bradshaw scored under the cross-bar, but Jolley :failed at goal, hitting an opponent with his kick. Half-time: Warrington, 2 goals 3 tries (13 points); Runcorn, nil. Runcorn started the second half a man short, a player having received marching • orders. Baker, well fed by his neighbours, got over nicely, but Jolley again, failed at goal, al- though the °kick was taken right in front. Bradshaw, running well, - passed to Brookes, who scored, and Jolley added the goal. Jolley dropped a goal, and,then Hughes rushed to the other end and -scored fOr Runcorn, A. Richardson missing the goal. Bradshaw re- sponded with another try for Warrington, but the goal-kick missed fire. W. Cunliffe scored just, before time and Jolley missed the goal. J. Jolley, jun., kicked a penalty .goal for Run- corn. Result :—Warrington, 4 goals 7 , tries (29 points); Runcorn, 1 goal 1 try (5 points).

div.p: AVARRINGTON AWAY.
Visit To Rochdale To-ft).

To-day Warrington pay a visit to Rochdale, and they will field the same team as that which did duty against Runcorn yesterday, with the exception that Tranter will play on the three- quarter line in place of Brookes. Warrington and Rochdale 'lave already met twice this , season. The first occasion was on September 19th, when the Hornets won at Wilderspool by eight points to five On NOVOIII- - 11th the Rochdale men agam visited War- rington in the third round of the Lancashire Cup, and once More they administered defeat, this time by 13 points to five:

div.head: BRAVO, ORFORD!
div.p: BRAVO, ORFORD!
Village Gives Freely Of Its Men For
The War.

• It would, perhaps, 'be iMpossible to And u district of the Small population of :Orford Vil- lage which has so, nobly given- of its sonS in response to the country's call. • Mr. Ingham, who is employed at the Orfordl Tannery-, and lives at.. Laburnum Villa, Orford, had the diStinction of Waring five sons who weie serving their country, three of whom are doing duty at present in the trenches, and one of whom, Corporal George, has (as was recorded in a 'recent issue), made • tilt greatest sacrifice that the patriot can offer to the land he loves, having died of 'wounds received in action. The oldest.i son,, Frederick, of the Grenadier 'Guards; went through the •whole of the 'South Afriean'eampaign„ without a scratch, although he saw his Comrades shot down on both sides iof him. .ile was three. years and ten months. in• South A frica. Frederick is-' now employed, at the Dallam Forge, is married, has a family, and is. too old to re-enlist. Private J. Bighorn, , another married son, went over to France with. his regiment on February 19th Gunner Wal- ter, of -the Royal Field Artillery ("C" 56th Brigade) is another son; while Corpl. George lligham (29) with his brother, Corporal William Bighorn (27), were both in "A" Company of the 4th (Territorial) South Lanca shires.

A young Orford soldier, Rifleman William RiAardson—krother to Mr. Yates, of the New Cottages, Orford, whose husband is also a soldier doing duty in the trenches—was for a time,. lying in hospital in France suffer- ing from an eye complaint. Mr. and Mrs. Swinton, Long-row, Orford, have two sOns in the Army, James and \Villiam.
Another gallant son of Orford -who is serving his country is Arthur .Leedale. who . is borne on th books of •II.11:S.

div.head: VISITORS' SOLITARY POINTS.
div.p: VISITORS' SOLITARY POINTS.

Another penalty kick falling to Dewsbury, Stringer added two more points to their swell- ing total, and almost immediately afterwards Ward went over from a pais by Rhodes, repeat- ing the performance a few minutes later, after transfers by Thomas and Rhodes. Holland and Price next figured prominently, an excellent move on their part leading to Dyson obtaining a try, upon which Stringer improved. Just before the interval still more points fell to the triumphant Yorkists, a beautiful made pass by Ward enabling Rhodes to cross the Warring- ton line. Changing ends with a useful lead of 21 points, Dewsbury fouild their job a rather more difficult one, for Warrington now had the wind in their favour. Indeed, the visitors made a desperate attempt at rallying, and more than

once in the early stages of the concluding moiety they very seriously embarrassed the defence, and Fearnley was able to land a pretty penalty goal. But Warrington's effort was something in the nature of a flash • in the pane and soon they were driven to act almost solely on the • defensive, and that they did not defend any too brilliantly is proved by the fact that two more tries and a, goal were totted up against them, the tries being secured by Price and Ward and the goal by Farrar. The final reading of the score board was: Dewsbury, 4 goals 7 tries (29 points); Warrington, 1 goal (2 points).

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
INTER-WORKS CUP COMPETITION TO BE
HELD "AS USUAL."

The advent of Easter signals the near approach of the commencement of the boWling season, and greens are being carefully rolled and trimmed in readine§s for the "gentle game and playe," which for hundreds of summers past has held a place in the hearts of lovers of outdoor sports. The Works' Amateur Bowling Association announce that despite the, -war— which, of course, will doubtless have some con- siderable warring effect upon the season—the Inter-Works 'Cup Competition will be held as usual, for teams of twelve aside. Entries must be sent in to the Secretary, gr. W. Patrick, not later than Saturday evening next.

LIBERAL BOWLERS' ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the Liberal Club Bowling Green members .was *held in the read- ing-room of the club on Monday etening, under the chairmanship of Alderman Tinnion. _ -

The following' officials were elected for the ensuing season: Chairman: Mr. J. T. Smith; vice-chairman, M. F. Walker; secretary, Mr. George Marshall; committee, Messrs. T. Shaw, J. Gibson, R. Kitehmough, J. Collins; T. O'Brien,- IL Johnston and E. Fogg.

div.head: FOOTBALL PATRIOTS.
div.p: FOOTBALL PATRIOTS.
St. John's Team Provide 33 Soldiers From 36 Members.
GOOD PLAYERS, GOOD FIGHTERS,

St. John's Association Football Club pro- vided the champion junior team of Warring- ton before the war started. They have proved that they are even better patriots than foot- ballers, for out of 36 members 33 have re- sponded to their country's call. • The •Seere, tarry called his men together, explained the situation, and, all who were fit and' eligible, enlisted. Twenty-five are 'actually in the fighting-line, and the last news received of them showed that only one had been wounded —Private T, Devine, who was employed at. glehmond's. ''he secretary is at present under Government making ammunition because after serving five months with the Army Service Cprps lie, met with an accident and came out of hospital rather weak. We are glad to say he is now in the best of health.

div.head: OPTIMISM IN THE TRENCHES.
div.p: OPTIMISM IN THE TRENCHES.
The following has been received by him from his brother, • Lance-Corporal Smith, who is at the Front:—

"March 16th,—Just a line to let you know I arrived at the Front all right and in the best of health, &c. I hope you are making rapid pro- gress also. :Lam very. ,glad to know that all the Orford St. John's members are in the pink and think they have set a good example to the foot- , ball circles of Warrington. I know our Ernest is over here because 1 have had a letter ,from him, Is that correct about the Warrington ` Terriers '? If it is I.m very very, but never mind, duty must be done. I can assure you with my little experience it is no joke out here. Of course I am in the pink and never felt any. better in my life.. I must say we had our barn. billets shelled the other'. night, kill- ing several. . I am just' returning from the . trenches after. 48 hours. ..You may know we cannot understand these French people, but all the Aame, we run short of nothing. You Might , send me 'The Examiner so that I can ' read, , about the doings over there., I must say I am enjoying this life fine, although I may get killed any moment, but I am glad to know that God has prepared a home for me." He then. con- 'chides with best respects, &c., and wishes to be. 'remembered to all ,his friends. It will be well known that Lance-Corporal Smith was a good worker in the interests of Buckley-street Mission. Before the war he was employed by Messrs. Armitage and Rigby as assistant loom overlooker.

The members of his family serving are Pte. John Smith (21), Ammunition Column (Richmond's). Lance-Corporal Fred Smith (19), Royal Min- ster Fusiliers (Armitage and Rigby's). Pte. Ernest Smith (18), 4th South Lancashire Regiment -.:Richniond's).

ceived a well-judged pass from Deakin and gained the lead for the Saints. Half-time: St. Barnabas', 2' goals; Central, 1 goal. GRAPPENHALL v. EARLESTOWN ST. JOHN'S MISSION.

The above teams met on the ground of the former • club, neither being fully represented. The home captain won the toss and Collins set the ball rolling. The home team, through Ford, made an attack on the visitors' citadel, but were repulsed, and the visitors raced to the home end. where Collins missed a good opening. Con- tinuing to have the best of the exchanges, the visitors again missed by Theobald shooting over the bar. From the goal kick the home team rushed to the visitors' end, and Ford scored the first goal. The Mission now made desperate efforts to get on equal terms, but failed owing to off-side, and shortly after were penalised for a. foul. This brought. relief to the home de fenders, and even play followed. half-time: Grappenhall, 1 goal; Mission, nil. On re-starting, the home lot soon became aggressive, and the visitors' defenders were hard pressed, but eventually got the, ball away. Then the home goal was in danger of being. captured, but the goalkeeper made several fine saves. Following even play the home team were penalised for off-Side, but; not to be denied, the home forwards rushed On the visitors'. goal and a second goal was added: The visitors made strong efforts to reduce the arrears, but their forwards shot very badly, and for hands the visitors were awarded a penalty kick. Smith, taking the, kick, hit the upright,.•and..the goal- keeper cleared. Play was again transferred to the visitors' end and the home forwards rushed the ball through. Another attack by the visit- ors ended in the ball being sent over the bar. The remainder of the game was of an even char- acter, but no further goals were scored, the result being: Grap.penhall, 3 goals.; Earlestown Mission, nil.

div.head: ELM WOOD CONGREGATIONALISTS v. HOLLINS GREEN.
div.p: ELM WOOD CONGREGATIONALISTS v. HOLLINS GREEN.

These teams met. On Saturday in -their return fixture on the ground of the former. The Con- gregationalists, winning the toss, decided to play with the wind in their favour, and at once visited their opponents' goal area, but had to retire to midfield, owing to strong defensive play by the visiting backs. End-to-end play followed, but both sets of • forwards finished liadly. After twenty minutes had elapsed the visitors improved -greatly, and .by good com- bination they beat the home defence and scored their first goal. The ensuing play up to the in- terval was evenly \ contested, the visitors retain- ing their lead, and the score being 1-0 in their rayon r. The second portion opened very briskly, the visitors being the initiators, and soon attacked the home goal. After several shots had been cleared, the Congregationalists took up the run- ning, and made several fruitless attempts on the visitors' citadel, where the defenders proved superior to the attackers. . Ashton and the visitors' centre-forward had the misfortune to collide with each other, and the game had tá be stopped a few minutes. From the throw-up the visitors gained possession, and ,combining well together, transferred play to the home quar- ters, where the inside right scored a splendid goal. Encouraged by this success the visitors. continued to have the best of the exchanges, and the home defence were hard pressed. Eventually Atkinson scored the third goal. The- concluding stages were chiefly in favour of the visitors. What attacks were made by the home forwards were easily repulsed. Result : Hollins Green, 3 goals; Elmwood Congregationalists, nil.

NEWTON CONGREGATIONALISTS v. ,LONGFORD' UNITED. - On the Newton Congregationalists' ground. The visitors won the toss, and Rowbotham set- . the ball rolling with the wind. Smart, inter- cepting, passed out to. Wainwright, and the latter centred, for Porter to make a smart clear- ance, from which the benne forwards gained the ball' and raced to the visitors' end, where a good effort was spoiled by off-side. SherFatt opened the score for the visiiing after twenty minutes' play, Wallace clearing the first attempt from 'Wainwright, when Sherratt obtained and sent the ball between the uprights. Following this reverse the home team played a very plucky game, but. met with a strong opposition, which they were unable to get past. Half-time: Long- ford, 1 goal:. Newton, nil. On resuming, the visitors were soon on the aggressive and kept up a steady pressure on the home goal, and the home forwards got few chances to show their attacking abilities The visitors udded further goals 'by Wainwright, Sherratt, and Fearnley, the last-named scoring with a splendid long shot. On the day's play the visitors showed marked superiority, Bennett, Sherratt, Wainwright, Fea,rnley and Stevens being most prominent, whilst Porter. Pilling and Bcresford were .the pick of the home team. Result: Longford, 4 goals; Newton Congrega- tionalists, nil. 'WARRINGTON CENTRAL v. ST. BARNABAS'. Owing to the unfit state of the Lovely-lane ground the fixture between the above clubs was arranged to be played in Victoria Park.' Central: Ashcroft; Glover and Williams; Emson, Gilbert and Williams; Mason, Critch- Icy, Webb, Ashcroft and Farrell. St. Barnabas' t Shaw; Jefferson and Long; O'Neil, Challinor and Robinson; Lemons, Ver- non, 'Deakin, Herbert and Ray. Referee, Mr. J. T. Hadkiss. The Saints won the toss and decided to play against the wind. The opening exchanges were very even. The Saints made the fitst advance, but were driven back by Glover and Williams. After a visit to the Saints' goal, the. play was again transferred to the home citadel, and from a melee in front of goal Vernon ored. The home team retaliated in brisk fashion, and after several attacks had been successfully repulsed by the visitors' defence they at last succeeded in equalising the scores, Farrell doing the need- ful. Both teams played strenuous football, and . the 'Saints gaining the upper hand, - Ray -re-.

div.head: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE.
div.p: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE.
Second Division.
STOCKTON HEATH v. WEST TIMPERLEY.

The Heathens played their return fixture with West Timperley on Saturday on the West Avenue, ground, before a fair crowd of specta- tors. The•Heatliens wen the toss 'and decided to play against the wind, and from the kick off they quickly laid siege to the visitors' goal. Smith opened the score with a good shot. The visitors retaliated strongly, and were awarded a penalty kickittrom which they equalised. The Heathens then again became aggressive, and Vernon scored a splendid goal with a shot from near the corner flag. Encouraged by these sue- cesses the home team had much the best of the exchanges, and Smith scored the third and fourth goals. Half-time:. Stockton Heath, 4 goals; West Timperley, 1 goal. ,On resuming, the Heathens slackened their pressure, and for twenty minutes play was chiefly in midfield. Then, in response to their supporters, the home players again took up the offensive, and during the last portion of the game goals were scored in quick succession by Noden (2), Smith, Vernon, Mortimer, and Lloyd. The home team were at full strength; with the exception of Hooper, while the visitors were not able to place their best eleven in the field. Result:. Stockton Heath, 10 goals; West Timperley, I goal.

div.p: 11ESTER AND RUNCORN LEAGUE.
WESTON V. FRODSHAM.

O'n the ground of the former. The visitors w'on'thetoss.and having a Strong breeze in their • favour quickly advanced• to the home end. •A good effort by Savage was cleared by Broome at the expense of a corner. This was got away, and the home forwards gaining possession of the .leather, raced to. visitors end, where Conway shot wide. ,of the goal. • The visitors ~were,.playing a good effective game in mid-field, but when., near goal- they met with •strong Brooine made ,many splendid saves, and was ably assisted in :defence by Jeffries and White. , Spencer, eV the visitors, was- well fed; but finished' erratically.: The • /fome team struggled hard' to :break through the visitors' defence, hut they rarely got to 'cloSe quarters,. Conway being their: most dangerous forward. After good midfield play the visitots combined well together, and Kinsey, 'Working for posi- tion, scored' n splendid goal •from7Wenty yards' . range. • • The heme team. -.'-now played. more strenuously, and made- several attacks on the visitors' goal, but their efforts were easily cleared by the defenders. Half-time: • Frodsham, 1 goal; Weston, nil. , • In thessecond half the home team had the wind behind them, but from the centre-kick the Visitors were the most aggressive, and Jeffries and White, defending well, got-the ball away. The home team transferred play to the visitors' end, where Hulse and Crane had their work Cut out to ~keep the home forwards at bay. The We,stonians were playing a more convincing guile than their opponents, and frpm- another strong attack Conway equalised the scores with a splendid shot. Play- con- tinued to be even up to the call of time, but no further scoring was done by either 'team. For the Weston team, Broome (in goal), Jeffries and White. div.head: HORIZONTAL HEAD LAMPS.
div.p: HORIZONTAL HEAD LAMPS.

Since the eyesight of practically every driver is different it is an extremely difficult matter to lay down any definite rule as regards tho best angle for the head lamps. If notice 'IS taken of many of the cars one passes on -:tho road, it will be realised what a great 'variation there is in the positions adopted. In some iii- stances.the beam appears to be far too high, in fact, spending itself in lighting up the trees overhead. In others, the roadway a few yards ahead of the car seems to have all the Light concentrated upon it. This Itlst position is ttse • ful enough in foggy weather, hut not on a clear night. I always have my lamps adjuste4 as to see as far as possible, and when just r2glati the beam is focussed in. a itorizontßl line to flap road,. To determine-- the best position -a V 474. dark road should he selected, and this shouli be traversed. a number of times; altering the adjustment before each trip, .until the eia&l; position is found in accordance with th-a driver's eyesight. The comfort of securing.lo right adjustment cannot be. over-estimated.

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
Women and the Liberation of Men For Fighting Purposes.
PIONEER BICYCLES.
Queries and correspondence should be addressed to "The Hub," c/o The Editor. Replies cannot be sent by past, and all queries will be'answered in our columns.

Mr. Max Pemberton believes that the in- fluence which the bicycle` has had on motors and motoring is very great indeed. There is certainly a lot of truth in his contention. The cyclist of the past was of a mechanical turn of mind, but at the same time the motor cycle and motor ear have proved, a valuable means of educating -people in all kinds of mechanics. Talking about the early motorists, Mr. Pem- berton says in a recent article in "The Field ": ,frrThese people were almost all old bicyclists. • Some of them had ridden the bone-shaker; others took •up what, were then called " spiders " because of the like- ness of their wheels ,to a web, and they re- discovered the roads of t ngland. What these men • did 'before the bicycle was in;. vented it is a little difficult to say; but I remember well that their presence upon a country road was an event in the old days, and I recollect very well being stopped by a shepherd near Bedford, who asked me if I was doing it for a wager. There were revelations to. be made in those days,, and our magnificent system of highways :to be ,• . ,discovered for a generation unaware of their existence. But that is thirty-five • • years ago or more; and the tale has become an ancient one. '

The bicycle demanded initiative and self- resource, at any rate in its earlier days. It was somewhat of an undertaking tr) learn to ride, say, a 56in. wheel, and many a bruise was painted during the .process. Nickel-plating- did not adorn the new contraption at the begin- ning, and weary hours were spent by the enthusiast polishing the briat steel which every shower rusted. The bicycles rarely got out of order if well treated, but any kind of collision was disastrous. Thus, upon a blasted heath, a man might bend a crank and aiscover, like Helen's Babies, that the wheels would not go round. Or he might buckle his rim, and have • to. get four or five agricultural labourers to sit upon the wheel's edge while it was straightened. Happily, there were no punc- tures, and the 'lvorst that happened to the old solid tyres was that they came off. For all that, the men who rode the fearsome things were, in a sense, mechanics, and indisputably. were possessed of the instincts of the pioneer. Their discerned the revolution that was to come and they defied the jeers of the populace and the contempt of the socially elect.

div.head: CURIOUS CASE AT BRIDLINGTON.
div.p: CURIOUS CASE AT BRIDLINGTON.

"In the opinion of the Bench, the sergeant was not justified in riding on the footpath. But as the Bench do not wish to harass the military, they have decided to dismiss this particular ease.", This was the decision of the magistrates after discussing, in private, the case of a sergeant and two privates riding on the footpath. The two latter came off when told to do so by the constable, but the sergeant refused to do so, since he claimed that he was acting within his rights. Lieutenant . Hood. representing the defendant's regiment, stated that the sergeant was under military orders at the time, and that it was sometimes necessary for an officer to ride on the path, so as better to supervise his men. Against this it was held that the regulations under the Defence of the Realm Act did not refer 'to public roads and public lands. Lieutenant-General Kerrison, in command of the regiment, said the defendant was acting under ' orders, and he held that military exigencies required the sergeant to ride on the footpath at the time. It is a peculiar point, but I think the Bench were correct in their decision under the circum- stances. ,

A ROTARY ENGINE MOTOR CYCLE. 'The conspicuous suCcess of the rotary engine for aeroplanes has emboldened manufacturers to experiment , with this .type in otb Pr directions. It has been tried in motor car construction and has, to a certain extent; proved successful.. I heard nearly • twelve months ago that an American maker had applied this principle to motor cycles, but it was only a short while ago , that I saw- his contrivance. The engine is placed in the back 'wheel. The stationary crankshaft is Concentric with the wheel, serving as an axle, the three cylinders thus revolving in the same plane as the wheel. • The cylinders are geared to the wheel by means- of two-speed . gears and • idler. The , engine revolves at four \ times the speed of ' the wheel. The 'least • that can be said for the construction is that it is in- genious, but somehow I do not fancy that the design will meet with much approval in this country. Motor cycles are ,becoming more and more standardised as regards general design. Such a revolutionary idea, even if it ever suc- ceeds, will take time to reaeh any degree .of popularity. What the rotary, in this ease, gains in transmission it loses in accessibility.

div.head: CHANGING GEARS.
div.p: CHANGING GEARS.

A point of importance is in changing .the gear when hill climbing. That .a number of riders do not apprecidto that there is a psychological moment when this should be done is apparent to anyone who observes cyclists on the road. The change- should be effected in the majority of cases at anything between fifty and seventy- five yards sooner than is usually done. The best way of determining the correct time is to have a. speedometer fitted. When the speed drops to a certain point, change the gear. If the 'needle remains steady the right moment was selected. If the needle swings upwards it shows that the change was made too late. Another way to test this point is to ride in company with an expert cyclist mounted on a similar machine and compare his speed on-the hills with your own. By negotiating the'sam.:, hill a number of times the lesson will be learnt.
