div.head: TREATS FOR BOLD-STREET WESLEYANS.
div.p: TREATS FOR BOLD-STREET WESLEYANS.
Interesting Re-Visits From Rev. H. G.
Roberts and Prof. Sssinnen.

Sunday was a red-letter day in the history of ,the Bold-street Wesleyan Church, for it saw two highly interesting events in the shape of return visits from the Rev. IL G. Roberts, who was formerly a minister in the town, and Professor Firmin Swinnen, the organist of the Church of St. Walburgis's, Antwerp, and deputy-organist of Antwerp Cathedral, who recently gave a delightful organ recital in the church in aid of the fund to help his unfor- tunate compatriots, and who now discoursed further sweet music in a good cause. The Rev. U. G. Roberts preached both morn- ing and evening, to a large congregation on each occasion. Special music was.sung by the choir.

_ ,Professor -gwinnen's organ recital was given in the afternoon, when Mrs. C. E. Parker pre- sided and i‘n the course of a few introductory remarks, urged the 'claims of the society funds, for which a substantial collection was sub- sequently taken. The Professor's programme was of a highly interesting description, and each item in it was played in masterly fashion, particularly interesting being his extremely' clever extemporary improvisations on two themes handed him by Mr Prank Hickman—the opening bars of the anthem "Let all the world in every corner sing" and•the Russian National Anthem.

• On Monday evening the Rev. H. G. Roberts leetured on "The War and the European Hereafter." The Present war, he said, was the most wicked in the history of the human race, on the one side; but on the other it was the most righteous. Although the Prussian bully was yet powerful—and was—to give him his dues—fightinvery bravely, he would be torn from his seat, by the justly incensed allied nations and •would be thrust down beyond the pos:iibility of ever rising again.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. APRIL 3, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. APRIL 3, 1915.

to the chap standing next to you in order to make yourself heard. The noise sounded like rapid fire from rifles, only ten times louder. Just 'think what the banging of five hundred big guns would be like. But that was not the worst! It was in clearing the village of Neuve Chapelle that we lost most men. There was a machine gun in nearly every house, and the streets were so narrow that we had to come along them all bunched up, and the enemy mowed us down like 'corn. . . . You never knew, even when you got inside a house and were clearing the Germans out, whether a shell would come over and blow you to bits.

div.head: WAR STORIES: BY LETTER AND INTERVIEW.
div.p: WAR STORIES: BY LETTER AND INTERVIEW.
"CURIOUS HAIR PARTING."
A Correction.

Last week we reproduced a portion of a letter that a young Territorial, Private Leonard Wood- ward, 3, Arpley-street, had written to his sister. We regret to state that we made him say that he had had his hair parted by a German bullet, whereas he wrote that a comrade on duty near him had had his hair parted by a German bullet.

div.head: HOME FOR WALKING DAY. Starts "Terriecs' Get When The Biu
div.p: HOME FOR WALKING DAY. Starts "Terriecs' Get When The Biu
Guns Boom.

Writing to Mr. IL Harrißon, .ehief booking and parcels clerk at Bank Quay (L. and N-W. Railway) Station, Lance-Corporal C. Booth, now of the 4th (Territorial) South Lancashire Regiment, and who was, before enlisting, employed at the station as a parcels-vanman, says "I have not been in the trenches yet, but I have been out trench digging, and also under rifle fire. Talk about a sensation! It was awful for the time being. One half of our battalion have been in the trenches for six days, and have come out again, with very few casualties. The weather is taking up' a bit, but it is still very cold. I think when the month is over we shall be able to do something with the Germans!

div.head: Expecting to be Home for Walking Day.
div.p: Expecting to be Home for Walking Day.

" We. have plenty of aeroplanes over here; in fact they are like flies knocking about, while the artillery behind us make us jump about when they start 'dishing the pills out.' I don't think we shall be out here very long now, we are expecting to be home for Walking Day!"
In a later letter, Lance-Corporal Booth says: "Since writing to you the last time, I have been in it, and have escaped unhurt'. I received a bullet-hole through my puttee."

div.head: "TERRIERS " HAIRBREADTH ESCAPE.
div.p: "TERRIERS " HAIRBREADTH ESCAPE.
Nearly Nlistaken for Germans.

In a letter to his mother, who resides at 46, West-street, Private Frederick William Lea, a Warrington Territorial, says:— " I will never forget the night of the 17th of Old Ireland (St. Patrick's Day). Number 4 platoon of "A" Company were lucky to come through alive. Forty of us were told to go with planks of wood and wire to a certain trench. We started off at about seven o'clock with a guide, and we kept on walking till one of the German lights went up, and then we dropped flat in the middle of a field, for the enemy's fire was very hot.
Guide Who Lost His Way.

"After a? while we started off again, and when we had walked about two miles we found that our guide had lost his way, and it was some tame before he found out a, better road. In the meantime, we found ourselves between two fires. We had to lie down again, and all at once another light went up. What a sight we then saw—dead bodies all ar aund us!

div.head: " For God's Sake Don't Shoot!"
div.p: " For God's Sake Don't Shoot!"

"Well, we could not stir an inch, for our Own men were firing over our heads, at the Germans, who were only ten or fteen yards from us. The first man to get away was F. Banner, but he had not gone far when one of our officers shouted ' Halt ! who are you?' he was thunuerstruck. and shouted back 'For God's sake don't shoot, you will kill your own men 1" When we got back into the trenches, we all gave a sigh of relief at having got out of such a terrible death- trap." In conclusion, the writer asks for cakes, sweets and writing paper.

div.head: WEIRD NIGHT.
div.p: A WEIRD NIGHT.
" Terrier " Gets Stnek In The Mud And Left Behind.

In a brief letter to his wife, who resides at 294, Knutsford-road, • Latchford, Private J. 'Bowden, who serving at the Front with the Warrington Territorials, describes an exciting experience which came his way on St. Patrick's night—" a night" he says "I shall never forget. We were on duty when we got lost. I was left behind and I got stuck fast in the mud, and had to stand under fire for a time without any cover. At 'last I saw a light and made for it as best I could and found that it came from a trench, but it was not ours. When I got out of the trench I discovered thatn, was between two fires, our own and the German's. I was only about twenty yards from the German lines and I was lucky to get away as I did, without being hit. When I came out of that trench I kept falling over dead bodies, and on my way back to our lines I fell into about eight lots of trenches. I was expecting to get shot every minute... . . Still I don't care what Igo through so long as I come out all right and get home safely, at last. . . On the 17th I was under fire, with hardly any cover, for about eight hours."

div.head: BOSCIIES WASTE FIFTY SHELLS.
div.p: BOSCIIES WASTE FIFTY SHELLS.
" Bug-out " That Refused To Be Blown Up. ,

Private William Allman, of No. 14 Platoon, "D " Company, 4th (Territorial) Battalion, South Lancashire Regiment, in the course of a 'short letter, written on St. Patrick's Day, to Mr. Harrison, chief booking and parcels clerk at Bank Quay Station, where he was formerly

employed as' a parcels porter, says :—" I am writing this in one of the dug-outs. The Germans have been trying to shell us out of it this afternoon, but it was all a case of good shot wasted. They used about fifty shells on us but they hit nothing. It is very quiet, save for the shelling! It is also very dangerous when getting in or out of the trenches. We are in them for twenty-four hours and out for twenty-four.. It is not as bad to be fighting as some people think. Everywhere we go every- thing is in ruins. We are now having some very nice weather,"

div.head: CHARMED LIFE.
div.p: A CHARMED LIFE.
Hit By Three Bullets, Yet Lites To
Tell The Tale.

In a letter to his sister, Mrs. Kettle, 19, Carlisle-street, C,ockhedge-lane, Private John O'Neill, of the 2nd Battalion of the East Lancashire Regiment, says :—" It is very cold here, the snow and frost being very severe. We attacked the enemy the other day with great success, but of course we lost a number ofdnen.

• • • One bullet struck me between the shoulders and turned out at my sleeve. but I was only (rrazed. The brass 'l)' on my equip- ment saved my life. Two more bullets went through my clothing, while a piece of shrapnel struck me on the chest, but I am still all right.

.. . I don't think the war will last much longer." Private O'Neill has also written a letter to his brother in which, after 'acknowledging the gift of a pair of gloves, he says:—" We are sometimes up to the waist• in water. .. . I wish you would send some candles, for we can- not get them here withent money, and when we go into barns in the dark they come in useful."

div.head: CLEARING :WINE CHAPELLE.
div.p: CLEARING :WINE CHAPELLE.
Valiant Local Rifleman In The Fiercest
Of The Fighting.

In a recent letter to Mr. Watson, of the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Company, Rifleman McDonald, of the Rifle Brigade—who formerly lodged with Mrs. Williams, newsagent, Wilderspool-road, and who, before • the war broke out and he enlistql, was engaged at the Cable Company's Works—says: "Just a few lines to let you know I am still alivp and back again in England. We have had it 3 bit rough out there. .. . I was at Neuve-Chapelle and it was simply awful, especially- on March 10th. That was the day we started, tAnd the bombard- ment was terrific.
The Deafening Guns. "You had to shout at the top of your voice

div.head: Difficult Task Cheerily Undertaken.
div.p: A Difficult Task Cheerily Undertaken.

" But for all these troubles we managed to clear them out. Our Hattalion of the Rifle Brigade had that job all on its own, and right merrily did we perform it." Rifleman McDonald is now in a Red Cross Hospital, at Bollington, near Macclesfield, nursing a wounded wrist.

div.head: • " AVE LIKE YOU ENGLISH!" Changed Opinions of Germans AViien At Bayonet's Point.
div.p: • " AVE LIKE YOU ENGLISH!" Changed Opinions of Germans AViien At Bayonet's Point.

Writing to his mother and father, who live at 21, .11eaton-street, Warrington, Rifleman. Alfred Bowden, of the 2nd Battalion of the Rifle Brigade, now serving in France, says that he has been too busy chasing Germans to drop a line before and adds that he is in the best of health. "I suppose," he continues, "you have heard of our success in taking a village and capturing about a mile of trenches. I was in it, and we got about eight hundred prisoners; we .made them glad to show the white flag. Some of them were old men, and some were mere boys. We rushed them out of their trenches at the point of the, bayonet, and that is something the Germans don't like. Once we got them out of the trenches we ran them . through the adjacent village, and as
they ran some of them threw away their rifles and shouted 'We like you English!'
Knocked Them Over Like Ninepins!

"Next morning the Gerinans tried 'a. counter- attack, but we were waiting for them and knocked them over like ninepins. They shouted 'Don't shoot; we are H.L.l."s' (High- land Light Infantrymen). I should think that we killed about four hundred that morn- ing . . . . and they didn't try it on us again !"

div.head: NAMELESS GRAVE
div.p: A NAMELESS GRAVE
And Sacral Symbols German Guns
Cannot Destroy.

"Our regiment has gained a very good name in this war!" Thus, with a touch of justifiable pride, does Private Mullins, of the King's Liverpools, 'commence his latest letter home to his mother, Mrs. Mary Mullins, 13, Dial-court, Warrington. "Every lad is happy," he continues, "so happy, that you would not think that Death lurked so near at hand,, If only the -young fellows at home properly realised the position they would rush to' join• Kitchener's Army at °once, and by taking the places of those already trained would enable reinforcements to dome out here. That would make our task easier. And what 'a task it is! We are up against an enemy that will stick at nothing in order tQ try and gain their ends. To see the lengths to which they have gone; to see the places' they haile reduced 'to ruins would astonish you.

div.head: Cross Standing Amid Chaos.
div.p: The Cross Standing Amid Chaos.

"Houses, shops and churches, all demolished, and, talking of churches, it is a curious 'fact that almost invariably' the crucifixes seem to escape. Near here, there is "a church that has been completely • destroyed, but the sacred cross still stands and from it the figure of the Man seems to be looking down upon our enency. calling upon him to repent his dastardly deeds. I am n writing this' near my dug-Out, and shot and, shell are, flying in all directions. Pathetic,indeed, is the grave about a couple of yards in front of me; a roughly-made grave holding the remains of some poor mother's son. A little wooden cross stuck at the head of the mound and inscribed 'ln memory of an unkndwn soldier,' tells its own sad story.

div.head: "I Am Not Downhearted !"
div.p: "I Am Not Downhearted !"

All the Warrington lads with us here," the writer adds, "are in the best of health . . . and I am not downhearted, so cheer up!" lie also tells how his letter was written in • the trenches, only fifty yards from the German lines; "so you may tell we have to keep a sharp look-out, for we are constantly under fire. However, there is not much danger from their rifle fire so long as one keeps out of sight. The great danger is from their shells. . . . . You may be laughing and joking with a comrade one minute and be may be blown to pieces the next."

div.head: CAPTURED BY GERMANS.
div.p: CAPTURED BY GERMANS.
Plight Of A Wounded Warringtonian.

Private T. Woolvine, of the 2nd South Lanca- shire Regiment, whose wife and family reside at 56, lloward-street, Warrington, has had a weird experience. Once he was reported as having died of wounds and then he was gazetted as missing. The latter description proved the more accurate. Mrs. Woolvine was upwards of three months without receiving tidings of her husband, When he did write it transpired that he was a prisoner of war in the German Camp at Paderborn.

div.head: Prisoners May Only Send_ Postcards.
div.p: Prisoners May Only Send_ Postcards.

Prisoners are only permitted to write post- cards, and Private Woolvine's last postcard, dated March• 3rd, was received by his wife on Friday, March 26th. He says "Just a few lines hoping to find you in the best of health, as it leaves me at present. I hope that you are doing as you said, viz., sending a parcel every week. I want to know what is the matter with you as it is six months now and I have received no parcel, save one from the railway people." Mrs. Woolvine says that she has sent a parcel weekly. Lady Greenall and also the Women's Liberal Association had also sent parcels.

div.head: Called Up With the Reserves.
div.p: Called Up With the Reserves.

Private Woolvine was eight years in the ?aid South Lancashire Regiment, and whilst on the Regerve worked as a goods porter on the L. and N.-W. Railway. Immediately on the mobilisa- tion of Reservists at the outbreak 6f the war he re-joined his regiment and was one of the first drafted out to France. He was in the battle of Mons, where, it appears, he was wounded and then taken prisoner. That is nearly seven months ago.

div.head: SHOT EIGHTY-FIVE " TOMAIIES." The Unmasking Of A Sham Farmer.
div.p: SHOT EIGHTY-FIVE " TOMAIIES." The Unmasking Of A Sham Farmer.

Private W. R. Miller, of the Royal Engineers (Postal Section), has just been on furlough for eight days, and visited his parents at Stockton Heath. Private Miller was connected with the Liverpool Post Office, and soon after the out- break of war joined the Postal Section of the Engineers. His duty at the Front is to convey the mails by motor cycle to the base, from whence they are delivered to the soldiers in the firing line. He went out to France early on in the campaign, and returned thither on Wednes- da.y 'night of last week, March 24th, after his brief holiday.
Private Miller had mucii to tell of his experi- ences. One story illustrates the "slimness" of the German soldier and will be of interest.
Mysterious Fatalities.

In one locality, the story runs, a man purport- ing to • be • a farmer was to be seen in the fields, pretending to be ploughing. Men were being continually-missed in .the neighbourhood in a most unaccountable manner. Suspicion at last 'fell .on the farmer. He was watched by an officer, who, having satisfied himself that .his suspicions were correct, promptly shot the man. On examination it was found that the pretended farmer had a small gun attached to his plough. He turned out to be a German, and when the body was examined it was discovered that he had actually kept a record Which showed that .he .had shot no fewer_tlian.Bs of our " Tommies," according to his own showing.'

div.head: MERCY, ENGLISH Germans Squeal As Their Trench Is
div.p: MERCY, ENGLISH Germans Squeal As Their Trench Is
Rushed.

Writing to, a, friend in Warrington, Sapper F. Coggins, who is serving with the Engineers at the Front, describes the charging of a German trench. "When par boys got into the trench," he says, "the ,Germaris shouted ' Mercy ! English?' We made about a thousand prisoners. I got several souvenirs, including a German helmet, a German bayonet, and a German water-bottle. .. . I saw the Prince of Wales yesterday (March 15th). He had been near to the firing line."

div.head: "IN THE THICK OF IT."
div.p: "IN THE THICK OF IT."
Burtomsood Man With The King's LiVerpools.

Private W. Powell, who is serving at the Front with the Ist Battalion of the King's (Liverpool) Regiment, writing to his mother— Mrs. T. Powell, of Yew Tree Cottage, Chapel- lane, Burtonwood—says : "We are in billets at present (March 12th), after having had a very rough time in the trenches. . . . . No doubt you will be able

to guess what sort of a time we had when you read our casualty list. But, I am thankful to say, I am safe and well." In a further letter, written two days later, the gallant private says I am alive and kicking, but I am very lucky to be so, I can assure you. We had an awful time a few days ago, but we are at present billeted in a big college. . . . I was sorry to hear about poor Andrew McKee, as I am sure everybody who knew him will be No doubt
you will have read of our big advance. . .
We were in the thick of it."

div.head: GIGANTIC FIREWORK DISPLAY.
div.p: GIGANTIC FIREWORK DISPLAY.
Local Officer Describes His Impres- sions of the Trenches.
In the course of an interesting letter to Mr. T. S. Steel, the well-known Warrington solicitor, an officer, belonging to the sth Cheshire Regi- ment, and who has many friends in Warrington, says :

"It seems a life time since I saw you at War- rington when I was on leave, and assuredly I have stuffed more into the last eight weeks than I ever dreamed of getting into the whole of my life a year ago. It is impossible to tell you all my adventures, but, perhaps, I can give you a brief sketch of the path we have taken. About a week after I last saw you, the Battalion left on a cold wet Sunday dawn, and took train to , where we embarked, and that same night put out to sea. Slowly we steamed into the channel . . . and crossed in com- parativo comfort.

div.head: Officers " Roughing It."
div.p: Officers " Roughing It."

" There was no accommodation for officers, and so we lay and dozed amongst the cinders and grit on the deck, and by daylight we were off the French coast. We landed later in the day, and were put into a rest' camp—cheerless tents on a bleak plateau; a sea of mud—wet wooden floor-boards and no blankets—and there we passed the night. That day we walked into the town and. ate a really rousing meal—the first since leaving England—and we returned considerably braced to our mud-bath on the hill top, where we slept like logs, as our blan- kets had arrived in our absence. The next day we entrained—the men in cattle trucks, 40 per truck—and for twenty-four hours were on the road.

div.head: "The Business" at Hand.
div.p: "The Business" at Hand.

, "At the end of that time we stepped out of the train at a 'railhead,' and a far-away ' and the reflection Of flares in the sky to the east, told that the business we had come on was at hand. That night we slept in some glass- houses belonging to some vineries, and .I had my clothes off and a cold sponge down for the first time since leaving England. When we woke I was pushed off with a party of cyclists to find billets for the Battalion in a, certain village, which You Will have often seen mentioned in the papers, and, as ue arrived; the sight of the Regimental Chaplaiii preceding a stretcher covered with the Union Jack, which was fol- lowed by a party of men with rifles reversed, told us that we were among things at last. The Battalion arrivell later- in the day and settled down for i good rest in billets.

div.head: First Experiences of the Trenches.
div.p: First Experiences of the Trenches.

Within two days of that the company cora- manders were in the trenches, the total period which had elapsed from our leaving England being seven days. Two days after that I, too, was in! How did I feel when I was in? I wanted to sleep most powerfully. I got into a cart that was going to the trenches with stores (floor-boards, sandbags, &c.), and having tucked my legs into the sandbags to keep them warm, I was quite comfortable. The front at night is one gigantic firework display. Bullets are continually going over you with a 'whizz.' In front of you there are glim- mers of a. light like little fairy lamps dotted about the ground. These represent our sup- pqrt trenches, which must be crossed before the if trenches are reached.
" Lines of Fairy Lights." "And then, again, you see a further line of fairy lights which show you the rear of the

firing line. The last bit of ground between the supports and the firing-trench is one mass Of shell holes, varying from the six-foot hole of the field-gun shell to the huge duck ponds of the 'Jack Johnsons 'or Big "Un's.' And this stretch has to 'be crossed with great caution, and, if a flare goes .us while you are doing it, you go on your stomach in the mud, without considering where your face is. Still, once you are in the trench you are safe, so long as you don't stick your head high enough for a ' sniper 'to get it. You keep awake at night and sleep in the daytime; at least if the shells will allow you!"

div.head: 1110 N CROSSES SOUVENIRS.
div.p: 1110 N CROSSES SOUVENIRS.
German Soldiers Gladly Part IVith Kaiser's Awards.

An interesting letter has been received by Mr. and Mrs. Fleming, of 18, Iloward-street, from their son George, who is only -nineteen years of age, and who enlisted at the outbreak of the war, along with a number of friends and work- mates. He belongs to the 2nd Battalion Rifle Brigade, and was formerly employed M the box room at Messrs. Crosfleld's.

Five Lines of German Trenches Captured. " I have just left the trenches with the Bat- talion for a few days' rest," he writes, "after a spell of twelve days in the firing line. I sup- pose you have heard about our success in cap- turing about five lines of German trenches, as well as the village of Neuve Chapelle. I was in two charges, and we lost a good many officers and men, including several who came with me.

div.head: Germans Trying to Break Sprint Records.
div.p: Germans Trying to Break Sprint Records.

"After a most terrific bombardment, we had the order to advance, and, although there were a lot getting knocked over, we were delighted to see the Germans trying to break sprint records towards their rear. Our company were in the first line of advance, and when we got to the village we took many prisoners from cellars, &c. They looked war-worn and gladly gave away souvenirs, such as watches, revolvers, sausages, helmets and iron crosses. At the other side of the village we had to dig trenches in broad day- light and we lost a good many men whilst doing so, for we were under fire all the time. About four hundred Germans began to wave the white Hag just in front of us, so we marched them away as prisoners.

div.head: Discovered by the Star Shells.
div.p: Discovered by the Star Shells.

"In the early morning, after our success, we lined the 'parapet, for we were expecting a counter attack. Our star shells were going up and bursting with ti glare likeelmtric light, and, sure enough; by the aid of these shells we could see that the Germans were making or our posi- tion like flocks of sheep. We soon began a rapid fire, and, it is believed, their casualties numbered, in our locality alone, something like four • the usand.

div.head: "Feel Quite Safe in the Trenches."
div.p: "Feel Quite Safe in the Trenches."

"We feel quite safe in the.trencheS, but it, is very dangerous when getting in or out of them. We have not had a wash for about a fortnight. I. received two cakes, some' cocoa and biscuits • . and they were quite a change from the biscuits we get in the trenches. We get plenty of jam, corned beef, tea, sugar, and as many clothes as we need."
NEGLECTED WORK.
Night Off On The Drink Costs
A Bolter-Down £ll.
WAR STORES HELD UP.
"A Good Lad " Who Was
Tempted By His Friends.

case of unusual character was before the Borough Justices on Saturday morning. The defendant was James parby, and he was described as being 34 years of age, and a bolter- down, of Plumpton-stre.et. He was summoned at the instance of the Monks' Hall Co. Ltd., to show cause why an order should not be made against him to pay .4.10 damages to the firm for loss sustained through his neglect to go to work.

div.head: CAUSED A MILL TO BE IDLE.
div.p: CAUSED A MILL TO BE IDLE.

Mr. T. S. Steel said he appeared to conduct the prosecution on behalf of the Monks, Hall Co.. acting on the instructions of Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co. The proceedings were taken under the Employers and Workmens Act of 1875, and the man's employers alleged that through his conduct in stopping away from work on March 23rd, without good or sufficient cause, he caused the machinery running in one of the mills to be thrown idle. The man was engaged on a night shift, and he should have started work at 6 o'clock, but, as a matter of fact, he did not turn up at all. The mill which he should have tended ought to have been running for twelve hours, but it only ran about an hour or two, and during that time, owing to defend- ant's absence, did not work at all.
Eighteen Workmates Penalised.

Not only was the mill rendered idle, but eighteen men and boys were thrown out of em- ployment, suffering financial loss to. the extent of a 4s. 10d., whilst the loss sustained by 35t•srs. Monks, Hall, was. over £lO. :Their Worships were asked to make an order upon the defend- ant to repay that sum of £lO. The man was not away through sickness, or any justifiable cause, for he (Mr. Steel) could, if necessary, call evi- dence to show that the man was drinking that day, and that, as a matter of fact, he was drink- ing at the time when he ought to have been at work; indeed, he was not only drinking that night, but the following day also. •

div.head: Very Serious Matter.
div.p: A Very Serious Matter.

This was regarded as a very serious matter, for the work that the man should have been doing was work that led up to Government work. As a result of his not working the shift in question, the Governthent work was con- siderably delayed. This was not the first time that the defendant had been guilty of similar conduct, for only the previous week he stayed away and caused a stoppage, thereby occasioning loss not only to the firm, but also to his fellow workmen. He was interviewed on the matter by Mr. Murray, the manager, and he then ad- mitted that he was away ,drinking. He gave a definite promise that it should not occur again, and on the strength of that he was allowed to continue his work. - It wasperhaps, unneces- sary to point out the seriousness of such: con- duct as the prisoner's, especially at the preNent time, and in view of the kind of work he should have been engaged upon.•

div.head: No Sympathy from his Union.
div.p: No Sympathy from his Union.

-- - . The trade society to which the defendant be- longed had issued a circular—a very fine circu- lar—appealing to their members nat to throw down their tools or neglf;ct their work, and pointing out that the "Pommies': in the trenches had got to go on with their work, and that it was up to their old workmates at home to do all they , possibly could to see :that the munitions of war were properly and regularly provided. On behalf of the society to which the defendant belonged—the Iron and Steel= workers' Association—he was instructed to say that they strongly resented the man's conduct, and regarded it, from their point of view, as well as the masters', as a very serious breach of duty on his part. This was not a case of a twin who was not earning good wages, for he'earned from -15 s. to 18s. per shift, and last week could have worked , a shift every night. The object of that prosecution was to bring home to the minds of the workers how necessary it was that work should be carried on continuously under the present circumstances.

div.head: FELL IN WITH A FEW FRIENDS
div.p: FELL IN WITH A FEW FRIENDS

Defendant told the Court that he was very sorry, and alleged that other men who had taken time off had not had anything said to them. On the night in question he fell in with a few friends, and was tempted from his work. "I am a good lad," lw added, "and I will see that it does not occur aagin." William Murray, manager to Messrs. Monks, Hall, said that owing to defendant's absence from his work there was a loss- in output of about 17 tons. The firm should have made a profit of about Ws. on each of those tons. Reckoning in repairs and maintenance charges the loss to the firm was more than .tlO.

div.head: ORDERED TO PAY £2 10s. A MONTH.
div.p: ORDERED TO PAY £2 10s. A MONTH.
The Magistrates' Clerk asked defendant bow Ile could pay the money, and he offered .22 a month.
The Bench, however. ordered that the sum of .22 10s. per month should be deducted in weekly instalments from his wages, until such time as the ,elO had been paid, plus <2l is. costs.

div.head: NON-CHURCHGOERS.
div.p: NON-CHURCHGOERS.
Need For Specific Place and Time of AVorship.

The anniversary of the foundation of the Golborne-street Baptist Church was celebrated by the'holding of special services on Sunday. In the morning the Pastor (the Rev. IL Ogden) preached from the words to_be found

, in the 11. Samuel, ii. 5, in which "Nathan is told to inquire of David if he would build for the Lord a house for God to dwell in." The preacher said that in these tithes of vague con- ceptions and indefinite notions about God and God's house, it was an inspiration to find a character whose vitlws about God and the wor- ship of God were definite and specific. With all the faults and failings ,which David un- doubtedly possessed, he had one desire through- out his life, and that was .to worship God and to manifest before the heathen world a definite place where God could be found. They might smile at the idea and say that God was of no particular shape or form, and that He did not dwell in any particular spot, but there was virtue in being able to concentrate their ideas of worship in One place The preacher said that he believed in the brother- hood off Man and Fatherhood of God.

div.head: Extravagant Price for Vagueness.
div.p: Extravagant Price for Vagueness.

There was little doubt that _Free Churchmen had paid an extravagant prtee for all the vagueness that had arisen from a misconcep- tion of such ideas. Men and women had been told that God could be worshipped any- where. He could, they were told, be found in the street, in the mart, by the babbling brooks and under the open skies; also that a barn for the Worship of the Lord would do quite as well as the most ornate cathedral. That was perfectly true, because those who worshipped God must worship Him in spirit and in truth. Generally-, those who •worshipped God, or pro- fessed to worship Him, by the side of the babbling brook or under the open .s:zies, merely made it an apology for no worship of God at all. • The idea was cursed with vagueness; it was like a river running into a marsh. Finest Charktee in the New Testament.

In the afternoon the service was conducted by Mr. W. It. Sherburn, of Stockton Heath, and Dr. Ferguson was the speaker. The con- gregaticm were delighted with the doctor's address, which included an original' presenta- tion of the character of Didymus. The Doctor suggested . that in . some :respects Didymus was the finest of all the New Testament characters, excepting • of course, the great outstanding Character. During the service excellent solos were rendered in effective fashion by Mr. Markham and Miss Hipkiss.
In the Pvening, the special preacher was Um Rev. T. Iles., of Liverpool. whose subject, wiT found in the words " For me to live is Christ."

Mrs. James Kenworthy sang very siYeetly and beautifully two solos---" Nearer; my God to, Thee " and "Calvary." The services • throughout the day were excellently attended, anfl all the collections were in advance of those taken the previous year. _
COMFORTS FOR SOLDIERS-.
GIRLS KNIT FOR NEW ZEALAND.

Miss F. E. Clarke, senior mistress at the Secondary School, has received the followins gratifying letter from Miss Helen Mackenzie- honorary ,eeretary to the New Zealand' AVl'r Contingent Association Ladies' Committee, 'Very many thanks for your letter and for the parcel of 13 scarves and 11 pairs of mittens, which your girls- have knitted for our Nov Zealand soldiers. It is • very \good of them to have given flieir spare time to knitting fer our men, and I should be glad if you would conveY to themlny warm thanks for their help—whieb they piny be sure is much appreciated."

div.head: PA,Oflo -FAGS" FOR SOUTH LANC• A
div.p: PA,Oflo -FAGS" FOR SOUTH LANC• A
11 rri tio ton's Welcome. Gift.

Captain Sydney T. Boast has written to the Town, Clerk, thanking him for a gift of 30,00° cigarettes forwarded to-the South Lancs. at th Front, through the Mayor's Tobacco Fund - The gallant Captain's letter is dated Ma'' 18th, - and says :—".The three cases, contailung the .30,000 cigarettes, arrived yesterday, abOt - an hour before we left to take auother',.turn o duty in the trenches. This came just at the right moment. Our men were rather short, And I was wondering how I could supply them for their. turn of duty when your cases arrived, an,", I at once distributed the contents'. On behan- of the men I send sincere thanks... Cigarettes are in more demand than tobacco, and are always acceptable and much appreciated by the men: The weather is much improved and things, generally, are livening up a "bit. Our 4th Battalion (the f Terriers ') has joined our brigade and is doing well. The battalion, at the present moment, is actually in the trencbcs --holding their own, and all very cheerful."

div.head: BAPTESTS ENTERTAIN BELGIANS. Tea and Song for Honoured Guests.
div.p: BAPTESTS ENTERTAIN BELGIANS. Tea and Song for Honoured Guests.

On Monday evening the Belgian refugees at present quartered in the comfortable home pr'- ruled for them at Black Bear House, were, at the invitation of the local 'Baptist Belgiall Refugees' Committee, entertained to a concert and tea at the Wash-lane Baptist Soho°lroom. The programme, which was 'bright and enter- taining throughout, opened with the playing- oil the pianoforte. by, Miss _Jones, of the Belgian and English National Anthems Miss Kendrick, of Chester, who, was recalled tital: after tiine, gave the songs " Here.we,are " Are We 'downhearted?" " For England," ".%;! ender the same flag," and "My dear old dad is Irish." Miss Weatherhead, of Keighley, heard to advantage in her rendering of .1 French song, as well as in the English son" " Down in the forest," and "Bird of love, divine." A. number of members of the girls Guild. who had been carefully trained by M-1. Fairhurst and Miss Wooton, rendered several action songs. Songs were also given. by Mr. - Dawson, whose contributions 'included " slumber song," " Glorious - Devon,", "The Drum Major" and "Shipmates o' mine," Mr. .Ashton, as "Mrs. Murphy," caused much amusement with his monologue descripti7e of "Lout and Marriage." He also gave thP' humorous recitation "How ,We Saved th°, Baru." and in response to encores ".Evar Dog-hospital" and " The Frenchman and tll6 At the close, Mr. .Tones proposed a f thanks to the artistes, which was carried witli hearty cheers.

During an interval in the programme, Mr. V- L. Jones; chairman of the committee cow' cernoti in promoting the entertainment, Faift that they were air glad to have the Belgians' among 'them, and if the letters which they had' vritten were any indication of their feelings- then they Were happy and satisfied in the home' had been found for them. Mr. Newton, one of, the officials at Black Belo. 11ase, .•;aid that he had tisited all the lionie in Warrington and, in his. opinion, the h(siet at Mack Bear Rouse was the best of tiv! 1-t.

SO IMPRESSED WAS LORD KITCHENER, on the occasion of his visit to Liverpool, with the fine display of, the "COMRADES that he has AUTHORISED LORD DERBY to raise A RESERVE BATTALION OF 1,000 MEN. The Men, will be in huts, trained together, and drafted, as required, to the yarious Bat- talions for reinforcements As far as possible, Men's Wishes will be Respected as to kvhich Battalion they are sent to. HOLMES, J.P. CLEANLINESS AND SMELLS. A word about cleanliness may not come amiss, And this is the rock upon which numbers of otherwise excellent poultry keepers come to grief. There should be •no smell at all; if there is the suspicion of ammonia in the air, depend upon.. it dirt is present. Now lime is cheap and an excellent deodoriser, and should be plentifully sprinkled upon .the floor of the house even if peat moss is used as well. If the latter is considered too extrava- gant lime can be used alone, and it will be found that the house is twice as easy to clean than if nothing were used at all. Poultry manure plus lime is a substance coveted by many gardeners and obtained by few, so there should be no diffic,ulty in dis- posing of it profitably, if stored in a dry place and kept dry. An old barrel with a lid is just the thing. Poultry manure has been known to realise 255. a ton, and a year's accumulation from even a small number of birds is pretty considerable. In conclusion I-might add,'if your neighbour complains of the smell of your poultry you may depend upon it the fault is yours.—" Feathered World."

PRIVATE HARRY HUMPHRIES. Wounded Man TelLs How Ills Cousin Died. Private Harry Humphries, another of War- rington's plucky "Terriers," and who was formerly a barman, residing with his wife and family of three small children at 64, Howard- street, has been wounded and is now hospital at the base. In a letter to his wife and family, received on Thursday morning, and bearing the date of March 29th. he says I am going on-champion under the circum- stances and am having 'a good time. Don't worry about my wound, because there is nothing dangerous. -Remember me to all inquiring friends. No information has been receive4,either by his mother or his wife as to the nafare of the gallant soldier's injuries. FIRST LYMNI " TERRIER " ‘VOUNDED. Popular Private Shot In Arm Last Week-end. • JOKE WHICH CAME TRUE. • The first Lymm Territorial to he wounded at the hands of the Germans is Private James Taylor, of 1, West Hyde, Newfields, Lymna. The news was contained in a letter received on .Thur4day morning by, Mrs. Clare at the Drill 'Hall. It was written by her -husband, Sergt. Harold Clare, and ran as follows : Monday.—We are having four days' rest from the firing-line--days which are greatly appreciated—after coming out of the trenches last night. I am sorry to say we had Private James Taylor, from Newfields, wounded in the arm. It is a flesh wound and will soon, we hope, be all right again. Otherwise we came out without a scratch. . . . Tell Mrs. Taylor, fpr I can quite under- .stand' bow anxious parents will be when 'they get news of their sons being wounded; tell her that Jim will soon be well and strong again. He is very popular with us, and we are all looking forward to the day when he will be well enough to join us again.
